#6282. Singapore Airlines’ New Business Class Finishes Look Cheap, Mismatched

Earlier I covered how Singapore Airlines unveiled its new first & business class, which should enter service in 2027 (hopefully). These products look like very nice improvements over the existing cabins, even if they’re not revolutionary.

That being said, I have to give Singapore Airlines some tough love on the new business class seats. Let me acknowledge that I’m a huge fan of Singapore Airlines as a brand. Any list I keep of the best airlines in the world (whether it’s the best airline brand, best first class, best business class, best inflight service, best inflight entertainment, etc.) has Singapore Airlines on it… that’s how highly I think of the brand!

But I’m also honest, regardless of how it fits my preconceived notions of a brand. I feel like I’m saying what everyone else is thinking, seemingly except for most influencers who are in Singapore for the launch event, who are just casually glossing over this… so much for attention to detail!

When I think of Singapore Airlines, the first thing that comes to mind for me is how deliberate the airline is. I don’t think there’s an airline that’s more intentional with every aspect of its guest experience, from the tone of voice with which staff speak, to warm and elegant design.

I’d say Singapore Airlines’ new first class actually looks really on brand. It’s a nice evolution of what the carrier has historically offered — it’s warm and elegant without being outdated.

And then you move to business class, and it looks like Scoot and Spirit Airlines had a baby. The gray and black is generic, the yellow accents look cheap, and then there’s so much going on with the blue and white bulkheads (if that’s actually how they’ll look).

And the Scoot reference isn’t even sarcastic. For those not familiar, Scoot is Singapore Airlines’ low cost carrier, and look at the seat finishes you’ll find there!

Usually there’s some consistency between seat finishes and wider branding, including the livery, flight attendant uniforms, etc. In this case, it’s not only not aligned, but they seem at odds with one another. There’s otherwise not a hint of yellow (or neon green, or whatever that is) in Singapore Airlines’ branding.

What so bizarre to me is how the first and business class finishes are completely mismatched, and you wouldn’t assume they belonged to the same airline. That’s because Singapore Airlines worked with different design firms (separate from the seating manufacturers as such) for the two cabins.

BMW Designworks was behind the business class seats, while PriestmanGoode was behind the first class seats. I think it’s safe to say there was no coordination between the two. I guess the argument from executives is that they want the cabin to look more modern and high tech, and go after a younger crowd, but I just don’t follow the logic.

It’s clear that Singapore Airlines put many years of effort into this product, and frankly I’m just surprised that Singapore Airlines executives signed off on this. Am I just in the minority in thinking this isn’t a good look for the airline? Did some marketer assure Singapore Airlines executives this was great branding, and they were wrong? Or did everyone just independently decide that this looks great?

If they at least eliminated the yellow stripes, it would no longer look cheap, but would instead look generic. I’m just surprised that this is the conclusion they came to.

Singapore Airlines of course had a big media event in Singapore to celebrate the launch of this product. I don’t attend media events, just as a general policy, because I don’t find them to be a great use of time. But I certainly do enjoy seeing the coverage from others.

What I find fascinating is the inherent bias that exists when someone is invited to something. For example, if you look at the comments on my post about the new cabins, the single thing most commented on by OMAAT community members is how bad the business class colors look.

If you watched the videos on social media about this, there’s oddly no commentary on that. Admittedly I haven’t seen all the coverage, but the worst coverage I’ve seen is someone saying they “don’t mind” the colors, and that it’s a “big departure” from the old look. Okay, that’s not exactly an endorsement.

I also haven’t found a single person who attended the event who said “I love the new colors,” which probably tells you everything you need to know. For that matter, it’s one thing if people acknowledged “I realize the colors might not look good in pictures, but in person, it’s a different story.” But I haven’t heard that either.

To me this gets at the rather complicated relationship between so many brands and influencer types. If you can say all the things you love about the product, shouldn’t you also feel totally comfortable criticizing the parts of the experience you don’t like, though?

While we’re on this topic, let me add one more point. Being able to sit in seats at media events like this is of course cool, but it really doesn’t actually give you an impression of what it’s like to fly in a product, and that’s why it’s not something I particularly value, as an experience.

Of course a big business class seat is comfortable when you sit in it for a minute, and you’re filming content. But the real test of a product is when you spend hours in the seat, when you recline the seat into a bed, when you try to move your laptop around while you’re being served a meal, etc.

I once had the opportunity to spend a night in an aircraft seat on the ground (I can’t really say more, since I signed an NDA, but it was to provide feedback to a seating manufacturer). To me that was fascinating, because it really gives you an understanding of what the experience is like. My feeling about the seat was very different after being in the seat for many hours vs. when I sat down.

Singapore Airlines has unveiled its new cabins, and there’s a lot to be excited about, as the hard products look very nice. However, Singapore Airlines’ new business class cabin finishes are a real mystery to me, because the yellow stripe looks cheap (I mean, it seems to be inspired by the carrier’s low cost subsidiary), and completely mismatched with first class.

The airline used different design firms for first class and business class. For an airline so focused on attention to detail and being very deliberate in terms of design, this strikes me as a misstep. Anyway, Singapore Airlines, I still love you and think you’re one of the best airlines in the world…

Where do you stand on Singapore Airlines’ new business class seat finishes? Does anyone love them?

#6281. Livery of the Week: JetBlue’s Florida Panthers Design

Editor’s Note: AirlineGeeks is proud to present our ‘Livery of the Week’ series. Every Friday, a team member will share an airline livery, which can be from the past, present, or even a special scheme. Some airline liveries are works of art. The complexity associated with painting around critical flight components and the added weight requires outside-the-box thinking from designers. The average airliner can cost upwards of $200,000 to repaint, creating a separate aircraft repainting industry as a result.

Have an idea for a livery that we should highlight? Drop us a line.

Since the beginning of its operations in 2000, New York-based airline JetBlue has always considered South Florida as one of its primary markets, with a presence at Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood Airport that has grown during the past 25 years to include up to 25 aircraft based overnight at the airport and over 2,000 people supporting its operations in Broward County.

As a sign of its commitment to the South Florida community, JetBlue has announced a multi-year extension for an expanded partnership with the Florida Panthers, the NHL’s southernmost franchise that captured back-to-back Stanley Cups in 2023-24 and 2024-25. The partnership will see JetBlue present a newly redesigned Champions Club at the Amerant Bank Arena in Sunrise, Florida, home of the Panthers, and to celebrate the announcement, the airline unveiled a special Panthers-themed livery for one of its Airbus A320 aircraft.

The new livery draws its inspiration from the Panthers’ jersey, therefore sporting the iconic Panthers’ red across the entire fuselage, with the outline of a golden panther all across the central part of the fuselage, right next to JetBlue’s logo. The Panthers’ shield logo is on the aircraft tail in navy and gold.

Bold red letters spelling FLORIDA appear on the bottom of the aircraft, where there’s also a leaping cat, the team’s logo. More symbols of the Panthers and the State of Florida appear in other parts of the fuselage: a simplified Florida flag appears near the front of the aircraft together with a palm tree and a hockey stick, which represent the secondary logo for the team.

“South Florida has been part of JetBlue’s story since our very first flight more than two decades ago, and we’re continuing to build on that history in a big way as Broward County’s largest airline,” said Marty St. George, JetBlue’s president, in a press release. “The Panthers know a thing or two about winning in South Florida, and we’re bringing that same energy as we expand our network, elevate the customer experience and deepen our commitment to the community. ‘Go Cats Go’ is a fun way to celebrate our shared passion for South Florida and team up with a franchise that knows how to make some noise.”

The aircraft chosen to display this special livery is an Airbus A320, registered as N784JB, delivered to the airline on Feb. 11, 2011.

The original name of the aircraft was “Blue And Infinity And Beyond,” which has been changed to “Go Cats Go” following the repainting in this new livery.

FOX Business correspondent Darren Botelho reports on Democrats' plans for congressional oversight of corporate America as business leaders weigh the potential impact.

A progressive policy organization led by former aides to President Joe Biden and former aides to progressive Sens. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass. assembled a detailed blueprint for potential Democratic congressional investigations to target President Donald Trump and his allies beyond the White House, which could foreshadow the goals of the 120th Congress.

Groundwork Collaborative's dossier, obtained and analyzed by Fox News Digital, maps Trump donors and corporate allies for potential Democratic congressional investigations. Leaders in big tech and CEOs of large corporations are likely to be among the targets of the anti-Trump crusade.

A longtime Democratic Senate staffer familiar with the process told Fox News Digital that the Democratic majorities on these committees already plan to exclusively focus on targeting allies and donors of the president, going as far as targeting the ones who donated to the new White House ballroom, once they move into the majority.

"We just had a midterm election where Democratic candidates across the country made the point that corporations have been doing very well for the last several years, while the typical family has been getting squeezed with higher prices and worse service," Bharat Ramamurti, a former deputy director of the National Economic Council who coordinated with Groundwork on the dossier, told Fox News Digital.

After some delays, United Airlines is one step closer to launching service on its posh new domestic plane.

The airline on Thursday evening announced it recently took delivery of its first Airbus A321neo “Coastliner” plane.

It’s a premium-heavy aircraft that will feature United’s new Polaris business-class suites and a true premium economy cabin.

And it will soon be a fixture on the carrier’s top transcontinental routes.

United shared a sneak peek of the new jet on social media Thursday evening —  well ... the outside of it, at least.

As expected, the exterior sports a special wrap featuring the “Coastliner” decal.

That’s because United plans to exclusively use this plane on its most premium coast-to-coast flights.

Once in service, you’ll see it on routes from Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR) to Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) and San Francisco International Airport (SFO).

It will likely also figure into the carrier’s plans at John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK), once United makes its long-awaited return to JFK.

While United had hoped to launch service on the Coastliner this past summer, delays at Airbus pushed the debut back a few months.

The jet is now slated to make its inaugural flight in early 2027, United said this week.

It will certainly be an upgrade to the airline’s prime transcontinental service.

Passengers flying in those suites will get access to United’s Polaris Lounge facilities.

There are also 12 Premium Plus recliners across three rows in a two-by-two configuration.

Plus, in economy there’s a walk-up snack bar.

The whole interior is very similar to the Airbus A321XLR that United debuted late this summer. That longer-range jet is slated to start flying to Europe in the coming months.

United’s looming introduction of the Coastliner comes as a growing number of U.S. carriers are upgrading their top transcontinental products.

This fall, Alaska Airlines revealed it will add lie-flat suites and premium economy to a future subfleet of Boeing 737 MAX 10 jets.

American Airlines last year launched coast-to-coast service with the A321XLR, which sports its latest-generation Flagship Suites up front.

Delta Air Lines, meanwhile, rolled out a version of the Airbus A321neo that doesn't have lie-flat seats (at least not yet) but does have a whopping 44 domestic first-class recliners.

Plus, JetBlue recently announced that passengers flying in its lie-flat Mint cabins would be entitled to enter its new airport lounges in New York City and Boston, even when flying domestically.

United has 50 of these Coastliners (along with 50 of the XLR jets) on order for the coming years.

So this aircraft will be a big part of the carrier’s most lucrative domestic service for years to come.

#6278. Red states have spent decades dominating a key corner of the economy — will the blue wave change that?

Texas could become America's next Singapore as business-friendly policies, lower taxes and an influx of wealthy residents fuel a new economic boom, according to an investment executive.

DALLAS — Red states have quietly outpaced their blue-state counterparts in commercial real estate investment returns for years, according to a new study highlighting stark differences in state economic policies.

But sweeping Democratic gains in Tuesday's midterm elections — even in traditionally deep-red strongholds — are raising questions about whether those states can maintain their economic advantages as the political landscape shifts in the new year.

Mitch Flax, founder and chief investment officer of Net Equity Capital, told Fox News Digital his research was sparked by the observation that commercial real estate investors based in blue states were reluctant to invest in their own markets.

The findings underscore a broader economic battle playing out across the country as businesses and wealthy Americans relocate across state lines, bringing jobs, investment dollars and tax revenue with them while potentially leaving financial holes in the states they abandon.

CEO SAYS DOING BUSINESS IN STATE ‘SUCKS’ AS COMPANY HEADS TO TEXAS AMID CALIFORNIA EXODUS

As businesses leave high-cost states, Texas has become the undisputed top destination. (Tom Fox/The Dallas Morning News/Getty Images)

"I had a large family office based out of Chicago who lives in California who said, we don't invest in real estate in blue states," Flax recalled.

Coming on the heels of the 2026 midterms, the study also raises questions about whether the state-level tax and business policies that have helped fuel growth in red states will remain intact as Democrats make political gains and begin to enact their agenda.

The encounter prompted Flax to examine nearly 24,000 commercial real estate transactions to determine whether political differences between states were associated with investment performance. Researchers used a proxy to estimate returns and classified states as red or blue based on their votes in the 2024 presidential election.

Flax attributed the performance gap identified in his analysis largely to differences in state-level business policies, arguing that those policies influence where companies relocate, jobs are created and, ultimately, where capital flows.

AMERICA’S NEXT ECONOMIC POWERHOUSE MAY BE RISING IN RED-STATE TERRITORY

The Texas capital attracted 88 corporate relocations from 2018 to 2025. (Brandon Bell/Getty Images)

The findings come as corporate migration toward lower-tax states rose in recent years, with Texas emerging as a major destination for companies relocating from costly coastal hubs.

Flax says that Texas is on track to be the next Singapore-style "tax haven" for companies, due to its policies attracting business and industry.

"We've all seen the movie ‘Crazy Rich Asians’ — get ready for Crazy Rich Texans, because that movie is coming," he said.

It's unclear how Tuesday's results will impact that prediction after Texas flipped a U.S. Senate seat blue with Senator-elect James Talarico beating Ken Paxton, who was backed by President Donald Trump, and Democrat Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa beating Republican Gov. Greg Abbott.

As Fox News Digital previously reported, a CBRE analysis found that 725 companies relocated their headquarters between 2018 and 2025. Dallas-Fort Worth led the nation with 111 relocations, followed by Austin with 88 and Houston with 31.

Meanwhile, the San Francisco Bay Area, a deep blue enclave, recorded a net loss of 163 corporate headquarters during the same period, as companies cited taxes, labor regulations and rising living costs among their reasons for leaving.

THIS STATE ISN’T JUST GROWING — ITS ECONOMY IS GETTING RICHER PER RESIDENT

Texas has attracted a wave of corporate relocations and business investment in recent years, helping fuel its emergence as a growing financial hub. (Shelby Tauber/The Washington Post/Getty Images)

Flax, however, also argued that population shifts and corporate relocations are symptoms of a deeper economic divide, with underlying business policies shaping investment decisions and determining where capital flows.

"Most of the large asset managers out there are underwriting population in this migration flow. But the reality is that's a symptom," Flax told Fox News Digital. "When you look at exactly what's causing it, it's pure structural business policy," he added.

Flax said those policies can trigger a ripple effect across the commercial real estate market as businesses relocate, workers follow and demand grows for housing, retail and office space.

"Migration is the symptom, but it's a cascade, right? So policy draws people and companies and then every kind of commercial real estate follows," Flax said. "Apartments follow migration, retail follows rooftops, office follows jobs, warehouse follows logistics."

Amanda Macias covers the intersection of business, economics and politics, with a focus on how policy decisions shape markets, businesses and American workers.

#6277. Southwest 737 Flew 44 Times Before Wind Damage Was Found

A Southwest Boeing 737 MAX 8 flew 44 times before maintenance crews discovered tail damage that investigators traced to a thunderstorm more than a week earlier. In a final report released Thursday, the National Transportation Safety Board said the damage went undetected through a scheduled maintenance check and caused a standby rudder control unit to operate abnormally.

The damage came to light after Southwest flight 746 experienced unexpected rudder movements on May 25, 2024, while flying from Phoenix to Oakland, California. All 175 passengers and six crew members were uninjured. The aircraft, registered N8825Q, sustained substantial damage.

The NTSB traced the damage to the night of May 16, when the jet was parked in New Orleans, and thunderstorms brought gusts of up to 73 knots, or about 84 mph. Investigators said the wind likely moved the rudder enough to damage ribs inside the vertical stabilizer where the standby rudder control unit was mounted.

At the time, Boeing’s 737 maintenance manual called for a special inspection after an extreme wind event but gave no wind speed at which the check was required. The manual listed signs such as an aircraft moving over its wheel chocks or leaving tire skid marks.

Southwest also lacked a process to notify maintenance control when a parked aircraft had been exposed to extreme winds. The jet flew the next morning without the inspection.

Over the next week, the aircraft completed 38 flights with no reported rudder or yaw damper problems. It then underwent scheduled maintenance in Houston on May 23, including a test of the standby hydraulic system. The procedure required a mechanic at the tail to verify that the rudder moved in response to pedal inputs.

Hangar video showed the rudder moving to the right but failing to move to the left. Investigators said no one was at the tail to verify the movement. Southwest’s maintenance records showed the test was signed off as passed, and the aircraft returned to service. The NTSB could not determine whether the test worsened the existing damage.

On the fourth flight the next day, a crew disconnected the yaw damper after reporting that it was overcorrecting in turbulence. The yaw damper uses the rudder to counter side-to-side motion.

The jet flew one more leg with the system listed as inoperative. It then passed a functional test, and the yaw damper was returned to service before Flight 746.

On the Oakland flight, the captain noticed momentary stiffness in the rudder pedals while turning onto the runway. Shortly after reaching 34,000 feet, he felt what he described as “a small amount of Dutch roll.” Both pilots felt the pedals move, and the oscillations recurred after the crew descended to 32,000 feet.

Flight data showed one episode of rudder and pedal oscillations lasting about 20 seconds, with no significant change in heading or bank angle. Investigators found that the abnormal movement appeared in the data from the first flight after the Houston maintenance check, before crews reported it. They observed it only when the yaw damper was engaged.

Southwest removed the aircraft from service after it landed in Oakland. The airline later inspected the rudder control unit mounting areas across its 737 MAX fleet and found no similar damage. It also added individual mechanic sign-offs to the hydraulic test and set up a process to alert maintenance control after extreme winds. Boeing revised its maintenance manual to require the special inspection at a wind threshold of 65 knots, or 75 mph.

#6276. The Airport Spending $335 Million So Connecting Passengers Stop Clearing Security Twice

Spokane International Airport, Simple Flying

Spokane International Airport (GEG) is preparing for one of the most significant transformations in its history, but passengers will have to endure several years of disruption before experiencing the benefits. A major portion of the airport's main terminal curbside closed on October 21, 2026, forcing motorists onto a temporary two-lane bypass road that is expected to remain in place until 2030. Inside the terminal, baggage claim facilities are also being relocated, while construction crews prepare the site for a new 255,000-square-foot building.

Central Hall is the project's centerpiece and is a $335 million project that will fundamentally change how passengers navigate GEG. The development is intended to eliminate the need for connecting passengers to leave the secure area and clear security again when transferring between concourses. But why has Spokane's existing terminal layout created this problem, and how will the airport maintain operations during such extensive reconstruction? The answers lie in its ambitious Terminal Renovation and Expansion (TREX) program.

Spokane International Airport's existing terminal configuration has a significant limitation that many passengers might not immediately recognize: its concourses do not provide the seamless post-security connections available at many larger airports. Travelers transferring between certain areas of the airport may have to leave the secure area and undergo TSA screening again before reaching their next departure gate. This unnecessarily complicates connecting itineraries, especially when passengers have limited time between flights.

The problem stems from the physical separation between Concourse C and the main terminal complex serving Concourses A and B. Although passengers can move between these areas using existing terminal infrastructure, the current arrangement does not provide the fully integrated airside circulation that Spokane wants to introduce. The airport's official TREX development plans identify the Central Hall as the solution, bringing together security screening, baggage claim, and passenger circulation in a centralized facility.

For airlines, the existing arrangement can also complicate the passenger experience when itineraries involve connections between different concourses. Travelers must account for extra walking, potential security queues, and the time needed to re-enter the secure area. While Spokane is not among the largest connecting hubs in the United States, improving these arrangements could make the airport considerably more convenient for passengers traveling through the Inland Northwest. The question is how a single new building can resolve a problem that has existed across several different terminal areas.

The 255,000-square-foot Central Hall will become the heart of Spokane International Airport's redesigned terminal. The estimated $335 million development is the centerpiece of Phase 2 of the TREX program and will consolidate security screening and baggage claim operations. According to the Spokane Journal of Business, the project will introduce a centralized security checkpoint serving all airlines, alongside a post-security connection linking Concourses A, B, and C.

This is a major change from the airport's current setup. Instead of requiring passengers to navigate separate security areas, the Central Hall will provide one consolidated screening facility through which departing passengers can access the different concourses. After passing through security, travelers can move between concourses without returning to the terminal's public side. The building will also consolidate baggage claim facilities, creating a more straightforward arrivals experience and improving access to airport concessions and other passenger amenities.

This project is intended to provide a more intuitive terminal layout, reducing the need for passengers to understand the airport's separate concourse arrangements. Airport CEO Dave Haring has described the development as offering the most significant improvement to passenger efficiency through consolidated screening services. As reported by KHQ, Haring has also emphasized the objective of giving passengers "one place to go."

255,000 square feet (23,690 square meters)

Both departing and arriving passengers will benefit from these improvements, although the new building will require substantial preparation before its construction can progress. That work has already started, and the first visible consequences are being felt outside the terminal, where the airport has had to introduce a completely different traffic arrangement.

Construction could begin as early as Spring 2027.

Building the Central Hall requires more than demolishing existing passenger facilities and building a replacement. Crews must first relocate important underground utilities, including water, sewer, and gas infrastructure, to prepare the site for the new building. This work has brought construction activity directly into the area around the main terminal, forcing Spokane International Airport to reorganize vehicle access.

On October 21, 2026, a substantial portion of the main terminal's curbside area was closed to vehicles and pedestrians. All vehicle traffic is now being directed through a newly constructed two-lane bypass road, which is expected to remain operational until 2030. According to The Spokesman-Review, the airport previously had three inbound traffic lanes, so the temporary configuration reduces capacity for vehicles entering the terminal area.

This bypass is intended to maintain access to the airport while construction crews work in the area previously occupied by the terminal's main approach roads. However, the reduced number of lanes could create additional congestion during peak departure and arrival periods. Passengers will need to follow updated signage to locate the available drop-off and pickup areas, while pedestrians using the parking facilities must access the terminal through the sky bridges. The airport has warned travelers to allow extra time for their journeys, particularly during busy periods.

The construction program also involves demolishing the existing hallway connecting the main terminal with Concourse C and Concourses A and B. Passengers will therefore use temporary pathways to move between the affected areas until the permanent infrastructure is completed. As KXLY reported on October 20, 2026, the airport expects the temporary traffic and passenger arrangements to remain in place through 2030.

This makes the current construction phase particularly challenging because the airport must maintain normal flight operations while simultaneously dismantling parts of its existing infrastructure. The situation is even more complicated for passengers using Concourse C, where the changes extend beyond pedestrian access and affect the entire baggage collection process.

Passengers flying with Alaska Airlines, Allegiant Air, and American Airlines are among those most directly affected by the changes at Spokane International Airport. These carriers operate from Concourse C, where the existing baggage claim facility is being decommissioned and demolished to make way for the redevelopment. Instead of collecting their checked luggage in the previous arrivals area, passengers will be directed to a temporary baggage claim facility in the Concourse C plaza.

According to The Spokesman-Review, the interim facility is expected to remain in use through 2030. This means that passengers arriving on the affected airlines will need to pay attention to airport signage after landing, particularly if they are unfamiliar with the temporary arrangements. The temporary baggage claim is part of the wider reorganization of Concourse C, which requires removing existing facilities before constructing the Central Hall.

The airport's parking arrangements have also changed. Its hourly parking lot has been closed for construction staging, requiring motorists to use alternative facilities depending on how long they intend to remain at the airport. Spokane recommends that visitors making stops of less than two hours use the short-term parking area on the first floor of the parking garage. Those collecting arriving passengers are encouraged to wait in the Cell Phone Lot until their friends or family members are ready for pickup. Further details are available through the airport's official parking information.

Passenger Arrangements During Trex Phase 2

Temporary baggage claim in Concourse C plaza

Temporary baggage claim in Concourse C plaza

Temporary baggage claim in Concourse C plaza

Use the first floor of the parking garage

Sources: The Spokesman-Review and Spokane International Airport.

Airport management also recommends that passengers arrive at least two hours before domestic departures. Although Spokane has traditionally been relatively straightforward to navigate, the construction program means that familiar routes through the terminal may no longer be available. The advice is particularly relevant for travelers who need to park, check baggage, or arrange special assistance. Nevertheless, the current disruption follows an earlier phase of TREX that has already expanded the airport's passenger facilities.

Allegiant Air drops service from 11 airports in September 2026, but seven return in October. See the full list and route changes now.

The Central Hall is the second major component of Spokane International Airport's Terminal Renovation and Expansion program. Before beginning the main terminal redevelopment, the airport completed an extensive expansion of Concourse C, providing additional gates and ticketing capacity. The first phase was completed in June 2026 after construction began in 2022, creating the foundation for the subsequent terminal improvements.

According to the airport's official TREX program overview, the Concourse C expansion added approximately 144,000 square feet (13,378 square meters) to the existing terminal. The development delivered three new gates, six additional ticket counters and a range of passenger amenities, including improved facilities for travelers requiring additional assistance. The project was completed through two major construction packages, Concourse C West and Concourse C East.

The original expansion was designed to provide additional operational capacity before the airport undertook the more complicated task of rebuilding its central passenger facilities. It also introduced improvements such as a nursing mothers' suite, companion care rooms, and upgraded passenger amenities. According to the airport's TREX program information, a joint venture between Garco Construction and Q&D Construction managed construction, with Architectural Alliance International Group leading the architectural design.

However, additional gates alone cannot solve the airport's existing security and connectivity limitations. The Central Hall is the program's most transformative element because it changes the relationship between the concourses rather than simply expanding their individual capacities. The airport's published schedule sets the start of Central Hall construction for the second quarter of 2027, after the current utility relocation and site preparation work.

The new Central Hall could fundamentally change the way Spokane International Airport operates, particularly for passengers connecting between flights. Rather than treating Concourses A, B, and C as separate passenger areas, the airport plans to create a more integrated terminal where travelers can move between gates without repeatedly passing through security. The benefits could extend beyond shorter connection times, making the airport easier to navigate for passengers unfamiliar with its layout.

The next major milestone is the anticipated groundbreaking in Q2 2027, with the temporary traffic arrangements and baggage claim facilities expected to remain until 2030. The airport's official TREX development program also identifies potential future modernization of Concourses A and B, although those improvements remain subject to additional funding. Consequently, the Central Hall is not necessarily the end of Spokane's terminal transformation.

For now, the airport must balance its construction ambitions with the practical needs of airlines and passengers. The success of the $335 million investment will ultimately depend on whether the completed facility delivers the promised consolidated screening arrangements and seamless connections between all three concourses. If it does, Spokane will have addressed a longstanding weakness in its terminal design, even if passengers must endure several years of construction to get there.

#6275. 'Money out of politics' ballot measure sparks First Amendment fight in battleground state

Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed details his Medicare for All plan while advocating for politicians to not take money from big corporations on ‘The Story.

Michigan voters approved a ballot initiative called Proposal 2, pitched to them as a way to curb pay-to-play donations and get money out of politics. But the measure has also triggered a federal First Amendment lawsuit alleging its separate speech and disclosure provisions could ensnare journalists, nonprofits and policy researchers who discuss elected officials.

Michiganders for Money Out of Politics, also known as MOP UP Michigan, said the lawsuit was expected after voters approved Proposal 2. Campaign manager Maura Cowley said the group is "confident Proposal 2 will withstand legal scrutiny" after organizers said they submitted more than 560,000 signatures to place the measure on the ballot.

The Mackinac Center for Public Policy, which filed the lawsuit, says it is not challenging the initiative’s central pay-to-play restrictions on political contributions from utility companies and government contractors. Its lawsuit instead targets provisions imposing reporting and disclosure requirements on certain communications that refer to candidates or "promote, support, attack or oppose" candidates or ballot questions, even without expressly urging voters to support or oppose them.

"Michigan voters deserve the freedom to research, debate, and report on the policies that shape their lives. But Proposal 2 is a Trojan horse: while it claims to target corruption, it would expose the Mackinac Center, its supporters, and ordinary Michiganders to criminal penalties and harassment simply for discussing public policy," Patrick Wright, the Mackinac Center’s vice president of legal affairs, said in a statement provided to Fox News Digital.

SURVEY REVEALS COLLEGE STUDENTS' GROWING INTOLERANCE FOR FREE SPEECH

Demonstrators protest the suspension of the "Jimmy Kimmel Live!" show outside the El Capitan Entertainment Centre where the show is performed in Hollywood on Sept. 18, 2025, in Los Angeles, California. (Mario Tama/Getty Images)

Under Proposal 2, any person — not just a campaign or political committee — who makes "electioneering communications" aggregating at least $5,000 in a calendar year would have to file a report within 10 days. Additional reports would be required after each additional $5,000 in covered communications. The reports would include the dates and costs of the communications, candidates mentioned, vendors paid and information about donors who contributed more than $100 for the purpose of making the communications.

Proposal 2 defines "electioneering communications" as public messages — including broadcasts, print publications, mailings, telephone calls, internet communications and other forms of general public communication — that reference a clearly identifiable candidate, regardless of whether they contain express advocacy, within 100 days of a general election or 30 days before a primary or special election. The communication must also be targeted to the relevant electorate where the candidate appears on the ballot, according to the provision.

Mackinac argues the measure leaves important questions unanswered, including which expenses count toward the $5,000 threshold, what it means for a donor to contribute "for making electioneering communications," and how the state will determine whether a communication is targeted to the relevant electorate.

SUPREME COURT STRIKES DOWN LIMIT ON PARTY CAMPAIGN SPENDING IN COORDINATION WITH CANDIDATES

The Michigan state capitol, on August 29, 2026, in Lansing, Michigan. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News)

The Mackinac Center’s lawsuit also challenges Proposal 2’s expansion of the definition of an election-related "expenditure." The amended definition includes public communications that "promote, support, attack, or oppose" a candidate or ballot question, regardless of whether they expressly advocate for or against the outcome. Under the proposal’s revised committee definition, an organization that spends at least $500 on such expenditures could be treated as a political committee if the state determines the spending was intended to influence voters.

Brett Nolan, an Institute for Free Speech attorney representing Mackinac, told Fox News Digital that the new electioneering-communications reporting provision contains no express exception for neutral reporting, legislative voting records or policy research. Proposal 2 does retain an existing exemption for certain news stories, commentary and editorials from being treated as campaign spending, but Mackinac argues that exemption does not resolve the reporting requirements for electioneering communications.

Mackinac’s complaint points specifically to its MichiganVotes project, policy scorecards, a neutral policy brief about Proposal 2, magazines, radio programs, podcasts and public-policy events as examples of speech that could be swept up in the new requirements because those materials sometimes discuss elected officials or candidates.

GOP LAWMAKERS URGE SUPREME COURT TO STRENGTHEN FIRST AMENDMENT PROTECTIONS FOR STREET PREACHERS

"The Supreme Court has said several times in recent years that disclosure mandates like this create an 'inevitable' chilling effect on free speech because the risk of political harassment (or worse) is so significant. The more costs we impose on those who want to exchange ideas and discuss public policy, the fewer of those people we will have," Nolan said.

"This law goes much further than addressing any interest the state may have in transparency about those who are funding campaigns and election advocacy," he continued. "The notion that the government has an interest in monitoring people who talk about public policy if they dare mention an elected official is antithetical to the First Amendment."

The U.S. Supreme Court cleared the way for the Trump administration to continue third-country deportations while the justices consider a legal challenge to the policy. (Getty Images)

The lawsuit against Proposal 2 seeks to block the electioneering-communications reporting requirement and the political-committee rules as applied to Mackinac — not to overturn Proposal 2 in its entirety. The measure is set to take effect 10 days after the official declaration of the vote, and no later than Dec. 3, according to the lawsuit.

"This lawsuit is no surprise," Cowley said in a statement to Fox News Digital. "The corporations bankrolling our opposition have been gearing up for this lawsuit since Proposal 2 first qualified for the ballot, if not before."

According to MOP UP Michigan, besides curbing pay-to-play political donations, Proposal 2 is designed to close what the group calls an "issue-ad loophole" — the ability to discuss candidates or ballot questions without expressly urging voters to support or oppose them in order to avoid certain disclosure rules.

"Last night, Michiganders spoke loud and clear, voting to pass Proposal 2 with an overwhelming majority and delivering a resounding mandate to end pay-to-play politics and put power back where it belongs – with the people," Cowley continued. "The bottom line is that we are confident Proposal 2 will withstand legal scrutiny, and we were fully expecting and are prepared to take on this challenge."

Alec Schemmel is a Politics Reporter for Fox News Digital who is originally from Charlotte, North Carolina but now resides in the Washington D.C.-Baltimore Metro Area.

I’ve held the (see rates and fees) for eight years, and despite carrying more than 25 credit cards, it’s one I’ll continue renewing year after year.

The reason is simple: World of Hyatt is my favorite hotel loyalty program, and this card makes it even more rewarding to stay with the brand. Between an annual free night, automatic elite status and the ability to earn valuable Hyatt points on spending, I consistently receive far more value than the card’s affordable $95 annual fee.

It isn’t the right fit for everyone. Hyatt has a much smaller global footprint than Marriott, Hilton and IHG, so travelers who rarely stay at Hyatt hotels may be better served by a more flexible travel rewards card. However, if Hyatt is already part of your travel plans — or you’d like it to become one — the World of Hyatt card is one of the best mid-tier hotel cards on the market. Card rating*: ⭐⭐⭐⭐

*Card rating is based on the opinion of TPG’s editors and is not influenced by the card issuer.

If you’re comparing several hotel credit cards, here’s what you need to know at a glance:

Unlike cards that earn transferable rewards, this is very much a Hyatt-focused product. If you’re loyal to Hyatt — or want an affordable way to accelerate your progress toward higher status — it deserves serious consideration.

If there’s one reason why I continue paying the World of Hyatt card’s annual fee, it’s the anniversary free night certificate.

Each cardholder anniversary, you’ll receive a free night award valid at any Category 1-4 Hyatt hotel or resort. Since Hyatt prices these properties between 3,000 and 25,000 points per night, there’s plenty of opportunity to extract well over $95 in value. Free nights expire 12 months after issuance.

I’ve redeemed my certificates at The Standard, Brussels, Hyatt House Manchester in the U.K. and Andaz Mexico City Condesa. In each case, paying cash would have cost considerably more than the card’s annual fee.

Even better, you can earn a second Category 1-4 certificate after spending $15,000 on the card in a calendar year.

That’s the spending threshold I personally target each year. It unlocks another free night and an additional six elite night credits toward Hyatt status for even more value beyond the points you'll earn from that spending.

Related: The best Hyatt Category 4 hotels to maximize your free night award certificates

Simply holding the card gives you complimentary Discoverist status.

While Discoverist isn’t Hyatt’s most rewarding elite tier, I still appreciate benefits like preferred room upgrades and late checkout (when available) and a 10% bonus on eligible Hyatt spending.

That said, for frequent Hyatt guests, this perk probably won’t be all that enticing since they’re likely to earn Discoverist status organically. The card becomes more valuable when working toward a higher status level.

Every calendar year, you’ll receive five qualifying night credits automatically, and you’ll earn another two qualifying night credits for every $5,000 spent.

I’ve found those elite night credits incredibly valuable. By combining the five annual elite nights from the card with my Hyatt stays and strategic spending to earn an additional six nights, I qualified for top-tier Globalist status in August 2025, which I’ll enjoy through February 2027.

One of my favorite things about the World of Hyatt program is that earning and redeeming points is refreshingly straightforward.

Unlike most major hotel loyalty programs, Hyatt still publishes an award chart, making award pricing more predictable.

When you stay at Hyatt hotels, these earnings stack with the points you earn as a World of Hyatt member. Since cardholders receive complimentary Discoverist status, you’ll also earn a 10% bonus on your base points, meaning you can earn up to 9.5 total points per dollar spent on eligible Hyatt purchases. That represents a solid 16% return on Hyatt purchases, per our November 2026 valuations.

I generally use this card for Hyatt stays and tax payments that help me reach the $15,000 annual threshold for the second free night certificate.

Otherwise, I typically use my  (see rates and fees) for most travel and dining purchases, then transfer those Chase Ultimate Rewards points to my Hyatt account whenever I need to top up my balance for an award stay.

That gives me the best of both worlds: I earn more rewards on everyday travel and dining while keeping my points flexible until I’m ready to book. If I don’t end up needing Hyatt points, I can always transfer them to one of Chase’s 13 other airline or hotel partners instead.

In my opinion, Hyatt points remain among the most valuable hotel points due to their flexibility.

Award nights start at just 3,000 points for a Category 1 property at the Lowest rate and range up to 75,000 points for a top-tier Category 8 property under Hyatt’s five-tier standard award chart.

I’ve used Hyatt points for everything from inexpensive city breaks to luxury resorts. Some of my favorite redemptions include:

Hyatt also lets you redeem points for Points + Cash stays, suite upgrades, club lounge access and Find experiences. While those options can make sense occasionally, I almost always get the best value by redeeming points for standard award nights.

Despite being one of my favorite hotel credit cards, the won’t be the right fit for every traveler.

The biggest drawback is Hyatt’s relatively small footprint. While Hyatt has more than 1,500 hotels and all-inclusive properties across 80-plus countries, that’s still far fewer than Marriott or Hilton. If you frequently travel to destinations without a Hyatt, you may struggle to maximize the card’s benefits.

Those who prioritize earning the highest possible rewards on everyday spending will likely find better options elsewhere. Beyond Hyatt purchases and spending toward the $15,000 threshold for a second free night certificate, this card isn’t particularly rewarding for dining, travel or everyday purchases.

Finally, travelers looking for premium perks like airport lounge access, annual travel credits and luxury benefits across multiple hotel brands should consider a premium travel rewards card instead.

For most travelers, I think the personal World of Hyatt Credit Card is the better choice than the (see rates and fees).

Both cards help you earn Hyatt points and elite status, but the business version is designed primarily for business owners. It offers bonus categories geared toward business spending and additional benefits for companies, while the personal card provides better long-term value for most travelers, thanks to its annual Category 1-4 free night certificate.

By comparison, I think the World of Hyatt Business card's $199 annual fee is harder to justify year after year because it lacks an anniversary free night. It does offer up to $100 in Hyatt statement credits each anniversary year, but that requires Hyatt spending and there's no way to get outsized value like you might with a free night.

Unless you own a business and can maximize the business-specific earning categories, I’d start with the personal card.

The annual Category 1-4 free night certificate has consistently offset the card’s $95 annual fee, while the elite night credits helped me qualify for Globalist status last year. Add in Hyatt’s strong redemption value, and it’s easy to see why this remains my favorite mid-tier hotel credit card.

If you regularly stay at Hyatt properties, I think the World of Hyatt card deserves a place in your wallet. If you rarely stay with Hyatt, though, you’ll probably get more long-term value from a flexible travel rewards card.

#6273. Reporter's Notebook: How midterms may change the House impeachment equation for Hegseth

Fox News chief congressional correspondent Chad Pergram reports on post-midterm calls from several Democrats to investigate President Donald Trump and his administration on ‘Hannity.’

Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., plans to reintroduce articles of impeachment for Pentagon Chief Pete Hegseth next week. The chances are increasingly high that the House could in fact impeach Hegseth.

Massie tried to impeach Hegseth before the midterms. But the House adjourned a day early in September, nixing Massie’s effort. House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., condemned the effort by Massie. But insisted that he didn’t send members home early because of fear that the House had the votes to impeach Hegseth.

So Massie’s articles of impeachment expired. But he will reintroduce them next week. Under the rules, the House must consider them within two days.

THE HITCHHIKER’S GUIDE TO MASSIE SAYING JOHNSON IS SENDING THE HOUSE HOME EARLY TO PREVENT HEGSETH IMPEACHMENT

Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., leaves the U.S. Capitol after the last votes of the week on Thursday, June 25, 2026. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

It’s possible the House could move to table the articles, or send them to committee, euthanizing the effort. But a growing number of House Republicans have grumbled about Hegseth. Any effort to dismiss the articles in the House might not work.

All Democrats are likely to vote to impeach. There are some Republicans who have said privately they’d like to impeach. Now, after the midterms, you have more Republicans hoping to build distance between themselves and President Trump. Moreover, the war in Iran contributed directly to the GOP’s thumping. So even more Republicans may be willing to impeach. Finally, the GOP may have attendance problems. Members who lost — or were shocked that they lost — might not show up. In other words, there may be more Democrats in the House next week than Republicans.

Don’t forget that some Republicans are now looking for a scapegoat after the election.

DEMS SEIZE THE SENATE AS BLUE TIDAL WAVE CRASHES DEEP INTO TRUMP COUNTRY, TOPPLES GOP STRONGHOLDS

U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth gives a State of the Force address at Marine Corps Base Quantico on September 30, 2026 in Quantico, Virginia. Secretary Hegseth delivered his State of the Force address to junior officers, enlisted leaders, and special guests including Anduril Industries co-founder Palmer Luckey. (Alex Wong/Getty Images)

A simple majority is necessary to impeach.

Then the House would send the articles of impeachment to the Senate.

Under Senate rules of impeachment, the Senate must at least receive and consider the articles. But it could move quickly to dismiss. That’s what happened when the Senate considered articles of impeachment for former Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas a few years ago. The bona fide "trial" part of the process never happened where the Senate heard arguments, listened to witnesses and took evidence.

It takes a simple majority to dismiss such articles. Again, this could happen under a Republican-controlled Senate. But how might outgoing Sens. John Cornyn, R-Texas, Thom Tillis, R-N.C., and Bill Cassidy, R-La., vote?

That’s to say nothing of Sens. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, John Curtis, R-Alaska, Todd Young ,R-Ind., and others.

STATE OF PLAY: BLUE WAVE SWEEPS DEMOCRATS INTO POWER, WITH KEY RACES STILL HANGING IN BALANCE

A split image of President Trump, Sens. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., and John Cornyn, R-Texas (Eddie Seal/Bloomberg via Getty Images; Aaron Schwartz/AFP via Getty Images; Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc;)

It takes a two-thirds vote to convict and remove in a Senate impeachment trial.

In addition, unlikely legislation, articles of impeachment carry over into the new Congress. Would a new Democratically-controlled Senate want to get bogged down in an impeachment trial from the start? Especially when new Democrats want to vote on affordability and health care?

Or, would a Democratic Senate embrace the idea of a full-blown impeachment trial for Hegseth – especially since the execution of the war in Iran seems to be one of the main reasons for this week’s electoral shellacking?

#6272. New Hyatt Credit Card Offer: Earn 4 Free Nights—Why I Spend On The Card Towards Elite Status

I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog. Be aware that websites may earn compensation when a customer clicks on a link, when an application is approved, or when an account is opened. Citibank is an advertising partner of this site, as is American Express, Chase, Capital One, and others. Any opinions expressed in this post are my own, and have not been reviewed, approved, or endorsed by my advertising partners. I do not write about all offers that are available -- instead focusing on miles, points, and cash back (and currencies that can be converted into the same). Terms apply to the offers and benefits listed on this page.

The World Of Hyatt Credit Card (See rates and fees) has a new initial bonus: earn 4 free nights at any Category 1-4 Hyatt hotel or resort after spending $5,000 on purchases in the first 3 months from account opening. That’s an improved offer from a card whose bonuses have usually been more modest than competing travel cards.

I have this card, and I put actual spending on it. Hyatt points are still valuable, but what gets me to use the card is the credit toward elite status and the rewards earned along the way. Hyatt status does more to improve my hotel stays than status with other major chains.

These are four separate certificates, so you can use them for one trip or spread them across different stays. You’ll need standard room award availability, and the certificates expire 12 months after they’re issued. The terms require checkout before the expiration date. Under Hyatt’s current award chart, a Category 4 standard room can cost as much as 25,000 points per night. Four certificates could therefore cover nights that would otherwise require 100,000 points. Their category restrictions and expiration date make them less flexible than having those points in your account. The card has a $95 annual fee. Chase excludes current holders of this card and previous cardmembers who received its initial bonus within the past 24 months. The usual Chase restriction on applicants who’ve opened five or more personal cards in the past 24 months also generally applies. Why I Keep The Card And Spend On It The annual Category 1-4 free night after each cardmember anniversary makes the $95 fee easy to justify. There’s also a second Category 1-4 night after $15,000 in purchases during a calendar year which makes that spending more rewarding. And these nights are transferable to another World of Hyatt member. If I won’t use one, I can give it to someone who will. For spending, the card earns 4 Hyatt points per dollar on qualifying Hyatt purchases; 2 on restaurants, airline tickets bought directly from airlines, local transit and commuting, and fitness club and gym memberships; and 1 on other purchases. More significantly, it comes with 5 qualifying nights each year, plus 2 more qualifying nights for every $5,000 spent. Those nights count toward both status and Milestone Rewards. Put $15,000 of otherwise unbonused spending on the card during a calendar year and you earn: 15,000 Hyatt points. An additional Category 1-4 free night certificate. 6 qualifying nights from spending, giving you 11 including the card’s annual 5. That means 49 qualifying nights actually spent in hotels, plus the card’s 5 annual nights and 6 from spending, gets you to the 60 needed for Globalist. And the $5,000 spent earning the initial bonus counts toward the $15,000 free-night threshold in the calendar year when you spend it. Milestone Rewards start at 20 qualifying nights and continue every 10 nights through 150. Some of the rewards on the way to Globalist are: Qualifying Nights Notable Rewards 30 A Category 1-4 free night, plus a choice of additional reward. 40 A Guest of Honor Award, plus a choice that includes a Suite Upgrade Award. 50 A choice that includes 2 Suite Upgrade Awards. 60 Globalist status, a Category 1-7 free night, 2 Suite Upgrade Awards, 2 Guest of Honor Awards, and My Hyatt Concierge. The value of another $5,000 in spending depends on where those two nights get me. Crossing a threshold for suite upgrades or Globalist can be worth giving up a higher earning rate on another card. Hyatt Status Is Stronger Than At Other Major Chains The card itself comes with Discoverist status. That’s better than a hole in the head as my grandfather used to say. But reaching Globalist has real value – as well as the milestone choices along the way. The biggest benefit is confirming a suite at the time of booking with a Suite Upgrade Award for up to seven nights when an eligible standard suite is available for the stay. That’s a huge value on family trips. I also value having a My Hyatt Concierge I can email requests to, actual delivery of 4 p.m. late checkout at eligible properties, and a more generous breakfast benefit than I get from other chains. At participating hotels without an available club lounge, Globalist breakfast generally covers a full breakfast for up to two adults and two children registered in the room, including tax and gratuity. Late checkout has exceptions, including availability limits at resorts, but I’m usually proactively offered late checkout everywhere else (and personally find it honored more often than not at resorts). The Free Night Certificates Should Be More Flexible The current version of this card launched in 2018. Its annual certificate is still capped at Category 4, while category creep has taken away many of the hotels where I’d most want to use it. Just this year, 14 hotels moved from Category 4 to Category 5, including Hyatt Regency Seattle, Hyatt Regency Grand Cypress and Hyatt Regency Jersey City. Five moved the other way, bringing options like Hyatt Centric Congress Avenue Austin and Dream Nashville within reach, but the certificate lost more hotels than it gained. I’d like Hyatt to at least let members add points to a certificate to book a higher category. The certificate works at a Category 4 hotel charging 25,000 points, but won’t work at a Category 5 hotel when it’s charging 15,000 points. And I wish Hyatt would let us combine these free nights with Suite Upgrade Awards or Guest of Honor Awards. I value them most traveling with my family when I’m paying for rooms out of pocket. That’s always when I want to use my suite upgrades! I don’t need a suite on a business stay (paid by someone else, when it’s just me) or to use the free night award. #6271. DOJ shake-up continues with head of national security division, US attorney in Miami resigning

Attorney General Todd Blanche, seen on Nov. 4, 2026, announced the departure of John Eisenberg and Jason Reding Quiñones on Nov. 6, 2026, adding to the shakeups at the Department of Justice. (Kathleen Flynn/Getty Images)

John Eisenberg, the head of the National Security Division at the Department of Justice, is stepping down from his post, becoming the third senior DOJ official to resign since the midterm elections.

Shortly after Fox News learned of Eisenberg's resignation, Attorney General Todd Blanche announced it on social media.

"He has served with distinction, strengthening our nation’s ability to address threats, both foreign and domestic," Blanche said. "Under his leadership, the Division advanced President Trump’s mission to make America safe by prosecuting terrorists and working with our law enforcement partners to disrupt planned attacks on the American people."

This was Eisenberg's second stint serving under President Donald Trump. In Trump's first term, Eisenberg was an assistant and deputy counsel to the president, as well as a legal advisor to the National Security Council, which advises presidents on foreign policy matters.

John A. Eisenberg responds to questioning from U.S. Sen. Mazie Hirono during Senate Judiciary hearings in the Dirksen Senate office building in Washington, D.C., on March 25, 2025. (Mattie Neretin/Sipa USA)

DOJ CIVIL RIGHTS CHIEF HARMEET DHILLON RESIGNS, SAYS WHITE HOUSE ASKED HER TO WAIT UNTIL AFTER MIDTERMS

Less than an hour before Eisenberg's departure was made public, Blanche announced the resignation of Jason Reding Quiñones, the U.S. Attorney for Florida's Southern District.

Quiñones was perhaps best known for securing an indictment against Raúl Castro, the former president of Cuba who took over after his brother Fidel Castro's nearly 50-year reign.

Raúl Castro, now 95, was indicted for his alleged role in the 1996 shoot-down of two unarmed civilian aircraft operated by Brothers to the Rescue, a Miami-based humanitarian group that searched the Florida Straits for Cuban migrants in distress. The four U.S. nationals aboard the two planes were killed.

"We are grateful for Jason’s leadership in combatting violent crime, drug trafficking, sex trafficking, and transnational crime," Blanche said. "Jason has served the Department multiple times over his distinguished career, and we thank him for his service to this country."

Jason Reding Quinones, US Attorney for the District of Southern Florida, speaks to the press outside the federal courthouse in the Brooklyn borough of New York City on July 20, 2026. (Leonardo MUNOZ / AFP via Getty Images)

DOJ LAUNCHES CRIMINAL PROBE INTO SUPREME COURT LEAK THAT EXPOSED RULING OVERTURNING ROE V WADE

The departure of Eisenberg and Quiñones came just a day after Harmeet Dhillon, who headed up the DOJ's Civil Rights Division, announced she'd be leaving as well.

In an interview with Fox News Digital, Dhillon said she attempted to resign three weeks ago but was asked by White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles to stay until after the midterms.

Dhillon moved to Washington following the deaths of her husband and father to "serve my country," but after roughly two years in the administration, she said it was time for her to leave.

Harmeet Dhillon, the then-Assistant Attorney General for Civil Rights, speaks onstage during the Hispanic Heritage Gala Washington DC by Latino Wall Street and Host Committee at Andrew Mellon Auditorium on Oct. 14, 2026 in Washington, D.C. (Leigh Vogel/Getty Images for Latino Wall Street)

Dhillon shifted her office's priorities toward issues including DEI and race-conscious policies, religious discrimination, transgender participation in women's sports, Second Amendment rights and election integrity.

In the lead-up to the midterms, Dhillon defended the Trump administration's investigation into noncitizen voters. She was also in charge of the DOJ's effort to send more than 1,000 election monitors to all 50 states.

#6270. Delta Air Lines Boosts Summer 2027 Schedule With New Routes & Expanded Weekend Frequencies

Delta Air Lines has announced another expansion of its summer 2027 network, featuring 11 seasonal routes, additional weekend frequencies on five domestic services, and increased flying to ten Latin American and Caribbean destinations. The changes announced today target leisure travelers heading to mountain resorts, national parks, and beach destinations.

The strategy builds on Delta's summer 2026 expansion, which introduced Saturday-only flights from Austin Bergstrom International Airport (AUS) and Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) alongside returning seasonal services elsewhere. Analysis of newly available US Department Of Transportation (DOT) data reveals that numerous routes achieved load factors exceeding 90%, explaining why Delta is maintaining its focus on weekend leisure demand while selectively increasing capacity.

Delta's latest announcement features 11 routes originating from Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport (ATL), Detroit Metropolitan Wayne County Airport (DTW), Austin and Los Angeles. All appeared in the airline's original summer 2026 plans, with destinations including Bozeman, Kalispell, Jackson Hole and Pensacola.

Most services begin in late May or June, although flights to Bangor will continue into October, extending beyond the traditional summer vacation period. Importantly, Detroit–Destin represents a reinstatement, having been canceled before summer 2026 operations began.

While a once-weekly service might seem very thin, it taps into the group of leisure travelers who want to get away for a week and are seeking out new destinations. This travel segment has surged post-pandemic, and Delta is betting that the trend will continue in 2027. Explaining the latest expansion, Amy Martin, Delta's Vice President of Network Planning, said:

“We’re continuing to tailor Delta’s schedule around where our customers want to travel. By adding weekend flights to some of the most sought-after leisure destinations, we’re giving customers more flexibility and more ways to make the most of their summer.”

The airline is also including eight previously loaded Boston Logan International Airport (BOS) routes, serving destinations such as Charleston, Savannah and Halifax, alongside two Florida connections from LaGuardia Airport (LGA). These additions complement Delta's wider Boston expansion, which includes new European connections for 2027.

The return of these routes suggests that Delta found success with them this past summer, and analysis of the DOT's T-100 data indicates this was definitely the case. Detroit–Pensacola achieved the highest June–July 2026 average load factor at 95.5%, followed by Atlanta–Bangor at 92.2% and Atlanta–Rapid City at 91.5%. Detroit–Bangor and Detroit–Bozeman also performed strongly, averaging approximately 89%, suggesting particularly robust demand from established Delta hubs.

However, newer routes didn't perform at those same high levels, with Austin–Bozeman, Austin–Kalispell, and Los Angeles–Jackson Hole all operating less than 80% full. Nevertheless, Delta has already extended Austin–Bozeman into winter, when it will operate daily during peak ski season. Such decisions illustrate why summer occupancy alone cannot determine profitability or a route's longer-term potential.

Delta is also increasing capacity on five established domestic routes, adding a weekend frequency to each. The changes include Orlando and Fort Myers service from Cincinnati Northern Kentucky International Airport (CVG), beginning in April, while Minneapolis–Kalispell receives more flying from June. These enhancements suggest Delta is selectively investing in established markets alongside its returning leisure experiments.

The airline will be adding 13 new Saturday-only routes from six of its hubs as part of its Summer 2026 schedule.

International leisure expansion forms another major component of Delta's plans. Ten routes across Latin America and the Caribbean will receive additional Saturday frequencies, extended operating seasons, or both. Atlanta accounts for half, with the airline highlighting a new Saturday flight to St. Lucia that will improve connections through its largest hub.

Delta's latest expansion consequently emphasizes refining existing networks rather than introducing large numbers of entirely new destinations. Its strong 2026 load factors on several routes help explain the strategy, although the return of slightly weaker performers suggests other considerations, including seasonal yields and aircraft utilization. With fuel costs encouraging greater capacity discipline, targeted weekend flying offers Delta a way to pursue leisure growth without substantial year-round commitments.

#6269. American Airlines Adds New App Option When Flights Go Wrong—Try For An Earlier Flight Without Giving Up Your Confirmed Seat

American Airlines is making it easier to try for an earlier flight when your travel falls apart. Its app and website will now offer standby options when you’re dealing with a travel disruption while keeping your new confirmed flight. You don’t need an agent for this – it’s part of their self-service tool. The change to list yourself for free standby on an earlier flight went into effect this week. During a disruption, the flight you can confirm may be hours later than one you could actually get on if a seat opens up. You no longer need to deal with customer service to get on the standby list. . How The New Standby Option Works American calls its tool Dynamic Rebooking. Here’s the sequence described in an internal company memo: Open your disrupted trip on aa.com or in the American Airlines app. Start with Flight Options or Rebook Trip in the disruption banner. If your flight was canceled and you don’t have a replacement, confirm one first. Choose a flight with availability, then return to Flight Options to look for standby. Look for earlier nonstop flights. Up to three standby options may appear when American can’t confirm the earlier rebooking. Pick one. You can join one standby list at a time through this tool. You can remove yourself or switch to another option without contacting an employee. Keep your confirmed flight while you wait. Your itinerary changes only if you clear onto the standby flight. If you’re confirmed for an 8 p.m. flight and the app can’t confirm you on the 5 p.m., you can standby for it while remaining confirmed on that 8 p.m.. If you don’t clear, your confirmed itinerary remains intact. Employees are told, Do not cancel the customer’s confirmed flight because the customer joined standby If you do clear standby you lose the confirmation on your original flight so if you can’t make it you need to remove yourself from standby. What American Is Actually Adding For Passengers American has offered same day changes and standby through its app since 2017. And keeping your original booking while standing by for an earlier flight was already part of published policy. The improvement is putting standby inside the flight disruption rebooking process. I’m pretty skeptical about AA’s IT for passengers. The week before last they did a pretty lousy job dealing with their problems. I was flying home from LAS with a connection in DFW. First flight was delayed repeatedly. The app kept promising to rebook me if my connection became non viable. By the time we boarded in Vegas my connection – with a change of terminals – was seven minutes. The app still did nothing so I switched flights myself. Then the flight out of DFW was severely delayed. Ended up home very late only to discover that my bag was mishandled and was still in Dallas. AA’s IT didn’t bother informing me until I was the last person at the baggage carousel at almost two in the morning.

That experience made me incredibly angry and gave me no confidence whatsoever in the technology that American is using.

@Christian — Yikes. Did you at least receive a perfunctory automated “sorry” after that ordeal? I mean, I know, like, actually receiving your checked bag(s) timely would’ve been preferred, and if not, reliable communication and reimbursement, but, you know, the ‘free’ market and lifting bootstraps is the best we can do for now… *facepalm* (this is why I try to do carry-on only.)

As recently as last week, the poor IT underpinnings of AA’s app effectively prevented its use even for confirming later rebookings. GAs and FAs are being told to tell disrupted passengers to rebook in the app rather than call or line up, only for the pax who listen to find themselves last in the queue when the app fails,

I’d prefer to see AA focus on getting the existing functionality working before they add new capabilities

@Frequent Delay Victim — There’s little incentive for AA or any major US carrier to properly invest in operational reliability because there’s no real financial penalty for them failing to deliver for you. (Oh, you’ll go to a competitor? Well, turns out, AA’s the only one operating that nonstop; oh, and Delta, United, Southwest, etc., also frequently delay and cancel with no real recourse other than a partial refund or expiring extremely limited silly credit.) We need major reforms that include actual consumer protections, or this will just keep getting worse and worse.

I think this is helpful, but I wonder if the alternatives offered are only valid for the original departing airport? In NY, LA, SFO and other airports I would not mind going to a different airport to catch an earlier flight, time permitting. But to date, alternatives have only been offered for the same airport you were originally booked from. Equally, I don’t NEED to get an alternative for LGA if I can catch an earlier option to JFK or EWR. Same for other destinations. I am sure AI could figure this out 😉
