#6268. Blue wave battered GOP strongholds across America, but one red state held the line

Bold conservative policies and crucial ballot measures helped Florida successfully mitigate the blue 'wave' during the midterm elections. Governor Ron DeSantis discusses how his state avoided a near extinction level event for the Republican Party.

On a night when Democrats made major gains across the country, South Dakota emerged as one of the few Republican strongholds where the GOP largely held its ground — even as Democrats made inroads around Sioux Falls.

Republican Gov. Larry Rhoden won roughly 63.5% of the vote Tuesday, nearly matching President Donald Trump's 63.4% performance in 2024. Republicans also swept the state's other statewide races and maintained overwhelming control of the legislature, despite Democrats picking up four seats.

Rhoden's victory came against Democrat Dan Ahlers, who described himself as a "conservative Democrat" and campaigned on affordability, rural healthcare, education and other kitchen table issues. But his moderate pitch did little to narrow the GOP's commanding statewide advantage, with Ahlers finishing at just 36.5% of the vote.

South Dakota's results stood in contrast to several other deeply Republican states where the GOP maintained control but saw its margins shrink considerably. In Idaho and Wyoming, Republican gubernatorial candidates won comfortably but finished with smaller shares of the vote than President Donald Trump secured in 2024. South Dakota's gubernatorial result, by comparison, remained virtually unchanged.

DESANTIS CALLS GOP MIDTERM LOSSES 'EXTINCTION-LEVEL EVENT' — AND EXPLAINS WHY FLORIDA SURVIVED

South Dakota Governor Larry Rhoden speaks during a rally at Mount Rushmore National Memorial on July 3, 2026, in Keystone, South Dakota. Trump is holding a rally and fireworks show at Mount Rushmore, kicking off a weekend of 250th Independence Day celebrations across the country. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)

David Jolly, the Democratic nominee in Florida, ran a campaign with similar themes to Ahlers' — pointing to the fact that he used to be a Republican and, like Ahlers, prioritized affordability and healthcare while on the campaign trail. Jolly cut the GOP’s vote share to just 50%, roughly six points below the party’s 2024 presidential performance. Tennessee's Democratic gubernatorial nominee inflicted a similarly sharp cut on Republicans' margins by employing a similar strategy.

Even down the ballot, South Dakota Republicans largely held their ground, though Democrats managed to flip four legislative seats in the Sioux Falls area, marking their first legislative gains in the state since 2008.

The losses were concentrated around the state's largest city, where a growing population and a less conservative political landscape have created more opportunities for Democrats, according to University of South Dakota political scientist Julia Hellwege. Opposition to large data-center projects also resonated with some voters in the area, according to a local Democratic official.

"South Dakota Republicans did well because we took on the issues that mattered to the people of our state and delivered real results for them," South Dakota's Republican House speaker, Jon Hansen, told Fox News Digital. "The bottom line is that we ran on tackling the issues that mattered to people, and then we delivered real results for the people on those issues. Not just talk, not just excuses, but real solutions. It’s what our people deserve, and it’s what we delivered for them."

FOX NEWS VOTER POLL: 2026 MIDTERM ELECTIONS USHER IN A BLUE WAVE AS DEMOCRATS WIN CONTROL OF CONGRESS

Former Republican Representative David Jolly, Democratic gubernatorial candidate for Florida, speaks during the National Action Network (NAN) 35th Anniversary Convention in New York on Thursday, April 9, 2026. (Victor J. Blue/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Hansen pointed to property tax cuts enacted by the legislature, regulations aimed at preventing utility costs from rising amid data center build-outs, curbing corporate eminent domain and balancing the state's budget, among other efforts, as crucial in the South Dakota GOP's success on Tuesday night.

South Dakota’s unemployment rate has been hovering around 2% since last September, roughly half the rate of the United States at large. Average wages also increased by about 4% in the state over the course of 2025. All of this occurred as South Dakota remained one of the most affordable states in the country, though rising rent costs outpaced wage growth in 2025, according to data collected by Realtor.com.

At the federal level, Republican Sen. Mike Rounds cruised to victory with 60.5% of the vote, though the GOP wasn't entirely immune to the national shift. South Dakota Attorney General Marty Jackley won the state's at-large congressional seat with roughly 64% of the vote, down from the 72% fellow Republican Dusty Johnson secured in 2024.

South Dakota's relatively modest legislative losses stood in sharp contrast to other Republican strongholds. In Texas, Democrats flipped 21 GOP-held state House seats, while Republicans in New Hampshire were on track to fall from the 222 House seats they won in 2024 to just 107.

DEMOCRATS SEIZE MAJORITY OF GOVERNORS’ OFFICES IN ELECTION-NIGHT SHIFT

The Texas State Capitol in Austin. A federal appeals court on Wednesday restored key parts of a 2021 Texas law governing mail-in voting and voter assistance. (AaronP/Bauer-Griffin/GC Images)

Republicans in Arizona, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin, Georgia, North Carolina and Michigan all lost control of at least one chamber of their state legislatures on Tuesday night.

"Those Republicans who lost on Nov. 3 did so because their actions (or inaction) didn’t match their promises to voters. We didn’t have that problem in South Dakota under our leadership," South Dakota's GOP House Majority Leader, Rep. Scott Odenbach, told Fox News Digital.

#6267. Singapore Airlines Unveils New Suites With Double Beds—Rollout Slips Again, And Many Planes Miss Out

First class is coming to the ultra-long-range Airbus A350s that operate the world’s longest flights. Business class gets doors, a different sleeping position, and more foot space. We’re not going to see the first aircraft with the new cabins until the second half of 2027, and several fleets won’t ever get these seats at all.

I flew to Singapore in November 2017 for the unveiling of their last new A380 business class and Suites. Nine years later, plenty of their aircraft still have an older product. And even the 380 itself didn’t finish installation until late 2023. Long haul A350 and Boeing 777 seats date to 2013. I flew to Seattle for delivery of the first 777 that had them.

Singapore’s new business class was designed with BMW’s Designworks and built by Recaro. It’s a bespoke seat, with a forward-facing, staggered 1-2-1 layout with doors and direct aisle access throughout. The biggest improvement is being able to adjust the seat continuously from upright to flat, choose a comfortable lounging position, and sleep without angling my body across the seat.

The A350 seat goes from 28 inches wide to 22 inches. On the wider Boeing 777-9, it’ll be 24 inches. So that’s a real tradeoff in seat width. Singapore’s old seat was exceptionally wide, but short and you had to angle your feet. A350 business class gets a 22-inch OLED screen, while the new 777-9 gets a smaller 20-inch screen without OLED.

The new first class, designed by PriestmanGoode and manufactured by Collins Aerospace, will have four seats on the ultra-long-range A350 and six on the 777-9.

The center pair can remain two independent suites or open into one shared space. Each passenger still has their own entrance, screen and table. Those seats can form a sofa for two or an 80-by-60-inch double bed. That’s the size of a standard U.S. queen mattress. Singapore calls it the largest double bed in commercial aviation. Individually, the beds measure 80 by 30 inches. The seats are 23 inches wide with the armrests raised.

Curved sliding doors, warm colors, Poltrona Frau leather and batik details make this look much more like Singapore Airlines than the new business cabin.

Companion dining is available at every first class seat, using the ottoman, which restores something missing from the current A380 Suites experience. The joined center suites can accommodate four people dining together.

Other features include a personal wardrobe, an illuminated vanity drawer, carry-on storage beneath the ottoman, wireless charging and a 32-inch 4K screen. Bang & Olufsen wireless headphones are supplied, and you can pair your own headphones. A small information panel shows flight details and lavatory availability without requiring you to turn on the main screen. Seat and lighting preferences can be saved for future flights.

This isn’t the A380’s separate armchair-and-bed concept. The chair becomes the bed. It’s a massive improvement over today’s 777 first class, while the A380 retains its current expansive Suites layout. There is only one center pair on each aircraft. Six first class seats on the 777-9 means four window singles and one potential double suite, not three double beds.

The announced program covers 41 existing A350s and Singapore’s 31 ordered Boeing 777-9s. Only the 777-9 gets all four new seat designs.

The A380, existing 777-300ER, medium-haul A350, 787-10 and 737-8 aren’t included in this seat program. Those aircraft keep their current cabin products under the announced plan. The A380 is separately getting Starlink.

The rollout has already slipped twice: the first refurbished long-haul A350 was originally due in the second quarter of 2026, then the first quarter of 2027. Now it’s the second half of 2027. The airline still targets the end of 2030 to complete the A350 retrofits.

Boeing’s delays explain why seats originally intended for the 777-9 are going onto A350s. But seat certification is also holding things up: the 777-9 seats have been certified, while the airplane hasn’t. The A350 seats still need certification. The ultra-long range A350 doesn’t have a firm separate debut date or announced launch route for its new first class.

The new premium economy seat offers 40 inches of pitch, up from 38, and nine inches of recline instead of eight. It’s 19 inches wide, in a 2-4-2 cabin, with adjustable leg and footrests.

777-9 economy cabin goes to 3-4-3 and 31 to 32 inches of pitch. It’s a wider cabin, but Singapore’s current 777-300ERs are 3-3-3. There are redesigned cushions, adjustable headrests and a revised recline mechanism intended to improve knee and shin clearance, plus 13-inch 4K screens, Bluetooth and USB-C.

Meanwhile, an A350 retrofit won’t bring these new premium economy or economy seats. Those cabins get refreshed upholstery and an updated entertainment interface, while keeping their existing seat hardware.

There will even be two hardware versions within the 777-9 fleet. Premium economy and economy on the first 12 aircraft get conventional 4K screens. The later 19 get OLED screens but lose USB-A. Economy also loses universal power outlets on those 19 aircraft, retaining USB-C. Premium economy keeps universal power. On those later jets, coach will have OLED while first and business won’t.

The early reaction is much warmer toward first class than business. In the FlyerTalk discussion folks like the larger bed, the return of companion dining and the ability to separate the middle pair into two proper suites. That’s a better arrangement for unrelated passengers than Lufthansa’s shared center suite. The business class thread is much rougher. Gray surfaces and bright yellow trim draw comparisons to Scoot, car interiors and a loss of Singapore’s warmth. Reddit reactions echo the complaints about generic styling and lost identity. Still, folks like the doors, storage and companion beds. Several Other Changes Arrive Before The Seats Singapore’s broader announcement bundles together upgrades with different schedules: Sleepwear and amenity kits. New kits begin rolling out this month on flights over six hours: Sisley in Suites and first, Byredo in business, INK & WATER in premium economy, and travel essentials in a batik pouch in economy. Business class gets pajamas for the first time, on all long-haul flights and selected overnight medium-haul flights over six hours. First class and Suites get new cotton sleepwear. Dining. The package includes more than 100 new or refreshed dishes, expanded drinks and Christofle serviceware in Suites, first and business. Lounge and ground-service improvements are also part of the broader investment. Entertainment and internet. The next KrisWorld system adds easier navigation, personalization, a wellness planner and more than 2,500 entertainment options, with hardware varying by cabin. Starlink begins rolling out from early 2027 on the A380 and long-haul and ultra-long-range A350s. The announced Starlink list doesn’t include the 777-9. The Biggest Commercial Change Is At The Back Of The Longest Flights The ultra-long-range A350 goes from 67 business and 94 premium economy seats to four first, 70 business and 58 premium economy. That’s 36 fewer premium economy seats or a 38% cut. Total passenger capacity falls from 161 to 132, or 18%. Singapore is replacing a substantial portion of its lowest-priced cabin on these aircraft with space it expects to sell for more. First class provides a new way to monetize the nonstop flights. Net net I expect this to mean tougher award space overall (certainly in premium economy). The early reaction is much warmer toward first class than business. In the FlyerTalk discussion folks like the larger bed, the return of companion dining and the ability to separate the middle pair into two proper suites. That’s a better arrangement for unrelated passengers than Lufthansa’s shared center suite.

The business class thread is much rougher. Gray surfaces and bright yellow trim draw comparisons to Scoot, car interiors and a loss of Singapore’s warmth. Reddit reactions echo the complaints about generic styling and lost identity. Still, folks like the doors, storage and companion beds.

Singapore’s broader announcement bundles together upgrades with different schedules: Sleepwear and amenity kits. New kits begin rolling out this month on flights over six hours: Sisley in Suites and first, Byredo in business, INK & WATER in premium economy, and travel essentials in a batik pouch in economy. Business class gets pajamas for the first time, on all long-haul flights and selected overnight medium-haul flights over six hours. First class and Suites get new cotton sleepwear. Dining. The package includes more than 100 new or refreshed dishes, expanded drinks and Christofle serviceware in Suites, first and business. Lounge and ground-service improvements are also part of the broader investment. Entertainment and internet. The next KrisWorld system adds easier navigation, personalization, a wellness planner and more than 2,500 entertainment options, with hardware varying by cabin. Starlink begins rolling out from early 2027 on the A380 and long-haul and ultra-long-range A350s. The announced Starlink list doesn’t include the 777-9. If you’re a frequent traveler, scoring elite status with a major carrier like Delta Air Lines can make your journeys more relaxing and rewarding.

However, deciding which airline loyalty program benefits you the most is difficult. This is mainly due to the variations between complimentary upgrades, bonus points or miles, lounge access and other valuable perks. Plus, is it even worth pursuing elite status?

This guide breaks down Delta’s SkyMiles Medallion program, including its four public elite status tiers, how to earn status in 2027 through both travel and non-travel expenses, and the benefits of each level.

Here is everything you need to know about elite Medallion status in the Delta SkyMiles program.

Delta awards elite status to qualifying SkyMiles members each year. Elite status offers a range of benefits — from seat selection to priority boarding — that make travel more comfortable and convenient.

The airline has four published tiers of elite status:

Delta also has an invite-only status tier called Delta 360. While the airline doesn't publish its standard qualification criteria, big spenders could get an invitation to this very special club. Delta also says, “Members that have reached the 5 Million Miler milestone will receive an annual complimentary invitation for Delta 360° Membership.” That's a pretty sweet perk.

Visit our Delta Medallion glossary page for more details.

Flyers earn Medallion status based on their eligible activity during the preceding calendar year. Delta tracks travelers' activity through Medallion Qualification Dollars, which they earn by flying with Delta and its partner airlines, spending on select Delta SkyMiles American Express cards and booking Delta Vacations packages.

For Delta-marketed flights operated by Delta or a partner airline, members generally earn 1 MQD for every dollar spent on the eligible ticket price (including the base fare and carrier-imposed surcharges but excluding government-imposed taxes and fees). For eligible partner-marketed flights, MQD earnings are generally based on a percentage of the distance flown and the purchased fare class, according to Delta's published partner earning charts.

Note: Delta Main Basic tickets generally don't earn MQDs or qualify for Medallion upgrades.

Related: Your guide to Delta Air Lines Million Miler status

You can also earn MQDs on eligible award tickets and through everyday spending on the Delta SkyMiles Platinum, Platinum Business, Reserve and Reserve Business American Express cards. All four cards offer an annual 2,500-MQD Headstart, while eligible spending earns 1 MQD per $20 on Platinum cards and 1 MQD per $10 on Reserve cards.

Your status is valid through Jan. 31 of the following year. For example, travelers who qualify in 2026 will earn 2027 Medallion status, which would be valid through Jan. 31, 2028.

You must meet the applicable Medallion Qualification Dollar thresholds each calendar year to maintain that status.

Delta used to have several ways to earn status, but now the carrier uses only MQDs as qualification criteria. Below are the requirements to obtain 2027 Medallion status:

Delta did not raise the status requirements for 2027 status.

Here are some key benefits of each of Delta’s status tiers.

This is the entry tier in Delta’s program, and you’ll receive benefits like:

Delta’s mid-tier status includes Silver Medallion benefits, plus:

In addition to the Gold Medallion perks, you’ll also get the following:

You’ll get everything detailed above, plus some even better perks:

Check Delta’s website to review the full list of benefits available to SkyMiles Medallion members.

To make it easier to earn elite status, Delta gives eligible frequent flyers who also hold the following cobranded cards a head start on MQD metrics with a boost of 2,500 MQDs (per eligible card type) toward status qualification at the start of the year (and each year thereafter, until further notice):

Since the MQD head start is awarded per eligible card type, you’ll enjoy more than one 2,500 MQD boost if you have multiple eligible cards. Additionally, you’ll be able to enjoy bonus MQDs based on everyday spending on these cards.

Specifically, the Delta SkyMiles Reserve Amex and the Delta SkyMiles Reserve Business Amex will accrue 1 MQD for every $10 spent. Meanwhile, the Delta SkyMiles Platinum Amex and the Delta SkyMiles Platinum Business Amex will accrue 1 MQD for every $20 spent.

Technically, you could earn Delta Medallion status without ever stepping on a plane, simply by putting enough eligible spending on a cobranded credit card. But that doesn't necessarily make it a good strategy,

Even with the MQD Headstart, reaching the higher status tiers through credit card spending alone requires a large financial commitment. Before putting everyday purchases on a Delta card to chase status, consider whether the rewards and benefits justify the cost, when there are lots of other travel credit cards that could offer better returns for you personally.

If you earned Delta elite status in 2025, it’s valid through Jan. 31, 2027. If you qualify in 2026, your status will last until Jan. 31, 2028.

It’s critical to consider how much you’ll be traveling in the future to decide if Medallion status is worth it. If you push hard to reach Diamond Medallion status, the valuable perks outlined above apply only when traveling.

With the high MQD requirements, you would need to spend a significant amount of money with the airline or on a cobranded card to earn this top-tier status. So, you should ensure you're traveling enough to enjoy it.

That said, if you wind up within striking distance of the next tier, consider whether the benefits are worth it for you personally. There’s no reason to go out of your way for perks that don’t matter to you. Pursuing elite status with an airline you can’t realistically fly regularly isn't a great move. Look at Delta’s offerings from your home airport and whether it would be feasible to rely on that airline.

This elite-status hobby has many trade-offs, and one of the most common is deciding whether to use your preferred airline or hotel chain when neither is the most convenient nor the cheapest. Would you book a one-stop Delta flight if Southwest Airlines had a cheaper, nonstop option? If the answer is no, it may not be worth going out of your way to earn Delta elite status (or any elite status, for that matter).

The final consideration involves travel rewards credit cards. Many airline cobranded cards offer perks that mirror what you’d enjoy as an elite member. For example, the includes a free checked bag worldwide and a second checked bag when flying domestic, priority boarding and a 20% inflight savings in the form of statement credit. The card has no annual fee for the first year, then a $150 annual fee (see rates and fees).

Meanwhile, when you fly with Delta, the Delta SkyMiles Reserve American Express Card provides 15 Sky Club lounge visits each year (Feb. 1 through Jan. 31). Cardmembers also qualify for various complimentary seat upgrades and receive an annual companion certificate (valid for round-trip domestic and short-haul international flights to Mexico, the Caribbean and Central America in economy, Delta Comfort, Delta Premium Select or first class). To earn unlimited Sky Club visits each year, the total eligible purchases on the card must equal $75,000 or more between Jan. 1 and Dec. 31 each calendar year.

If you can pay a flat annual fee for one of these cards and gain access to perks that matter to you without going out of your way to earn elite status, that may be a good plan.

Delta Medallion status can make flying more comfortable, particularly if you're a frequent Delta customer who can take advantage of all the perks. But the value of those perks really depends on how often you fly and how much you're willing to spend to earn them.

For most travelers, the goal shouldn't necessarily be "reach Diamond Medallion." Instead, focus on the status tier that offers benefits you'll actually use and avoid spending more or booking less convenient flights just to earn a higher level of status.

If you’re considering switching your loyalty, we hope this detailed review of Delta’s elite status program has helped you make your decision.

#6265. Denver Airport Taco Bell Worker Sues For Pay While Waiting At Security — And They May Win

A former Taco Bell food preparer at Denver International Airport is suing the restaurant’s operator for pay for time spent going through security and getting to the restaurant before clocking in. According to Law360, the Colorado state court lawsuit also alleges that hourly employees weren’t provided paid rest breaks. I’d normally be skeptical of a claim for pay while passing through an airport checkpoint. Government-required screening looks like part of getting to work. However, Colorado law is unique and more generous here than even California. This Wouldn’t Fly In California In January, I wrote about a Delta Sky Club worker at Los Angeles International Airport seeking pay for time spent going through TSA. A similar claim by an Admirals Club employee had already lost. In Cazares v. Host International, the Ninth Circuit upheld dismissal because the employee hadn’t alleged facts showing employer control during federally mandated screening. Federal law is also favorable to employers here. The Supreme Court’s Integrity Staffing Solutions v. Busk decision held that warehouse workers didn’t have to be paid for certain employer-required security searches. Simply requiring an activity doesn’t automatically make it paid work under federal law. Colorado Specifically Includes Security Screening As Work Colorado’s wage rules list “security or safety screening”, including waiting for it, among activities that can count as paid work. The state’s labor department explains that screening required to work for an employer can qualify “whether discretionary with the employer or legally required.” Its example is federally required radiation screening for nuclear plant guards. In Rael v. Q3 Contracting in 2024, a federal judge dismissed claims involving vehicle inspections and commuting under federal law, while allowing claims for that same time under Colorado law. The Taco Bell concessionaire’s best argument is that a shared airport checkpoint remains part of the commute: it serves aviation security generally, outside the restaurant’s premises and supervision. The worker’s answer is that this is a required screening to reach the assigned workplace, exactly the sort of activity Colorado treats as work. It’s not a frivolous theory the way it was for California airport lounge employees. Interestingly, the time security to the restaurant could count as work, too. Colorado generally excludes ordinary commuting and the initial trip to a workstation. However, its travel rule includes an exception once compensable work has begun. If the security checkpoint is work, then travel from that work location to the next one can be work, too. The state’s travel time guidance even discusses walking from an entrance to a workstation after paid activity starts. I’ve written plenty about the time it takes to get around Denver airport. So this could be a lot of time. My bet is that this dispute is more likely to produce a negotiated payment than a clean employer win based on who runs the checkpoint. But that’s just going to encourage more similar suits. Yeah, they are screened but the employee line is usually very short. Pilots and flight attendants, though, have “known crew member” status. At most airports, there’s an employee parking lot with a shuttle (as needed) to take them to the “front door” of the airport. At major hubs, the airlines usually have a SIDA required employee lot with a “secure” shuttle to drive them inside the SIDA, thus bypassing the TSA/KCM/employee line. In short, I don’t see how the employer should pay the worker until they clock in. The long TSA line is no different than a traffic jam or mass transit breakdown that slows the worker getting to…work! One leaves home at a time that would ensure that the worker arrives at work and on time. That is called “personal responsibility”. One does not get paid for lack of personal responsibility.

So, Dhedouville, your premise is that if an employee is late to work due to a traffic jam, blocked train crossing, overturned 18 wheeler, snow storm and the like or..OR… long TSA line, the employee should be paid. Did I get that right? So, Mr. Dhedouville, business owner, where do you draw the line on “late to work because…”? Obviously you have never owned a business before. Just, “Hey…show up when you can, OK? I’ll keep the doors locked until you get here. The customers will surely wait, don’t you think? I owned a very successful and honorable family business with 50 employees. Some were salaried. Some were “on the clock”. How should I regulate that? Our customers need their products delivered. That means if my “on the clock” warehouse and drivers show up whenever they can, how do I tell our customers, “We’ll deliver the items you need for your dinner service tomorrow…whenever we can.” You know the old adage, “Ignorance can be educated…stupid is forever.” Which one fits you?

@Win Whitmire — Two times on here you attempt to insert plausible deniability against the worker’s position, then decide to go off on @Jeffrey Dhedouville who simply said he hopes the worker ‘wins,’ but pre-supposed a bunch of nonsense onto him?

*wee woo wee woo* “PULL OVER! This is the false-equivalence police, again! You’re under arrest for making up a completely imaginary argument just so you can yell at it.” *weewoo*

Jeffrey literally wrote seven words, and you built a whole multi-paragraph fantasy novel about snowstorms and locked warehouse doors to call him stupid.

You think you’re teaching “personal responsibility,” but you’re just deep-frying your own brain over a Taco Bell worker wanting to get paid for time Colorado law explicitly says might be work.

If you want to drop tired old tropes and pick a fight, pick on someone who will actually fight you back, bruh. Cry harder.

#6264. British Airways $710 Million Tax Fight Could Leave Members With Less Valuable Points

British Airways’ parent has €638 million tied up in a fight over taxing Avios. The government wants 20% value added tax when the points are issued. For members, that creates a risk of fewer points for their spending, weaker bonuses or more expensive redemptions (even if the tax authority never sends them a bill). IAG’s November 6 financial results update a dispute with the British tax authority over how its loyalty business should have been taxed going back to March 2018. While IAG is the legal taxpayer, a tax on the business selling your rewards can reduce what those rewards deliver. And VAT is something ultimately passed onto the consumer but collected throughout the value chain. What Britain Wants To Tax IAG historically accounted for value added tax based on what members redeemed their Avios for. Most redemptions were flights attracting a zero rate. The tax authority’s position is that IAG Loyalty is being paid to develop, administer and maintain a loyalty program. On that interpretation, the issuance of Avios attracts 20% tax regardless of what the member eventually books. IAG’s more detailed half-year disclosure says its treatment relied on an earlier ruling from the same tax authority and existing case law. It’s challenging the assessment and whether the government can reverse that treatment retrospectively. And the November filing identifies two amounts: €516 million of historical payments, net of input-tax recoveries, recorded as an asset IAG expects to recover if it wins. €122 million of subsequent payments disclosed as a contingent asset. Some of these amounts reduce the revenue IAG ultimately recognizes from Avios. Together that’s €638 million (US$710 million). IAG expects a tax tribunal hearing during the remainder of 2026 and a decision in 2027. Members Can Pay Without Receiving A Tax Bill Suppose a bank buys Avios to give customers for using its credit card. If supplying those Avios becomes more expensive, several things can happen: IAG receives less after tax. Existing contracts may prevent it from immediately charging partners more, leaving shareholders with lower profits. The bank pays more. It can absorb that cost, buy fewer Avios, reduce earning or initial bonuses, raise card fees, or steer spending toward a different rewards product. The member gets less from the points. Changes to award prices, cash charges or redemption availability can lower the cost of honoring rewards—but also make the currency less attractive to collect. IAG’s disclosure flags payments it doesn’t consider recoverable from commercial partners. That leaves IAG holding those costs initially. But it forces a reevaluation prospectively of those agreements, or revaluing the points themselves. In other words taxing the creation of rewards makes it more expensive to offer the same rewards. So disappointed by the constant sane-washing, corporate shilling, and inserting of plays deniability to absolve these major multibillion dollar/pound megacorps from paying their fair share, in taxes and in wages, and actually operating reliably.

Consumers and workers should be saying ‘enough is enough’ and demand better. The UK already has a decent baseline, but even it can be improved; the US really needs to catch-up, fast. No more deceptive practices; no more excuses for lying, cheating, stealing. We’ve gone in the opposite direction over the past two years especially, but all that can and should change.

#6263. Dallas Wants More Gates At Love Field—And To Give Southwest Airlines A Bigger Monopoly

Dallas is opening the door to more gates at Love Field airport. Two things stand in the way. Federal law caps the airport at 20 gates, and Dallas has already negotiated a lease that would offer most of the additional gates to Southwest Airlines if the law were to change. Southwest already controls nearly all of the gates there. More room for adding Southwest flights is different than more competition for Southwest. Dallas needs a larger airport and to open itself to competition. The Dallas City Manager raised the prospect of additional gates at an aviation event last week. The airport is undergoing a $2.5 billion redevelopment that doesn’t include more gates. Former American Airlines Chairman and CEO Doug Parker defended the existing arrangement on this week’s Airlines Confidential podcast. His argument rests on the existing five-party agreement, federal law and investments made in reliance on both: “agreements are agreements.” That’s only why changing the rules will be difficult, not a reason to keep limits on competition forever. Why Dallas Can’t Just Build More Love Field Gates Southwest Airlines had to fight to operate from Dallas Love Field when it first launched. It flew its first flight in 1971 after being tied up in the courts. Existing airlines agreed to leave Love Field for DFW airport. Southwest wasn’t a party to that agreement. In 1979, the Wright Amendment was passed to limit competition from Southwest Airlines. Deregulation meant that Southwest could fy beyond the state of Texas, and other carriers feared that the close-in airport they operated from would be more desirable than DFW. The upstart Southwest that fought for the right to fly was mature and pivoted to using government to its own advantage by the time they succeeded in securing the Wright Amendment Reform Act of 2006. It was a compromise among Dallas, Fort Worth, DFW Airport, American Airlines and Southwest Airlines. Southwest gained the ability to sell connecting service beyond the old geographic limits, followed by nationwide domestic nonstop service in October 2014. Love Field’s gate count had to be reduced from 32 to 20. Southwest kept most of the gates. The airport couldn’t offer nonstop international passenger service. Basically Southwest got more flying from Love Field and a monopoly there, while American Airlines got a monopoly on international service from Dallas and a cap on how much service could compete from Love Field. Initially, Southwest effectively couldn’t even fly out of Dallas – Fort Worth offering direct competition with American. The five party agreement specified that any gate Southwest operates at DFW (or another airport within 80 miles) would require giving up a Love Field gate, up to 8 total gates. That restriction ended in 2025. The provision even covered affiliates and flights carrying Southwest’s code, with exceptions for existing DFW–Midway codeshare service. Southwest couldn’t even codeshare with partners who flew to DFW, and could set up a regional affiliate to operate there. Dallas Already Gate Southwest An Option On More Love Field Gates The city council approved Southwest’s October 1, 2028 – September 30, 2040 Love Field lease covering 18 of the existing 20 gates. One gate is under Delta’s control and the final gate is under city control and can (theoretically) be used for new service. Delta Air Lines Gate At Dallas Love Field Delta Air Lines Gate At Dallas Love Field The lease anticipates what happens with a change in federal law: Southwest and the airport both agree not to oppose an increase in gates at the airport. Dallas can then seek or support the effort. If the law changes, Dallas can pursue four, eight or twelve additional gates without the usual review by major incument airlines (‘majority-in-interest’ airline review, effectively Southwest) as long as each new gate won’t cost more than $50 million in 2025 dollars. Southwest receives an option on three of four, five of eight, or eight of twelve new gates. Even after changing a law that protects incumbents, Dallas would offer most new gates to its dominant airline. Parker Explains Why American Would Fight This Parker attributed two percentage points of Delta’s margin advantage, in an internal analysis from his American tenure, to Atlanta’s lack of a competing airport like Love Field or Midway. American has a lot to lose if some Dallas travelers gain better alternatives to DFW. Parker acknowledges his bias. American has made enormous investments at DFW, and predictable rules matter when financing airports. But I’d note: The agreement is more than 20 years old. Investors who bet on government keeping out competition also take the risk that the government changes its mind. Twenty years of protection is a substantial benefit, not a guarantee of protection in perpetuity. American hsa benefited from other subsidies, too. Parker was a prime mover behind American’s receipt of $12.8 billion in pandemic payroll support, the vast majority of the second and third tranches displacing payroll the airline was going to pay anyway. American chose not to fly from Love Field. American ended service in 2009 and subleased its gates to Delta. Its later merger settlement required divestiture of the gates, but American had already stopped operating. American preferred concentrating its network at DFW but that shouldn’t give them a permanent veto over competitors serving a different airport. The Government Destroyed Gates To Make This Deal Work Parker correctly recalls the demolition of six gates at the former Legend Airlines terminal. The overall reduction was twelve gates from 32 to 20. Six of those were at the separate Lemmon Avenue facility. I covered the litigation over that terminal and its leases. The Court of Federal Claims awarded the owners $133.5 million when the city took it back through eminent domain. The Federal Circuit reversed in 2018 arguing that the fact the gates couldn’t legally be used meant it had no value. It might soon have had value. The terminal was turned into a Lincoln dealership. North Texas Has Outgrown This Bargain DFW is growing. Its new Terminal F is planned for 31 gates, all serving American, with the first 15 expected to open in 2027. Meanwhile, McKinney is preparing to launch scheduled commercial service on November 11. Different parts of the Metroplex support different airport choices. DFW, Love Field and McKinney aren’t interchangeable for a passenger near downtown Dallas. Noise and road access are real though anyone living near the airport knew there was an airport there. Additional gate construction would necessarily involve an operational, environmental and access plan. American Airlines certainly didn’t walk away from the Naples, Florida airport just because residents there don’t like commercial air service! Love Field should be allowed to grow. The additional preferential gates should be open to airlines that bring new competition, rather than committing ex ante to enlarging Southwest’s existing control. These lease commitment is an impediment to that, and actually gives American Airlines its strongest argument against expansion. Southwest built its business by fighting attempts to keep it out. American chose to leave Love Field. Neither of those things justifies keeping other competitors out of the Dallas market, or serving each of the local markets in North Texas separately. The Court of Federal Claims awarded the owners $133.5 million when the city took it back through eminent domain. The Federal Circuit reversed in 2018 arguing that the fact the gates couldn’t legally be used meant it had no value. It might soon have had value. The terminal was turned into a Lincoln dealership. North Texas Has Outgrown This Bargain DFW is growing. Its new Terminal F is planned for 31 gates, all serving American, with the first 15 expected to open in 2027. Meanwhile, McKinney is preparing to launch scheduled commercial service on November 11. Different parts of the Metroplex support different airport choices. DFW, Love Field and McKinney aren’t interchangeable for a passenger near downtown Dallas. Noise and road access are real though anyone living near the airport knew there was an airport there. Additional gate construction would necessarily involve an operational, environmental and access plan. American Airlines certainly didn’t walk away from the Naples, Florida airport just because residents there don’t like commercial air service! Love Field should be allowed to grow. The additional preferential gates should be open to airlines that bring new competition, rather than committing ex ante to enlarging Southwest’s existing control. These lease commitment is an impediment to that, and actually gives American Airlines its strongest argument against expansion. Southwest built its business by fighting attempts to keep it out. American chose to leave Love Field. Neither of those things justifies keeping other competitors out of the Dallas market, or serving each of the local markets in North Texas separately. Parker attributed two percentage points of Delta’s margin advantage, in an internal analysis from his American tenure, to Atlanta’s lack of a competing airport like Love Field or Midway.

American has a lot to lose if some Dallas travelers gain better alternatives to DFW. Parker acknowledges his bias. American has made enormous investments at DFW, and predictable rules matter when financing airports. But I’d note:

The agreement is more than 20 years old. Investors who bet on government keeping out competition also take the risk that the government changes its mind. Twenty years of protection is a substantial benefit, not a guarantee of protection in perpetuity. American hsa benefited from other subsidies, too. Parker was a prime mover behind American’s receipt of $12.8 billion in pandemic payroll support, the vast majority of the second and third tranches displacing payroll the airline was going to pay anyway. American chose not to fly from Love Field. American ended service in 2009 and subleased its gates to Delta. Its later merger settlement required divestiture of the gates, but American had already stopped operating.

American preferred concentrating its network at DFW but that shouldn’t give them a permanent veto over competitors serving a different airport.

#6262. U.S. Airlines Face New Collusion Lawsuits-Sharing Data To Keep Ticket Prices High

Airfares rose 22.4% over the past year, according to the government’s September inflation report. And American Airlines, Delta, United other major carriers are accused of using shared airfare and customer shopping data to keep ticket prices high. Two new class action lawsuits say the airlines have built a way to spot competitors’ discounts and discourage the price cutting that could save passengers money. There’s a plausible antitrust claim here. There’s also a straightforward explanation for much of the same activity: airlines need to know when they’re charging more than competitors so they can lower their prices. The kind of information sharing that’s happening does not – on its own – amount to a legal violation. I just wrote about former American Airlines CEO Doug Parker explaining how airlines use Wall Street analysts to pressure competitors to stop growing, even while denying that executives signal each other. These lawsuits raise a related question about the systems pricing departments use every day: whether airlines have agreed to share information in a way that helps them avoid competing. Cory Garner flags two new complaints: Ward v. ATPCO, filed in federal court in Seattle, and Brown v. ATPCO, filed in Virginia. Between them, they name American Airlines, Delta Air Lines, United Airlines, Southwest Airlines, Alaska, Hawaiian and JetBlue, along with the Airline Tariff Publishing Company and its 3Victors subsidiary. ATPCO is owned by airlines and has long distributed fares and fare rules. These cases target its newer shopping data business. Airlines increasingly generate offers that vary by channel, itinerary, bundle and customer. Those offers can be harder for competitors to observe than a published fare. Iris collects shopping data. Airlines and other participants contribute information and receive competitive information in return. PriceEye makes offers easier to compare. It supplies competitive data and alerts that draw attention to differences in pricing. DemandView identifies demand before it becomes bookings. Search activity can show where customers want to travel even when they haven’t bought tickets. 3Victors describes the information exchange as “the more you contribute, the more you receive.” And it says Iris collects all the offers returned by a shopping request, including different brands, cabins and prices which is more than an airline would get scraping a limited website search result. The lawsuits argue this gives competitors visibility into competitor pricing they wouldn’t otherwise have, including for offers that haven’t resulted in sales. An airline that might discount to fill seats instead knows rivals can quickly discover and respond to the offer, so they do not make it. If an airline expects every price cut to be matched almost immediately, it may see less opportunity to win business by cutting in the first place. The same information can make tickets cheaper. If an airline is selling a flight for $100 more than a competitor, getting an alert that they’re being underpriced lets them adjust their fares to avoid losing a sale. And better demand information can support an extra flight or a larger aircraft, adding seat supply which supports lower fares. As I’ve explained when American, United and Southwest all showed the same $523 fare, independently responding to a rival’s price isn’t an antitrust violation. Similar prices aren’t enough to establish an agreement. An airline can generally observe a publicly available price and decide to match it. Competitors agreeing to keep prices above a certain level is price fixing. An agreement to exchange sensitive information that makes competition less vigorous is somewhere in beteween – it’s alleged here that the agreement violates the Sherman Act by unreasonably restraining competition. The lawsuit itself doesn’t establish that happens – they need to get to the discovery stage and come up with something juicy. In United States v. Container Corp., the Supreme Court found reciprocal exchange of recent customer-specific prices even without an agreement to adhere to a price schedule to violate the law. On the other hand, the Court also recognized that information exchanges can improve competition. Garner points out that the old government case against ATPCO involved airlines circulating proposed fares before customers could buy them. Airlines could see whether competitors would go along with an increase before exposing themselves to losing sales. PriceEye’s ability to show current offers for future flights isn’t the same thing. A price you can buy today for travel next June isn’t advance notice of a planned price increase. I’m skeptical that what the airlines are doing here actually breaks the law. At a minimum, their defenses are pretty good. A faster, more reliable way to observe bookable fares can help airlines compete. These systems don’t make pricing decisions. There’s no common agent fixing fares. Higher fares alone don’t show this system caused them. Fuel prices and resulting capacity discipline have mattered a lot. Meanwhile, airfares have actually been falling in inflation adjusted terms and even with the recent run-up are lower than they were pre-pandemic. Assuming the cases make it through to discovery, actual contracts airlines signed and feeds will show agreements and the real data being shared, as well as how the services are marketed and discussed at the airlines. If the case goes very far, I’d imagine we’d see a settlement involving money and tighter limits on data sharing to avoid triple damages plus fees. Belinda Luksic is an Australian travel journalist with words published across the globe, including in Conde Nast Traveler, Travel + Leisure Asia and Robb Report. Her work has taken her to all seven continents and both poles, where she has swum with whale sharks in Ningaloo Reef, plunged into the icy waters of the North Pole, eaten crickets in Siem Reap, hiked ancient trails in Bhutan and cycled the Balkans solo. There’s now a new reason to travel to the bottom of the world.

Silversea on Thursday officially opened The Cormorant at 55 South, a new luxury hotel near the southern tip of South America designed to transform the experience of traveling to Antarctica.

Located in Chile's Patagonia region near Puerto Williams, the world's southernmost settlement, the 150-room property will serve as a luxury base and launch pad for Silversea's high-end fly-cruise trips to Antarctica — journeys that begin with a flight from Puerto Williams to a research station at Antarctica's King George Island.

Once there, travelers board a Silversea expedition ship to explore Antarctica.

Related: How to get to Antarctica: The pros and cons of flying vs. cruising

“Silversea has always been about going further, and for our guests heading to Antarctica, that journey now begins here at the southernmost hotel on Earth, with the kind of welcome they’ve come to expect from us,” Silversea president Bert Hernandez said during an unveiling event at the hotel.

TPG is one of just a handful of travel media outlets getting an early look at the property this week.

Until now, Silversea's fly-cruise passengers have stayed in non-Silversea hotels in Punta Arenas, Chile ahead of a charter flight to King George Island. The less-than-ideal arrangement meant guests were booked across various hotels, while the line was left scrambling for additional rooms whenever bad weather delayed or grounded flights to Antarctica.

Now, with The Cormorant at 55 South, guests can relax in modern luxury overnight — or sit out bad weather — just minutes from their charter flight. Better yet, the expedition begins well before they step aboard their ship.

While at the hotel, guests will be able to try on or swap their Silversea-provided Antarctica polar gear, complete biosecurity checks that are necessary before visiting the continent, and clean any personal equipment they plan to take ashore, as well as attend an initial Antarctica briefing — activities that usually take place on the ship.

Related: I just camped on the ice in Antarctica; here's how you can, too

They'll also get a chance to explore Patagonia’s breathtaking wilderness on guided excursions around the hotel, including kayaking, hiking, birdwatching and horseback riding. A shuttle bus will also take guests into Puerto Williams.

“The idea was that this wasn’t a stopover hotel. This is the first and last impression that we make on our guests, and so we wanted that to be memorable,” Hernandez said at a press conference ahead of an official ribbon-cutting ceremony.

Initially conceived in 2018 as a turnaround hub for Antarctica, the Cormorant at 55 South has become a destination that by Hernandez’s own admission is “more beautiful than anyone ever envisioned."

Designed to blend in with the environment, the low-slung hotel features soaring ceilings, concrete floors, natural wood, stone and earthy textiles punctuated by pops of orange, yellow and green — colours that echo the surrounding terrain.

Floor-to-ceiling glass means the view is never far away, be it forest, sea or snow-scratched mountains, stretching from the jagged peaks of Dientes de Navarino to the Andes in Argentina.

Related: The best Antarctica cruise vessels

“It was always incredibly important that the hotel reflect the environment,” Silversea senior vice president of expeditions Conrad Combrink said during unveiling events. Elements of fire and ice inform the design, alongside the darkness of the Drake Passage and the Beagle Channel, just beyond the hotel.

Being in the “land of fire”, the hotel fittingly has a massive indoor firepit, surrounded by lounges and easy chairs. An outside terrace offers more places to sit and take in the scenery.

Rooms are simply designed, with a view of mountain or sea, and pair a soothing mix of local wood, natural textiles and green upholstery. There’s a Nespresso machine and a small bar fridge with water and craft beer from a brewery in Punta Arenas.

Latitude 55, the onsite restaurant, showcases regional flavors, including excellent empanadas and a stand-out asado barbecue served on the first night of any stay, slow-cooked over an open fire in the hotel grounds.. At Bar Sur, guests can sample Chilean wine, enjoy a pisco sour tasting or try a cocktail made with calafete, a berry indigenous to Puerto Williams. The Uncharted Boutique is the place to stock up on beautifully made Chilean handicrafts or last-minute polar gear.

More than a hotel stay, The Cormorant at 55 South marks a wider shift for Silversea,which will now base all its Antarctica expeditions out of Puerto Williams. Previously only sailings that crossed the Drake Passage left from Puerto Williams.

While most Antarctic operators base their fleets out of Ushuaia, Argentina, Silversea is the only cruise line running operations out of Puerto Williams. Located further south along the Beagle Channel, Puerto Williams provides a shorter, more direct launch point into the Drake Passage.

Silversea's fly-cruise trips allow Antarctica-bound travelers to skip a ship-based voyage across the Drake Passage — the notoriously rough, 600-mile-wide waterway separating the tip of South America and Antarctica.

Guests fly from Santiago directly to Puerto Williams for an overnight stay at The Cormorant, before taking a charter flight across the Drake to King George Island in Antarctica's South Shetland Islands, where their expedition ship awaits. Upon return, guests spend another night at the hotel before flying back to Santiago.

Related: The ultimate guide to expedition cruising to Antarctica and beyond

The opening of the Cormorant at 55 South coincides with Silversea's largest Antarctic season to date. Fly-cruise itineraries now dominate the line’s offerings in Antarctica, accounting for 29 of its 40 total sailings across three expedition vessels: Silver Endeavour, Silver Wind, and Silver Cloud. The hotel will currently stay open from October through March, but there is talk it will open year-round, for travelers to southern Chile looking for a soft landing after adventures.

More than a place to stay,  The Cormorant makes the journey south feel like an experience in its own right — a fittingly rugged starting point for what lies ahead, plus unique bragging rights of having stayed at the southernmost hotel on earth.

#6257. U.S. Now Requires Ebola Attestation For Flights From Abroad — How To Complete It And Who Can Be Denied Boarding

Flying to the U.S. from abroad now requires an Ebola attestation. You have to confirm that you haven’t been in the Democratic Republic of the Congo during the previous 21 days before boarding your flight even if you’ve never been anywhere near Africa. An internal American Airlines memo explains how they’re collecting it, including what happens when a kiosk sends you to your phone and what to do if you can’t use the app. For most passengers, this is another check-in step. For someone who’s recently been to Congo, it can mean being unable to board a flight home even with a U.S. passport. Who Has To Complete An Ebola Attestation? The federal requirement took effect for flights departing for the United States at or after 11:59 p.m. Eastern Standard Time on November 3, 2026. It applies across airlines, including foreign airlines. You provide a declaration about recent travel history. That’s it – there’s no Ebola test or vaccination certificate. U.S. citizens, foreign visitors and green card holders are covered. Passengers merely connecting through the United States are covered, too. Departures from airports with U.S. immigration preclearance still count. Domestic flights aren’t covered. U.S. territories aren’t foreign countries under this rule, so a nonstop flight from Puerto Rico to the mainland doesn’t trigger it. The form requires an attestation for each individual, including children. A parent or another authorized representative can complete it for a child or someone unable to do it themselves. The current order runs through 11:59 p.m. Eastern Standard Time on December 18, 2026. The March 31, 2027 date printed on the form is the expiration of its paperwork approval, not the scheduled end of the travel requirement. How To Complete It On American Airlines American’s October 30 internal advisory lays out the airport procedures. Use the app or aa.com during check-in. The app requires you to complete the attestation before you can finish checking in. Once submitted, American adds a completion marker to your reservation. Don’t expect the kiosk to collect it. American says kiosks don’t support attestation collection. They’ll display a QR code directing you to the mobile app, and you’ll need to finish the attestation before completing kiosk check-in. No working phone? Ask for paper. American allows passengers to bring a completed paper form or request one at the airport. You can download the official fillable form here. An agent can also record a verbal attestation. You must first review the attestation wording. The agent then asks you to confirm your travel history and records that you reviewed the language and attested. Both American’s memo and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s instructions permit this. For paper, enter the name, select the appropriate option for yourself or someone you’re authorized to represent, and sign and date it. Read both pages and give the completed form to the airline. American must retain completed paper attestations for 42 days. If the app won’t let you proceed, ask an agent to check whether the attestation is recorded. American calls the completion marker ADOC. Ideally complete this before heading to the airport. If the technology fails, ask for the paper form. If You’ve Been To Congo, The Form Can Stop Your Trip The question is whether you’ve been physically present in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, not whether you feel healthy or believe you were exposed. Even a connection at a Congolese airport counts, including a stop where you stayed on the aircraft. The State Department confirms that U.S. citizens are also barred from boarding commercial flights to the United States during the waiting period. Limited government exemptions exist, including authorized medical transport and limited humanitarian cases. The calendar calculation is easy to mess up: Day 0: The day you leave Congo. Days 1–21: The full calendar days you remain outside the country. Day 22: The first day you can board a flight to the United States, assuming you meet other entry requirements. Leave Congo on November 1, for instance, and the first eligible boarding date is November 23. The CDC illustrates the waiting period this way: Uganda and South Sudan have separate rules. Under the current entry restrictions, non-U.S. citizens and non-U.S. nationals, including green card holders, who’ve recently been in either country must also wait outside the United States. U.S. citizens and nationals who’ve been there, but not Congo, can return through New York JFK, Washington Dulles or Atlanta for public health screening. Airport connections count for these rules as well. How Serious Is The Ebola Outbreak? The CDC’s November 3 update, reporting data through November 1 lists 10,563 confirmed cases and 5,130 confirmed deaths almost all in Congo which is the second-largest Ebola outbreak recorded. Outbreak Cases Deaths 2014–2016 West Africa epidemic About 28,600 reported About 11,300 2018–2020 Congo outbreak 3,470 reported 2,287 2026 outbreak, through November 1 10,563 confirmed 5,130 confirmed he current outbreak also passed 1,000 confirmed cases within 40 days of response activation; the 2018 outbreak took about 235 days. Conflict, weak health services and difficulty tracing contacts have helped it spread. Kenya and Nigeria reported imported cases in October. Ebola is extremely serious if you become infected, but the risk of becoming infected is low. The CDC reports no U.S. cases associated with this outbreak and considers introduction into the United States very unlikely. (But they aren’t always right about these things…) Ebola spreads through infected blood and other body fluids. It’s not airborne and it isn’t believed to spread by pre-symptomatic people. Taking a flight with someone exposed to Ebola isn’t going to get you sick. You need exposure to their fluids. Then illness can progress from fever, aches and fatigue to severe vomiting, diarrhea, dehydration and organ failure. The outbreak’s reported fatality rate has been around half (but probably overstates things because those dying of Ebola wind up as identified cases, while many who don’t die likely to do not). When 2021 Ebola travel restrictions were put in place, there were approved vaccines and antibody treatments. Those were for the Zaire type of Ebola while this is caused by Bundibugyo virus, for which there’s no approved vaccine or specific treatment. How Much Will The Attestation Help? Ebola can take up to 21 days to cause symptoms. Someone can be infected, feel well and pass a temperature check while still incubating the disease. Waiting after leaving the outbreak country gives that infection time to become apparent before a U.S. flight. During the earlier epidemic, about 38,000 travelers received enhanced assessments at U.S. ports of entry. One was later diagnosed with Ebola who had no symptoms when he arrived and reported his illness afterward. A declaration’s effectiveness depends on truthful reporting. Requiring three weeks of extra time outside the United States creates an incentive for untruthful reporting. What To Do If You’re Restricted From Flying If you’re barred because of recent travel to an affected country, the Transportation Department’s October 28 enforcement notice preserves passenger protections: For a communicable-disease travel refusal, the passenger can choose qualifying rebooking within 90 days without penalty at the original applicable fare, or a refund for unused flights. A required significant itinerary change, such as rerouting for health screening, triggers a refund if you decline the changed trip. The separate public health travel restriction rules provide transferable credits valid for at least five years. You select the applicable refund or credit remedy, rather than collect both. If you’re refused travel on this basis, get it in writing. The airline must provide that explanation within 10 days of your request. Requiring three weeks of extra time outside the United States creates an incentive for untruthful reporting. What To Do If You’re Restricted From Flying If you’re barred because of recent travel to an affected country, the Transportation Department’s October 28 enforcement notice preserves passenger protections: For a communicable-disease travel refusal, the passenger can choose qualifying rebooking within 90 days without penalty at the original applicable fare, or a refund for unused flights. A required significant itinerary change, such as rerouting for health screening, triggers a refund if you decline the changed trip. The separate public health travel restriction rules provide transferable credits valid for at least five years. You select the applicable refund or credit remedy, rather than collect both. If you’re refused travel on this basis, get it in writing. The airline must provide that explanation within 10 days of your request. Leave Congo on November 1, for instance, and the first eligible boarding date is November 23. The CDC illustrates the waiting period this way:

Uganda and South Sudan have separate rules. Under the current entry restrictions, non-U.S. citizens and non-U.S. nationals, including green card holders, who’ve recently been in either country must also wait outside the United States. U.S. citizens and nationals who’ve been there, but not Congo, can return through New York JFK, Washington Dulles or Atlanta for public health screening. Airport connections count for these rules as well.

The CDC’s November 3 update, reporting data through November 1 lists 10,563 confirmed cases and 5,130 confirmed deaths almost all in Congo which is the second-largest Ebola outbreak recorded. Outbreak Cases Deaths 2014–2016 West Africa epidemic About 28,600 reported About 11,300 2018–2020 Congo outbreak 3,470 reported 2,287 2026 outbreak, through November 1 10,563 confirmed 5,130 confirmed he current outbreak also passed 1,000 confirmed cases within 40 days of response activation; the 2018 outbreak took about 235 days. Conflict, weak health services and difficulty tracing contacts have helped it spread. Kenya and Nigeria reported imported cases in October. Ebola is extremely serious if you become infected, but the risk of becoming infected is low. The CDC reports no U.S. cases associated with this outbreak and considers introduction into the United States very unlikely. (But they aren’t always right about these things…) Ebola spreads through infected blood and other body fluids. It’s not airborne and it isn’t believed to spread by pre-symptomatic people. Taking a flight with someone exposed to Ebola isn’t going to get you sick. You need exposure to their fluids. Then illness can progress from fever, aches and fatigue to severe vomiting, diarrhea, dehydration and organ failure. The outbreak’s reported fatality rate has been around half (but probably overstates things because those dying of Ebola wind up as identified cases, while many who don’t die likely to do not). When 2021 Ebola travel restrictions were put in place, there were approved vaccines and antibody treatments. Those were for the Zaire type of Ebola while this is caused by Bundibugyo virus, for which there’s no approved vaccine or specific treatment. How Much Will The Attestation Help? Ebola can take up to 21 days to cause symptoms. Someone can be infected, feel well and pass a temperature check while still incubating the disease. Waiting after leaving the outbreak country gives that infection time to become apparent before a U.S. flight. During the earlier epidemic, about 38,000 travelers received enhanced assessments at U.S. ports of entry. One was later diagnosed with Ebola who had no symptoms when he arrived and reported his illness afterward. A declaration’s effectiveness depends on truthful reporting. Requiring three weeks of extra time outside the United States creates an incentive for untruthful reporting. What To Do If You’re Restricted From Flying If you’re barred because of recent travel to an affected country, the Transportation Department’s October 28 enforcement notice preserves passenger protections: For a communicable-disease travel refusal, the passenger can choose qualifying rebooking within 90 days without penalty at the original applicable fare, or a refund for unused flights. A required significant itinerary change, such as rerouting for health screening, triggers a refund if you decline the changed trip. The separate public health travel restriction rules provide transferable credits valid for at least five years. You select the applicable refund or credit remedy, rather than collect both. If you’re refused travel on this basis, get it in writing. The airline must provide that explanation within 10 days of your request. #6256. Democrat who toppled GOP incumbent will head to court on felony charge just days after election upset

Republican strategist Barak Lurie and radio host Mark Davis join ‘The Will Cain Show’ to analyze Democrats’ sweeping midterm victories, including James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa’s wins in Texas. The panel also examines Democrats taking control of Congress, Hakeem Jeffries’ bid for House speaker and what the election results signal for Republicans moving forward.

Just one week after pulling off a surprise victory over incumbent Republican Rep. Tim Moore in North Carolina’s 14th Congressional District race, Democrat LaKesha Womack is set to appear in court on a pending felony charge.

Womack secured 51.1% of the vote in the House race, while Moore received 48.9%, according to election results reported by The Associated Press.

The Mecklenburg County Sheriff’s Office previously confirmed to Fox News Digital that Womack had been served a criminal summons on Oct. 11 by a deputy with the Polk County Sheriff’s Office on a pending felony charge alleging she failed to return a rental vehicle valued at $20,000 in 2019.

The criminal summons was issued in January 2020 but not served until 2026, according to WBTV. Womack is set to appear in court on Nov. 10, The New York Post reported Thursday.

REDISTRICTING EFFORTS BLOW UP IN REPUBLICANS' FACES AMID HISTORIC HOUSE LOSSES

LaKesha Womack is running for Congress in North Carolina's 14th congressional district, challenging incumbent Rep. Tim Moore, R-N.C. (LaKesha Womack campaign)

Womack previously acknowledged failing to return the rental car on time, saying she was experiencing homelessness at the time and was unaware that a criminal case had been filed against her.

"This historic victory is bigger than me. It is a testament to the power of ordinary people who believe that their voices matter and that leadership should be rooted in service, accountability, and opportunity for all," Womack told Fox News Digital in a statement on Friday. "As a Black woman, a single mother, an entrepreneur, and someone who has spent more than two decades helping communities grow, I understand both the challenges people face and the possibilities we can create together."

Representative Tim Moore, a Republican from North Carolina, at the National Guard Armory polling location during the North Carolina primary election in Gastonia, North Carolina, US, on Tuesday, March 3, 2026. (Cornell Watson/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

DEMOCRATS SEIZE HOUSE CONTROL IN STUNNING BLUE TSUNAMI, VOW RETRIBUTION AGAINST TRUMP ADMIN

"We didn't just make history in North Carolina's 14th Congressional District; we opened the door for a new generation of leaders who listen, learn, and lead for the people," she continued.

When asked about facing the felony charge on Friday, Womack declined to comment to Fox News Digital.

Under North Carolina law, the charge is a Class H felony that can carry a prison sentence exceeding two years, depending on the defendant's criminal history and other sentencing factors.

Under House rules, members formally charged with a felony punishable by two or more years in prison are expected to step aside from committee assignments and party leadership positions while the charges remain pending, a provision that could become relevant to Womack once she takes office in January.

Rep. Tim Moore, R-N.C., leaves a meeting of the House Republican Conference at the Capitol Hill Club on Tuesday, March 17, 2026. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

Moore's campaign did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

"My opponent needs to explain these pending felony charges to the voters of North Carolina District 14," Moore wrote in an Oct. 28 post on X. "With a court date literally the week after the election this is a big deal."

#6254. New Federal Reserve Research Finds Cutting Merchant Swipe Fees Even Hurts Consumers Who Don’t Earn Rewards

You can earn no miles, no points and no cash back from your credit card and still lose if the government cuts credit card merchant swipe fees. Research from two Philadelphia Federal Reserve economists explains why: the money banks collect when you spend helps pay for better borrowing terms. That’s a problem for the retailers’ argument that consumers who don’t collect rewards are simply paying for everyone else’s vacations. I wrote this week about why the legislation threatening card rewards isn’t dead, even with Dick Durbin retiring and Roger Marshall losing his Senate seat. The political sales pitch is that reducing merchants’ payment costs saves consumers money. That isn’t true and has never been true anywhere in the world it’s been tried. It’s cover for retailers who want the benefits of accepting credit cards, but think the government should require the service be offered to them for less money. But credit cards aren’t just a convenient way to make purchases. They also provide financing for those purchases, and the merchant fee helps support that. Even A Card With No Rewards Can Give Something Back Satyajit Chatterjee and Burcu Eyigungor’s Credit Effects of Credit Card Interchange Fees uses bank supervisory data to examine an overlooked part of the debate: what interchange does to credit itself. The June 26 paper was highlighted in a new Bank of Japan summary. In the data, rewards cards have higher credit limits. Cards without rewards have lower interest rates despite higher default rates. They argue that rewards make repayment more attractive because default means losing access to future rewards. And when a bank keeps interchange instead of paying rewards, competition encourages it to offer better rates and limits to attract the customer’s business. They find that both rewards and non-rewards cardholders gain, even after accounting for higher retail prices. A bank earning money when that person buys groceries has another reason to want the account. Eliminate that revenue and the account becomes less attractive at the same borrowing terms. The adjustment could show up in the interest rate, credit limit or card approvals. Limiting interchange hurts access to credit and credit costs for the most vulnerable> Most Cards Earn Rewards—And Most Interchange Already Goes Back Out Rewards aren’t confined to a small group of people flying first class. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau’s latest market report says that in 2024: 80% of general purpose credit card accounts offered rewards. 92% of spending on those cards was on rewards accounts. And a separate New York Fed study finds that banks receive interchange averaging 1.82% of purchase volume and incur rewards costs averaging 1.57%. That’s about 86% of issuer interchange revenue going back out as rewards expense. Limits on credit card swipe fees actually redistribute from consumers to merchants, even as proponents seek to villify the banks. Points Aren’t The Whole Reason To Use Credit Instead Of Debit If an airline takes your money and doesn’t provide the flight, the card you used matters. So does whether a fraudulent charge has already emptied your checking account while everyone sorts out what happened. Credit cards come with federal billing dispute rights, including for purchases that weren’t delivered as agreed. With a billing error dispute, you can withhold the disputed amount during the investigation. Debit cards have fraud protections, too. But the money can already be gone from your account. Having a claim for reimbursement isn’t the same as keeping your cash available for rent while the claim gets resolved. Then there are the benefits particular cards add: purchase protection against theft or damage, extended warranties, return protection, rental-car coverage and insurance for covered travel disruptions. Interchange helps fund the card’s economics: rewards, fraud losses, dispute handling and benefits. Cutting interchange doesn’t repeal federal consumer protections athough those were imposed on an economic model that included them. And it an change what banks charge for the product, which optional benefits they offer and which customers they want. #6249. Airline Lobby Chief Says Up To 99% Of Flyers Are Happy—His Own Survey Disagrees

The head of the U.S. airline lobby says 98% to 99% of passengers are “very happy.” His own organization’s survey says 72% are satisfied (28% aren’t!) and just 31% are very satisfied. It’s good to know that most people are satisfied with flying, although the sameness of business models especially in the domestic market and variable wait times at airports, long walks through terminals, and air traffic control delays are frustrating and we’re making relatively little progress. Air travel is largely safe and affordable. Chris Sununu, the former New Hampshire governor who now leads Airlines for America, made the 99% claim on this week’s Airlines Confidential podcast. He was arguing against a return to economic regulation and saying the industry needs to do a better job telling its success story. With Democrats retaking Congress, airline re-regulatoin becomes a target for Senators like Elizabeth Warren. Here’s What The Airline Lobby’s Research Found Airlines for America commissioned Ipsos to conduct its latest annual air-traveler survey. Overall in 2025: 31% were very satisfied. 41% were somewhat satisfied. 16% were neutral. 9% were somewhat dissatisfied. 3% were very dissatisfied. That’s 72% satisfied, up from 69% in the prior year (which is flat). 28% aren’t at least somewhat satisfied. Getting Someone There Isn’t The Same As Making Them Happy A passenger can reach their destination and still have spent hours dealing with flight changes, seat assignments, or cancellations and waiting in line to check bags. People are more happy when flights operate on-time. They’re happier when the middle seat next to them is empty. They’re happy when the employees they interact with seem not to hate their jobs. Airlines are now trying to get passengers to spend more for their product, move their loyalty and put the airline’s credit card at the top of their wallet. Delivering on-time transportation is baseline – necessary, but not sufficient. The Industry Has A Better Argument Available Sununu is right to reject a return to government deciding which airlines can fly which routes and what they can charge. Customer complaints aren’t a reason to restore that system. We need competition, fewer barriers to entry into the industry for new carriers and more innovative business models and aircraft. The airline industry has been subsidized, and it’s largely sclerotic. More regulation would make that worse – but simply denying that air travel could be better – that ‘99%’ of consumers are happy – isn’t the right case to be making.
