#6201. Tom Petty and The Who box sets reveal two sides of rock history

Two great box sets being released for the holiday season from Tom Petty & the Heartbreakers and The Who showcase different approaches to exploring an artistâs back catalog with strong results on both sides. âOrigins 1971-1978â chronicles not just the Heartbreakersâ first two albums but also documents the journey that brought them there, while âThe Who By Numbers 50th Anniversary Editionâ documents the bandâs seventh album in a more traditional box set presentation. Both of the releases successfully accomplish their goals and deliver a worthwhile experience for interested listeners, but follow different paths to reach their respective sonic destinations.

âItâs not Tom Petty good.â Thatâs how Adria Petty described the standards against which decisions were made about what to include and not to include in the outtakes record. âCould this be any band? If so, itâs not in there . . . itâs gotta be something that really adds to the canon or weâre just detracting from the canon.â

In the case of the Petty box set, the records at its heart are the newly mixed and remastered editions of the first two albums: the eponymous first release and record number two, âYouâre Gonna Get It!â Then thereâs âLive from the Record Plant,â originally broadcast on KSAN-FM in 1977, a DVD of the bandâs appearance on the BBCâs âOld Grey Whistle Test,â and finally (and most importantly for this release) a disc of unheard tracks: âNo Sleep Til L.A.â and âThe Cut Out Bin.â (On the LP edition of the box, the latter two are separate albums, but on the CD-only version, the two are consolidated.)Â

Rounding out the set is a Blu-Ray with hi-res stereo, Dolby Atmos and 5.1 immersive mixes, and importantly, a full-color 46-page âfanzineâ called âHeart Attackâ that serves as the liner notes for this box, with photographs, essays, interviews and commentary from members of the surviving Heartbreakers. There are other editions with additional advanced artifacts like posters or simulated Polaroids â my favorite is probably the âPunk to New Waveâ trading cards â but if youâre in the target market for those kinds of fun treats, youâve probably already ordered your copy.

Whatâs notable about the unreleased music featured on âNo Sleep Til L.A.â and âThe Cut Out Binâ is that it isnât just a simple compilation of demos and rough takes in a logical order of some kind, but instead is deliberately curated into the shape of an album. Itâs intended to convey the journey Petty and the band took to get to the place where theyâre going into the studio to record that first record, capturing tracks from the Mudcrutch era (Pettyâs pre-Heartbreakers band that also featured future Heartbreakers Mike Campbell and Benmont Tench) as early as 1971 and then as the Heartbreakers in their early days, learning to work in the studio in L.A. and in Tulsa, where their label Shelter Records sent them to learn how to make a record instead of running the meter on a L.A. studio.Â

The outtake record isnât trying to fabricate something that doesnât exist or inject fiction into the Heartbreakers legend, but rather, to show you how the band evolved from a bunch of kids in Florida who picked up and went out to L.A. to seek their rock ânâ roll fortunes on a wing and a prayer into a band that would end up being inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. Itâs expanding the legacy, not rewriting history.Â

âItâs not Tom Petty good.â Thatâs how Adria Petty, who oversees Petty Legacy, the business concern thatâs handling her late fatherâs catalog, told Salon as she described the standards against which decisions were made about what to include and not to include in the outtakes record. âCould this be any band? If so, itâs not in there . . . itâs gotta be something that really adds to the canon or weâre just detracting from the canon.âÂ

And the collection absolutely burnishes the canon. Itâs hard to listen to the selection of music and understand how any music business professional didnât think this band had serious potential. Thereâs so many standout tracks: âParade of Loons,â which opens the record, from the great rock ânâ roll tradition of writing a song from the perspective of watching the craziness unfolding around you is borderline new wave, but it also isnât â itâs easy to understand why an industry struggling to understand the new guard needed to figure out where these new guys fit, exactly â and perusing some of the photos included in âHeart Attackâ you can extend some grace on that front, because â as Adria Petty laughed, âThese are not guys you want to date your daughter, you know?â But as you learn from some of the news clips included in the booklet, Petty did not want to be co-opted into anyoneâs movement or limited by any genre.

âYouâre Gonna Learnâ is reggae-influenced at a time when that wasnât a widely known, let alone embraced, genre in American rock, and they manage to pull it off without embarrassing themselves. âUp In Mississippi Tonightâ could be an outtake from âExile on Main Street.â There are also a couple of earnest and successful Dylan homages: âWild Eyesâ and âI Canât Fight It.â If youâre going to borrow, borrow from the best (and from a guy youâre going to be on the road backing in 10 years).

Then thereâs âUnheard Kind of Hero.â This is a song that Heartbreakers keyboardist Benmont Tench had previously mentioned as a song he saw the band perform before he was in it, and how he was astounded that a band in Gainesville, Florida, was writing original material like that. In âHeart Attack,â Tench offers, âI was following Mudcrutch around because they were so good, and they played a lot of really cool covers and they played some stuff of their own,â he remembers. And when he heard âHero,â he asked a friend working for the band who sang it originally. When he was told it was an original, his reaction was, âOK, good lord. Because if you listen to that, whether he was 17 or 19 when he wrote it, the storytelling in it is the beginning.â

The box set is configured to bring the listener into the story, opening with the outtakes before taking you to the officially released albums, then live radio show and then, finally, the 1977 âOld Grey Whistle Testâ performance. But Iâd like to make the case that you should begin with the OGWT performance because it is utterly electrifying. Anglophiles are already familiar, but in case youâre not, the âOld Grey Whistle Testâ is a legendary BBC music program that was the opposite to âTop of the Popsâ in that its focus was on albums as opposed to hit singles. But this isnât an OGWT where a band plays a couple of songs; this was one of their special editions where the band gets the full show. So this is a 40-minute performance by a band that was already famous and well-liked in the U.K., a status they were still fighting to achieve back home.

Theyâre dressed in black (Benmont Tench rocking a red shirt underneath his suit jacket), Petty looking more like a gunslinger, Ray-Ban aviators and studded guitar strap, Stan Lynch singing harmony vocals over Pettyâs shoulder, Mike Campbell dropping guitar riffs and solos without breaking a sweat, Ron Blair sharing the center mic for harmony vocals but otherwise staying low-key back against the drum riser. Itâs a time machine back to 1977, with camera work more evolved than weâre used to seeing because it was a TV show about music, not a variety show that featured a band. The colors are a little over-saturated, but people who are used to watching archival rock ânâ roll clips wonât be phased. The most jarring element is whenever the camera cuts to the audience, who look like theyâd rather be anywhere else. A U.K. source shared that this was because this wasnât an audience of Tom Petty fans but rather random people whoâd put in for tickets and wouldnât have been encouraged to be enthusiastic. Petty gets his revenge, though, at the last number. (No spoilers!)

The Who box sets are intended to be complete documents of individual records. So thereâs the disc of the remastered album (which sounds fantastic), then the initial Townshend demos.

âThe Who By Numbersâ was released in 1975, but this is still being declared a 50th anniversary artifact. It features 92 unreleased audio tracks, a recording of the band live in Swansea in 1976, the requisite Atmos and stereo mixes, and a video of the full concert of The Who at the Silverdome in Pontiac, Michigan, in 1975.Â

Also included is what has become a trademark for the bandâs reissue sets, a gorgeous full-color 100-page book of liner notes, interviews, lyrics, photographs and other assorted documentation. Even if you buy the CD box, youâre still getting the full-sized book because they put the CDs into an album-sized enclosure. The archivist this time is Andy Neill, one of the two names you want to see behind a Who reissue.Â

The Who box sets are intended to be complete documents of individual records. So thereâs the disc of the remastered album (which sounds fantastic), then the initial Townshend demos. Townshend was approaching 30 when he began work on the songs for âBy Numbers,â and he was in the middle of a number of personal dilemmas, as well as struggling with his and the bandâs place within rock ânâ roll: âI felt detached from my own songs,â he confesses. He also rued the fact that he felt he owed his best material to the band, instead of being able to pursue more of a solo career, which all of his bandmates had done. Townshendâs âWho Came Firstâ came out in 1972, but there hadnât been anything since.

(Michael Ochs Archives/Getty Images) The Who, 1975

The demos are lovely, ethereal sketches, documenting Townshend breathing life into his creations for the first time. There are two demos of âKeep Me Turning,â which didnât make the cut and we wouldnât hear until it appeared on âRough Mix,â the warm and affectionate project he recorded with Ronnie Lane of the Faces two years later. A fun game is to take the Townshend demo of âSlip Kid,â where heâs kind of half-speaking, half-singing, and then compare it to Daltreyâs delivery on the finished version, which is the one song from this record that was built on the original demo. (This is a release that youâll want the good headphones for.) The highlight is probably âHow Many Friends,â which is the heartbreaker on the album; Daltreyâs read of it nails the pathos, but this version makes you wish that Pete maybe hung onto it for himself.

Up next is âTracking Sessions,â which are initial loose takes with the whole band, but not finished vocals. Itâs basically how the band taught themselves the new material, and it includes listings like âRamport Jamâ where they (sans Keith Moon, still making his way back to the U.K. after hanging out in L.A. and working on his solo record) fart around on a variety of instrumentals and a Faces song. This lasted about half an hour, but weâre getting only eight minutes; given the nature of the release, just give the fans the entire unedited mess. Throughout the sessions, you hear the band members making jokes and laughing; you hear Glyn Johns in the control room offering his thoughts; you hear Pete Townshend complaining about not being able to obtain a suitable breakfast. This stuff is gold.Â

Whereas the Tom Petty box set is intended to show you how they got to the first two albums, this release is trying to show you why this was the record between âQuadropheniaâ and âWho Are You.â

There are also lovely early run-throughs of âImagine A Manâ with a solo Townshend on acoustic and Nicky Hopkins on piano, and similarly, âThey Are All In Loveâ (a song that Daltrey did not initially want to sing) is also offered solo Pete. A prototype of âBlue Red and Grayâ is here as well, thanks to Glyn Johnsâ insistence: âI find that the hardest thing for me to do as a writer is to express optimism, general warmth and a feeling of good will to all men in a song,â Townshend said. âIt feels trite and I hate it. That song, âI Love Every Minute Of The Dayâ . . . is a prime example. Glyn Johns wanted it on the album; I cringed when he picked it. He heard it on a cassette and said, âWhatâs that?â I said, âNothing.â He said, âNo. Play it.â I said, âReally, itâs nothing. Just me playing a ukulele.â But he insisted on doing it. I said, âWhat? That fu*king thing. Hereâs me, wanting to commit suicide, and youâre going to put that thing on the recordâ.â

Disc 4 is billed âEarly Mixes & Guide Vocalsâ and is by nature more structured than the Tracking Sessions. The songs are taking shape now. Entwistle offers his approach to his âSuccess Story,â Pete sings the lead on âHowever Much I Booze,â thereâs a version of âSqueezeboxâ that the liner notes state is âaccented by tambourineâ but sounds like the cowbell on the âSNLâ âDonât Fear The Reaperâ sketch, and âDreaming From The Waistâ is a fantastic illustration of why Pete Townshend needed Roger Daltrey to sing most of his songs.Â Â

As a way to track the evolution of the song from start to finish, the inclusion of all of these different versions is an established and useful presentation device, but given their formative nature, itâs not likely that youâre going to go back to them with regularity. But thatâs not why this record exists. Whereas the Tom Petty box set is intended to show you how they got to the first two albums, this release is trying to show you why this was the record between âQuadropheniaâ and âWho Are You.âÂ

But itâs probably more accurate to state that âThe Who By Numbersâ was the record between the âTommyâ movie and âWho Are You,â which isnât a small distinction; the âTommyâ movie made the band into a larger and different flavor of rock star, one that brought in the girls because of shirtless golden god Daltrey and delivered your average punters who might not have found their way past the tunes theyâd heard on the radio. And itâs not unimportant to note that the âTommyâ movie brought the band the kind of money they hadnât yet seen.Â

Thatâs part of the cri de coeur you hear on âBy Numbers.â Itâs by no means the main thread, but it absolutely underpins Townshendâs personal anxieties. Heâs annoyed that his bandmates are off doing their own thing. Heâs perturbed that he doesnât have the time or material to make another solo record because he has to offer his best songs to The Who (and conversely, itâs kind of hilarious that he then seems panicked when he presented Daltrey with the songs heâd written for the record and ended up shocked that Rog picked âthe more personal onesâ.) NOTE: Daltrey is not responsible for the abomination that is âSqueeze Box,â that we have to blame on Ronnie Lane, who was enchanted by it.Â

The Swansea show from 1976 here isnât complete, but it is Keith Moonâs last proper show before a U.K. audience. (It was recorded with the intention of being released as a live album, and one of the original tapes went missing at some point in the 1990s, which is why the first two songs are missing.) âMy Wifeâ will sound familiar to anyone who owns the âMaximum RnBâ box set, âSqueezeboxâ is palatable because of Townshendâs giant power chords, âIâm Freeâ (introduced by Moon, who dedicates it to the occupants of the prison across the street from the venue) sounds more like the version from the âTommyâ soundtrack, and thereâs a hilarious comedic bit over âBellboy.â

But itâs the last live artifact here thatâs a truly delightful surprise. Itâs on the last disc with the Atmos remixes, and at first I feared it would be poor-quality footage added simply because it existed. But itâs far, far better than that. It is the complete show from the Pontiac Silverdome in December of 1975, cleaned up and remastered. This show set the record for the largest ever indoor rock concert attendance of 76,896, which would be broken by Led Zeppelin in the same place two years later. Because of the size of both the venue and the crowd, a large screen was set up to project closed-circuit video, a thing weâd think absolutely nothing of now, but at the time was a revolutionary development.Â

There were four cameras, and they do a more than decent job of capturing the action but donât expect any fancy camerawork or closeups of guitar solos. The sound is in mono â as the liner notes point out, âthe sound was captured via a direct line mono feed from the PA â no attempt was made to professionally record the concert for synching purposes.â Part of the âJoin Togetherâ / âRoad Runnerâ / âMy Generationâ medley ended up in âThe Kids Are Alright,â but this is the first official release of this footage.

You know what? The sound quality is more than adequate, and where it falls down the electricity coming off of that stage in this performance makes up for a multitude of sins. Roger is in Woodstock buckskin fringe, and even this primitive setup can capture that those trousers were, shall we say, form-fitting. (Wait for âMagic Bus,â which swings so much harder and better than it did later.) Daltrey introduces the âTommyâ portion by noting, âThis is how we used to do it,â and then the band proceeds to light the stage on fire. The band seems perplexed and concerned about the size of the crowd, with both Roger and Pete each taking turns to ask the crowd to take a few steps back.

This Silverdome footage is absolutely a text, and even this rudimentary capture that was meant to make sure the 76,896th guy in the back could see something is still full of electricity and life. If you were lucky enough to see the band with Keith Moon in those days, youâll remember, and if you werenât, this at least brings some of that fairy dust into your life and your house. Put it on, turn it all the way up, and enjoy it without 76,896 people stepping on your feet.

#6200. Will the midterms live up to the hype? 6 key stories we’re watching

Across the country, voters are making their way to the polls in the climax of a vitriolic midterm election cycle set against the backdrop of an electorate souring on Donald Trump and Republicans. Inflation is up, consumer confidence is down, gas and diesel prices are through the roof, largely due to the president’s war of choice in Iran. The cruelty of his MAGA agenda has roiled the country and left a bad taste even in the mouths of some of his erstwhile supporters.

Each election is billed as being consequential; this one lives up to the hype. As we await the results, it’s worth taking note of several questions:

A tsunami, a trickle — or something in the middle? All are possible, but signs are pointing to significant Democratic gains, likely up to 25 seats in the House, as well as a Senate majority. Dr. Abdul El-Sayed looks increasingly likely to win in Michigan, and James Talarico has Democratic hopes up in Texas. Senate races in Maine, Kansas, Iowa and Alaska are in play, and it’s worth keeping an eye on South Carolina, Mississippi and Louisiana as well.

One sign will come at 6 p.m. when polls close in Kentucky’s 6th Congressional District, where Democrat Zach Dembo is facing off against Republican Ralph Alvarado. Once a Democratic stronghold, the seat went Republican in 2012 and, despite a close call in 2018, has remained in GOP hands since. Although the district has been gerrymandered to favor Republicans, the energy on the ground is with Dembo. If he posts and maintains a healthy lead, look for significant Democratic gains to unfold throughout the night.

What effect did redistricting have on the GOP’s chances?

The midterms will be the first test of the GOP’s redistricting strategy, which saw the party redraw congressional districts in Florida, Texas and other states, partly in response to the gains Trump made with Black and Latino voters in 2024. But polls show those margins have been largely erased as the electorate has turned on the president after nearly two tumultuous years in office, while Democratic legislatures in California and Virginia have imposed their own gerrymanders. According to a Politico poll, the GOP increasingly sees the coalition that returned Trump to office as “crumbling,” and may have gained little or nothing from all this adventurous map-drawing.

Will progressives be bolstered or chastened?

Losses — or even narrow wins — by progressive candidates could be used as more evidence by the party’s establishment wing of the need to tack toward the middle ahead of the 2028 presidential election. Larger wins would provide rocket fuel to the movement.

The size of the blue wave could well come to be seen as a measure of progressives’ influence and power within the Democratic Party. Losses — or even narrow wins — by progressive candidates could be used as more evidence by the party’s establishment wing of the need to tack toward the middle ahead of the 2028 presidential election. Larger wins — and victories in unexpected places, such as Michigan’s 7th Congressional District where William Lawrence, co-founder of the Sunrise Movement, stands a real chance of unseating incumbent Republican Tom Barrett — would provide rocket fuel to the movement.

Progressive groups are already on the offensive, getting a head start on spinning tonight’s election results, particularly in anticipation of a narrow El-Sayed win in Michigan. “Expect to hear narrow victories cited as evidence of weak electability,” a Progressive Change Campaign Committee memo obtained by Politico reads. “But a candidate’s first winning margin is not their electoral ceiling.”

Will the Haley Stevens drama matter in Michigan?

Haley Stevens, the Democratic congresswoman who narrowly lost to El-Sayed in Michigan’s Senate primary, has brought the drama in the race’s closing days. As late as Saturday night, she pledged to colleagues and friends that she was backing El-Sayed, only to turn up hours later at a church service with his Republican opponent Mike Rogers, and endorse the former congressman in a video. The cold-dish move has virtually drowned out El-Sayed’s closing message, with Stevens being formally kicked out of the Michigan Democratic Party.

The question now is if any of it will matter, especially in light of a New York Times/Siena poll taken before Stevens’ move that showed El-Sayed leading Rogers by 11 points. Michigan Republicans seem to think it won’t, telling Politico they wish the congresswoman had crossed the aisle earlier. The nonpartisan Cook Political Report agrees, moving the race in their ratings to “Leans Democratic,” a shift that was already in the works before Stevens detonated her bomb.

Still, the results in the state’s Democratic primary were far narrower than the polls showed, with El-Sayed besting Stevens by only 1%, or 14,893 votes.

The New York Times reported yesterday that the world’s first trillionaire has dropped a staggering $474 million this election cycle, an historic first. The amount has been spread out across a variety of groups, PACs and funds, but it doesn’t include the “dark-money donations” the Times reports he has also made. Most of the $168 million he contributed to the Senate Leadership Fund has served to shore up Ken Paxton, the GOP nominee for Senate in Texas, who is locked in a tight race with Talarico.

Musk has a lot riding on Tuesday’s results. Beyond the simple math of whether he got enough bang for his buck, there is also the issue of what will surely face him in the event of a Democratic congressional majority: investigations.

Musk has a lot riding on Tuesday’s results. Beyond the simple math of whether he got enough bang for his buck, there is also the issue of what will surely face him in the event of a Democratic congressional majority: investigations. If the blue wave materializes, Musk can expect congressional inquiries of his activities, including his reported interventions in Russia’s war against Ukraine and his leadership of DOGE during the early months of Trump’s second administration.

Each election brings surprises. Think not one but both of Georgia’s Senate seats going to Democrats in 2020, or Republicans making big gains in New York two years later.

This is the year we could hear the echo of Georgia’s 2020 election results in another Southern state. Despite boasting large Black populations, Senate seats in South Carolina, Mississippi and Louisiana have long been out of reach for Democrats. But there is now a path to victory for the party’s candidates in each of those states.

In South Carolina, the GOP incumbent Darline Graham, who was appointed to the seat at Donald Trump’s command following the death of her brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham, has proven to be a lackluster candidate, alarming even some Republicans with her performance in debates and on the stump. Democrat Annie Andrews has run a more nimble campaign, and between Graham’s performance and the national state of affairs, she appears to have narrowed the gap.

Mississippi’s incumbent GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith has also run a lazy campaign, expecting to coast to victory. But the national political environment under Trump, coupled with campaign gaffes, large Black turnout in the aftermath of the Supreme Court’s decision to gut the Voting Rights Act and clever campaigning by Scott Colom, her Democratic opponent, have helped to put the race in play.

Louisiana is also a wild card. The state, which is one-third African American, has also seen a surge in early voting among Black residents, and according to a recent poll, the race between Republican Julia Letlow and Democrat Jamie Davis, who is Black, is tied.

Polls are not predictive. The political history of these states continues to favor Republicans, but any of them could deliver one of 2026’s electoral surprises. If that happens, it will signal that the blue wave has become a blue tsunami.

#6197. For Ukrainians, U.S. Midterm Results Bring Some Hope

This issue is preventing our website from loading properly. Please review the following troubleshooting tips or contact us at [email protected].

Dispatch: For Ukrainians, U.S. Midterm Results Bring Some Hope

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

Understanding the conflict four years in.

KYIV AND WASHINGTON—The outcome of the U.S. congressional elections this week, which gave Democrats control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives, will be welcomed in some countries more than others, including Ukraine—which has quarreled with Republican-controlled Washington off and on for two years now.

So what are ordinary Ukrainians saying about the results?

KYIV AND WASHINGTON—The outcome of the U.S. congressional elections this week, which gave Democrats control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives, will be welcomed in some countries more than others, including Ukraine—which has quarreled with Republican-controlled Washington off and on for two years now.

So what are ordinary Ukrainians saying about the results?

In Kyiv, which is now preparing for a brutal winter, some residents seemed cautiously optimistic. But on a day marked by sweeping power and water cuts following a barrage of Russian attacks on critical infrastructure, Ukrainians appeared far more focused on ensuring their daily survival.

“The main thing for us is that there’s water and electricity—and no war,” said Yulia, who declined to give her last name. “I hope things will be better.”

The U.S. midterm results come as Russia has ramped up its campaign of hybrid warfare in Europe and escalated its attacks against Ukraine, damaging critical infrastructure and regularly upending daily life across the country. In Kyiv on Wednesday, disruptions to energy and water supplies prompted officials to establish emergency centers in hard-hit areas and urge residents to get their water from public fountains.

Those impacts were visible at one café in the city, which was forced to rely on a generator for power. A staff member told Foreign Policy that the generator had already been running for eight hours. Elsewhere in the café, a row of power packs for rent testified to the difficulty of doing much without electricity.

Maxim Yersigngeyev, who had brought his young daughter to have breakfast at the café due to a blackout at home, said he didn’t particularly follow the U.S. election. “But if it’s good for Ukraine, that’s good,” he said.

In the southern Zaporizhzhia region, search-and-rescue operations have been underway after Russian forces bombed a humanitarian hub on Monday, killing at least 40 people and leaving dozens more missing under the rubble. The attack could rank among one of the deadliest against civilians in nearly five years of war.

The timing of that strike, as well as other Russian strikes earlier this week, drew a sharp response from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who said that it was “very telling” that the attacks coincided with the U.S. congressional elections.

“The Russians believe that America will not notice this signal from them. But such terror must be noticed and stopped,” Zelensky said in a post on X on Tuesday. “It is essential to help build peace honestly and reliably, and America can do that.”

Tensions have been high between Zelensky and U.S. President Donald Trump, with one sticking point being the powerful Patriot air defense interceptors that can shield against Russian ballistic missile attacks.

Zelensky has warned of shrinking supplies of the weapons and accused the United States of slow-rolling deliveries, and the Trump administration has previously backtracked on pledges to share the technology underpinning the missiles with Kyiv.

The Trump administration last week approved a proposed $2.1 billion sale of the missiles for Ukraine, although Zelensky has said that it could take “several years” for the weapons to arrive. The sale runs through a U.S. program and would be completely funded by Canada, Norway, and Germany.

And further negotiations are on the horizon. On Wednesday, the European Commission is set to host representatives from Ukraine, the United States, France, Germany, the United Kingdom, NATO, and the World Bank for talks on postwar reconstruction and security guarantees.

Next week, Washington is also expected to mediate talks between Kyiv and Moscow in Abu Dhabi, with discussions focusing on “post-war security arrangements, de-escalation, humanitarian efforts, and next steps toward peace,” U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff announced in a post on X.

Back in Kyiv, Valeriy Shevchenko told Foreign Policy that he was happy with the Democrats’ wins but had his eye more on the 2028 presidential election.

“But as you see, we are constantly being attacked, specifically through power outages—we need to rely on ourselves,” he said, referring to Ukrainian air defenses.

#6194. Elon Musk is using Anakin Skywalker to cope with the midterm forecast

Move over, Haley Stevens: There’s a new competitor for the most pathetic reaction to plummeting political fortunes. Elon Musk, the former Trump administration member and the world’s richest man, has seen the midterm election forecast for conservative candidates, and he’s responded by petulantly playing with his toys.

The X owner started “Anakin-posting” on Monday. The purely online phenomenon finds far-right and MAGA nerds recasting Star Wars’ Anakin Skywalker, the man who will become Darth Vader, as a tragic hero and paragon of traditional values. A typical post uses generative AI to reframe the “Star Wars” films’ genocidal space monk as a masculine, hyper-conservative, attentive father. Musk’s post shows Anakin, as played by actor Hayden Christensen, sitting on a throne surrounded by his children, Luke and Leia, and his wife, Padme. The AI illustration has pulled liberally from all three trilogies, placing the adult faces of Mark Hamill and Carrie Fisher on the children. Natalie Portman’s Padme appears to be wearing her makeup and crown from “Black Swan.” The Sith first family is surrounded by 1970s-era storm troopers and 2010s imperial guards.

“This is what they stole from us,” Musk captioned the computer-generated photo of his sci-fi fan fiction.

For the unfamiliar, Anakin was a member of an order of space knights. As a young man, he began having prophetic dreams of his wife dying in childbirth. Consumed by ambition and anger, and desperate to avoid the fate he envisioned, he was manipulated by several elderly politicians into betraying his chivalric order, killing many of his fellow knights and slaughtering an entire school full of squires for fear of retribution. Unable to save his wife, and grievously injured from a battle with his former mentor, he became a running dog of a fascist empire that aimed to rule the entire galaxy.

Right-wing young men have warped that story through the established MAGA lens of “returning to tradition,” picturing a world where having the conviction to kill a bunch of toddlers is celebrated.

The typical example of “Anakin-posting” expresses rage at a stagnant economy or lack of prospects by sharing images of Christensen’s Anakin looking stoic. MAGA influencers like Jack Posobiec have added a dash of intergalactic racism, sharing images of a young Anakin surrounded by literal aliens to hint at a pro-segregationist message. Others have reimagined Anakin’s mentors as chiding liberal scolds, grafting pink hair and a keffiyeh onto Obi-Wan Kenobi. In the pathetic galaxy of Gen Z men, anything from mid-century magazine ads to a Disney-owned sci-fi epic for children can be a stand in for their cultural grievances.

Enough time has passed between the prequels and the present that Anakin can be presented as a brooding badass. The primary criticism of the movies at the time concerned Christensen’s portrayal of Anakin as a whiny child throwing a deadly tantrum. The knotty and boring political intrigue subplots of the films have been forgotten, making it easy to gloss over Anakin being a stooge for politicians playing a game beyond his ken.

Musk, in particular, does have reasons to empathize with the “Star Wars” villain. After believing he had found a way to reshape the government toward his own ends via DOGE, he was booted when the program proved deeply unpopular. Seeing visions of a blue wave washout, he used his financial superpower to try and avoid what appears to be an oncoming loss. Separated from the levers of power and now half a billion dollars poorer, Musk has been forced to play-act a scenario where he won. His image-generating toy gave him the happy ending that politics, relationships and wealth couldn’t.

But all the AI bots can’t undo the facts of Anakin’s story. He was ultimately killed by the evil emperor he served, dying in front of the son he abandoned. His “return to tradition” was a last-minute awakening, when he was forced to confront all the harm he had done and the miserable life he had led. Now there’s something for Musk to aspire to.

U.S. Vice President J.D. Vance on Wednesday offered an extraordinarily frank assessment of why he believes Republicans got clobbered in the 2026 midterm elections. He blamed the Iran war.

“The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night,” Vance said on X.

U.S. Vice President J.D. Vance on Wednesday offered an extraordinarily frank assessment of why he believes Republicans got clobbered in the 2026 midterm elections. He blamed the Iran war.

“The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night,” Vance said on X.

“If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest,” Vance added. “But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.”

It’s not often that a sitting vice president comes out so forcefully against a defining policy decision made by his boss—especially when that boss is as notorious for punishing perceived disloyalty as U.S. President Donald Trump is.

But Vance, who is widely expected to be interested in running for president in 2028, appears to have calculated that the political cost of continuing to defend the Iran war outweighs the potential risk of drawing Trump’s ire.

In the lead-up to elections, polling consistently showed that the Iran war was unpopular among voters and that the cost of living was their top concern.

As Vance noted, Trump himself has acknowledged that the Iran war was a “piece” of what contributed to the historic defeat. But the president remains unapologetic about starting the war.

“I did the right thing. I would have done it again,” Trump told the Wall Street Journal.

Trump also blamed the quality of Republican candidates on the ballot, stating that some could’ve been “better.” In a separate interview with Fox News, Trump acknowledged voter discontentment over the war’s economic consequences, including high gas prices, but suggested the pain at the pump was worth it in the long run.

“People agree with what I’m doing on Iran, but they really, probably weren’t willing to do the short-term consequence of paying more for gasoline,” Trump said. “And, you know, I understand that. I don’t agree with it, and I would say to people, you know, ‘It’s a short-term problem but for long-term gain.’”

But Trump and Vance have never done a particularly good job of selling the Iran war to the American people. Since the very beginning, the administration has presented muddled and often contradictory explanations for why the United States needed to launch a full-scale war on Iran in February.

Even in his final speech on the eve of the election, Trump undermined the war’s main justification by saying that Iran’s nuclear program had already been destroyed by U.S. military action last summer.

“I hope people realize that when they go into the voting booth, because we had to stop Iran from having a nuclear weapon. If, if we allowed Iran to have a nuclear weapon, this country could never function the same way. The whole world would be a different place, so we’ve stopped that. We stopped that a year ago with those beautiful B-2 bombers, which hit every single mark, and just put hundreds of tons of rock on top of everything,” Trump said.

Vance is believed to have strongly opposed the war behind closed doors; yet he outwardly maintained support for it. It seems that American voters’ unequivocal rejection of the war has convinced him that he no longer has to pretend.

John Haltiwanger is a staff writer at Foreign Policy. Bluesky: @jchaltiwanger.bsky.social X: @jchaltiwanger

#6188. “It’s them, not me”: Trump rages at Fox News over election coverage

President Donald Trump fumed at Fox News on Election Day, accusing the conservative network of turning against him, giving Democrats too much airtime and driving away its own viewers.

“FoxNews Ratings are way down (27%!) because they’re spending too much time covering the Trump Deranged Dumocrats!” Trump wrote Tuesday on Truth Social. “All of those people who used to watch Fox, and no longer do, get it. It’s them, not me.”

﻿

Trump insisted his own popularity remained strong, claiming his numbers were “better than they have ever been” and citing a CNN poll that he said showed overwhelming Republican support for him.

The president also accused Fox News of deliberately undermining him through its polling.

“The FoxNews Poll, always the worst, is so insulting with the questions they ask,” Trump wrote. “Every question is a hit job, and every answer is ‘BULLS***!'”

His grievances extended beyond the network’s programming. Trump questioned why Fox Corp. was financially supporting Democratic politicians and organizations, naming House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, Reps. Jamie Raskin, Ted Lieu and Pete Aguilar, along with several Democratic campaign committees. He did not provide figures to substantiate his allegations.

Trump also singled out Jessica Tarlov, the Democratic strategist and co-host of Fox News’ “The Five,” with a personal insult while watching the network’s election coverage, a complaint he brought up in previous posts.

“I can’t stand Jessica Tarlov’s voice — DUMB AS A ROCK, but it’s the voice that gets me,” Trump wrote, adding that he would change channels until she was off the air.

Fox News has experienced a ratings decline, although Trump’s explanation for the drop is unsubstantiated. Nielsen data showed the network’s total-day audience fell 27% in October compared with the previous year, according to TheWrap. Fox nevertheless remained the most-watched cable news network.

Fox Corp. CEO Lachlan Murdoch attributed the decline to viewer fatigue during an earnings call Monday.

Trump, however, insisted the network’s coverage of him was responsible.

“They’re way down, not because of me, but because they are AGAINST me!” he wrote. “This happened once before, and Fox almost collapsed. It’s happening again!”

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at how a Democrat-controlled Congress might impact U.S. foreign policy, the start of coalition-building talks in Israel, and Ukraine’s timeline for European Union accession.

Democrats took back control of the U.S. Congress in Tuesday’s midterm elections in a dramatic rebuke of President Donald Trump and his Republican Party. With Democratic candidates making big gains in historically deep red states, even top White House officials have recognized that Americans appear to be tired of the administration’s playbook and want significant change.

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at how a Democrat-controlled Congress might impact U.S. foreign policy, the start of coalition-building talks in Israel, and Ukraine’s timeline for European Union accession.

Democrats took back control of the U.S. Congress in Tuesday’s midterm elections in a dramatic rebuke of President Donald Trump and his Republican Party. With Democratic candidates making big gains in historically deep red states, even top White House officials have recognized that Americans appear to be tired of the administration’s playbook and want significant change.

“[E]veryone knows why we lost,” Vice President J.D. Vance wrote on X on Wednesday. “And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.”

According to Vance, many voters’ frustration centered on the Iran war. Since U.S. and Israeli forces first launched strikes on Iran in late February, fuel costs have skyrocketed to record highs, making inflation and pricing concerns the No. 1 issue for more than one-third of Americans, according to an Economist/YouGov poll published in September. The cost of living for the average U.S. household has grown by around $2,000 since the war began, according to economists at Moody’s Analytics. And dozens of U.S. products, from medical supplies to computers to condoms, have suffered strains to their supply chains.

On Election Day, Trump appeared to make a last-minute bid to convince voters that his Middle East policies are adaptable, abruptly announcing that Washington will cut off $4 billion in aid to Israel by the end of this year.

However, that did not seem to assuage voters. Kansas saw a Democrat win a Senate seat for the first time in nearly 100 years, with other big party flips occurring in Texas, Iowa, and North Carolina. Michigan elected the country’s first Muslim senator, Georgia elected the country’s first Black woman governor, and New Hampshire elected the country’s first openly gay man to serve as a senator. All of them are Democrats.

With the left now poised to hold a majority in the Senate and House of Representatives when the new Congress is sworn in on Jan. 3, experts expect that Democrats will crack down on some of Trump’s most controversial policies. That could include challenges to sweeping tariffs, new limits to military spending for the Iran war, and investigations into alleged corruption within Trump’s inner circle. Pursuing the impeachment of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth could well be at the top of that list.

Other foreign-policy priorities for Democrats may include improving the U.S. relationship with NATO; providing greater support for Ukraine; reining in U.S. boat strikes in Latin America; and requiring greater regulation of Big Tech, artificial intelligence, and data centers.

Trump has flip-flopped in recent days between agreeing to work with Democrats and vowing to veto everything placed on his desk. House Democrats, meanwhile, have already outlined a 100-day agenda to bring down the cost of groceries, reverse cuts to healthcare programs, and launch investigations into some of Trump’s cabinet members.

“Lawyer up,” Rep. Robert Garcia, who will chair the House Oversight Committee in the next Congress, said on Tuesday.

Many foreign leaders appeared optimistic that Democrats’ midterm mandate will “introduce a new era in world relations,” as South African President Cyril Ramaphosa said. Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store stressed that U.S. politics may now better align with European priorities, and Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez compared the results to last month’s left-wing victory in Brazil.

Still, analysts anticipate that the road ahead will not be easy for Democrats. “[N]o one should kid themselves that the next two years are going to be anything other than ugly, chaotic, and brutal,” FP’s Michael Hirsh wrote. “Looking ahead to 2028, many of those newly alienated former Trump voters will be up for grabs. The question is whether a badly divided Democratic Party will be in a position to draw them in.”

Coalition talks begin. Israeli President Isaac Herzog on Wednesday formally accepted last week’s parliamentary election results, paving the way for party consultations to begin. His announcement came after Israel’s election commission said that a thorough investigation found “no evidence of irregularities that compromised the integrity of the election or affected its results.” A separate Shin Bet investigation into alleged foreign interference is still ongoing.

Herzog’s decision deals a blow to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s efforts to sow distrust in the results, which saw his hard-right bloc lose its majority in the Knesset. Netanyahu and his allies have repeatedly touted unsubstantiated claims of Arab-led parties stealing the election, including by allegedly receiving aid from Qatar; Qatar has denied any involvement. Nonaligned Arab-led parties won a record 19 seats in the Knesset in late October.

Now, Herzog will begin meeting with party leaders to determine who will be named prime minister-designate. Most individuals are expected to back either Netanyahu or Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of the opposition bloc. However, that will likely depend on who the Arab parties choose to support. Several of Eisenkot’s allies have balked at the idea of allying with Arab groups, yet Arab parties have largely ruled out joining any coalition that includes Netanyahu.

Not on target. The European Commission warned Ukraine on Wednesday that it needs to speed up its reform efforts if it wants to meet its European Union accession goal, which is to conclude membership negotiations by the end of 2028. “The Commission is committed to support this ambitious objective ​but considers that to meet it an acceleration of ⁠the pace of reforms is required,” the body wrote in a report seen by Reuters.

EU membership remains a core foreign-policy priority for Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. Kyiv has long argued that joining the bloc would give Ukraine greater long-term security against Russia; the EU granted Ukraine candidate status in June 2022, mere months after Russia launched its full-scale invasion. However, on Wednesday, the bloc outlined only seven policy areas out of 35 in which Kyiv could conceivably finish reforms before its 2028 deadline expires.

According to the commission’s report, Ukraine must now focus on improving rule of law standards, delivering an action plan on national minorities, and tackling corruption. Several major scandals have undermined Kyiv’s reform efforts, including controversial cabinet reshuffles as well as evidence of politicians and other elites having received kickbacks from defense contractors.

“Act of treason.” Indonesia deployed more than 20,000 troops and personnel to the capital of Jakarta on Wednesday. Although military spokesperson Maj. Gen. Muhammad Nas insisted that the movements were “a normal occurrence,” their timing comes as local authorities are investigating an alleged illegal wiretapping operation targeting President Prabowo Subianto.

Earlier this week, Indonesian police detained three senior police generals suspected of intercepting communications, accessing electronic systems, and deleting electronic data between 2025 and 2026. The incident allegedly targeted Prabowo and dozens of other prominent figures, including journalists, activists, and business executives.

“Based on the progress of the investigation so far, there are signs and indications pointing toward an act of treason,” Yusril Ihza Mahendra, the Indonesian coordinating minister of law, human rights, immigration, and correctional institutions, said on Wednesday, adding that the operation could have been part of a broader effort to undermine the government.

Already, Gen. Listyo Sigit Prabowo, who was appointed as the presidential chief of staff just last month, has been dismissed. Listyo was a known loyalist of former President Joko Widodo, who is Prabowo’s biggest rival and remains highly influential despite no longer serving in public office.

The dachshund has long been a favorite dog breed among the wealthy and famous, from Queen Victoria to Andy Warhol. Now, a German art museum is celebrating the sausage dog’s influence across the ages. On Saturday, the Kunsthalle Bremen unveiled “The Dachshund: An Icon Off the Leash,” an exhibit featuring paintings, photography, stuffed toys, and other works of art by fans of the four-legged hunting dog. The dachshund was “like a muse,” museum director Christoph Grunenberg said, pointing to the impact that it had on artists such as Pablo Picasso, David Hockney, and Thorsten Brinkmann.

#6184. Jon Ossoff projected to handily win reelection in Georgia

Sen. Jon Ossoff easily defeated a challenge from Republican Rep. Mike Collins to hold on to his Georgia Senate seat on Tuesday, according to AP projections.

After Donald Trump carried the state in 2024, early forecasts predicted tough sledding for Ossoff. But during a brutal government shutdown — the longest on record — the senator signaled he was willing to stake his candidacy on protecting Affordable Care Act subsidies, and he proved an adept campaigner who was hyper-focused on Georgia issues. Ossoff focused his stump speeches around affordability, skyrocketing inflation and foreign entanglements, hammering Trump for his costly war with Iran.

For his part, Collins’ candidacy was hamstrung by controversies involving his payroll and affiliation with alleged white nationalists.

Frequently floated as a 2028 contender, Ossoff adopted a fighter’s stance at his campaign events. Like feisty Michigan candidate Abdul El-Sayed, the senator took every opportunity to land a jab against Republicans, occasionally causing some monocle-popping among centrist commentators still holding on to the idea of the dignity of the presidential office. In August, he drew jeers and applause for making light of the rumors surrounding Trump aide Natalie Harp.

“So [Trump] doesn’t want to do this job,” Ossoff said . “He wants to build his ballroom and travel with Natalie on their apparently defenseless flying palace gifted by the Emir of Qatar.”

Ossoff, for his part, has said he has “zero interest in running for president.” His victory speech, which will come later tonight, will be studied by pundits seeking to divine his intentions.

#6182. Keisha Lance Bottoms set to become first Black woman governor in US

Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms defeated Republican billionaire Rick Jackson in Georgia‘s gubernatorial election Tuesday, becoming the first Black woman elected governor in American history and ending more than two decades of Republican control of the state’s highest office.

The contest pitted two sharply different candidates to succeed term-limited Republican Gov. Brian Kemp, whose departure opened the governor’s office for the first time in eight years.

Bottoms, a former Atlanta mayor and adviser to President Joe Biden, campaigned on expanding access to health care, improving public education and addressing the rising cost of living. Jackson, a billionaire health care executive and political newcomer, emphasized cutting taxes, reducing government spending and bringing his private-sector experience to state government.

Jackson invested more than $200 million of his own money into the campaign, making his bid one of the most expensive self-funded gubernatorial campaigns in American history.

The election also ended Republicans’ decades-long control of Georgia’s governorship. The last Democrat elected governor was Roy Barnes in 1998. Barnes lost his reelection bid to Republican Sonny Perdue in 2002, and Republicans have held the office since Perdue took office in January 2003.

Georgia’s changing political landscape added another dimension to the contest. Once a reliably Republican state in presidential elections, Georgia narrowly backed Democrat Joe Biden in 2020 before returning to President Donald Trump in 2024. Democrats also captured both U.S. Senate seats in 2021, with Raphael Warnock subsequently winning a full term in 2022.

On Tuesday, Georgia voters also reelected Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff, demonstrating the state’s continued willingness to support Democrats in statewide contests.

Bottoms is the first Black governor elected in Georgia, the first woman to hold the state’s highest office and the first Black woman elected governor anywhere in the United States. She is also the first Democrat to win Georgia’s governorship in 28 years, breaking a Republican winning streak dating back to 2002.

#6179. Andrews defeats Graham in South Carolina Senate shocker

Dr. Annie Andrews will be the first Democratic senator from South Carolina since 1998, according to AP projections. In a stunning upset, she defeated the incumbent Republican Darline Graham, who was hand-picked by Donald Trump to succeed her brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham, following his death in July.

A pediatrician, Andrews positioned herself as an antidote to Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s MAHA agenda. Her campaign launch video hinged on measles outbreaks and the harm of anti-vax sentiments at the highest levels of public health. She described Kennedy as the “brain worm guy” and slammed Trump’s Cabinet as uniquely unsuited to their positions.

The race was never supposed to be close. South Carolina is about as red as you can imagine. The haven of cheap gas and fireworks hasn’t elected any Democrat to statewide office since 2006. Trump carried the state by 17 points in 2024.

Unlike her sibling, who shifted from staunch Trump critic to late-in-life ally, Graham was joined at the hip to the Trump administration from the outset. The president’s high disapproval ratings worked to turn the typical GOP lay-up into a closely contested race.

But Graham, a novice politician, did herself no favors. She flubbed softball questions around foreign affairs on the debate stage, a strong suit of her hawkish brother. Her dismal poll numbers pushed Trump to rally for Graham repeatedly in the state, cementing even stronger associations between the Republican nominee and Trump’s unpopular policies.

High early turnout among Black voters in the state also spelled trouble for Graham. The community, which is largely Democratic, turned out in high relative numbers and helped swing the race toward Andrews.

The Democratic candidate worked to avoid the associations with national party leaders that hamstrung Graham, refraining from appearances with prominent Democrats in the race’s final weeks. Andrews painted herself as a pragmatist, willing to work with national Republicans to score wins for South Carolinians. Late last month, Andrews received a shocking bipartisan endorsement from two former governors of South Carolina. Republican David Beasley joined Democrat Jim Hodges to support Andrews over Trump-backed Graham, saying Andrews was the only candidate focused on “making things better.”

#6178. Dems pivot from ‘affordability’ pitch to DHS probe threats after midterm wins

At a House Homeland Security Committee hearing, Rep. Delia Ramirez, D-Ill., delivers a powerful and emotional statement, questioning if any parent wouldn't go to extreme lengths for their dying child. Ramirez attacks for-profit prison corporations and makes a direct call to abolish ICE and dismantle DHS, citing concerns over inhuman conditions.

Several prominent Democrats who ran on an "affordability" message were largely silent when pressed by Fox News Digital on their sudden pivot to foreshadowing investigations into the Trump administration, including in many cases its immigration enforcement efforts.

Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., who is poised to lead the House Oversight Committee, responded to Democrats' win Tuesday with a statement: "Lawyer Up", despite having pledged to prioritize household costs alongside government accountability.

Garcia told CNN before the election that "Democratic priorities" would be lowering the cost of "gas, groceries, the mortgage, the rent," alongside combating government corruption.

PROGRESSIVES FUME AT HAKEEM JEFFRIES FOR SAYING DEMOCRATS WON'T 'GET EVEN' WITH TRUMP

Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., speaks to members of the media July 15, 2026. After the Democrats retook the House, he is set to become the chairman of the House Oversight Committee. (Graeme Sloan/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

In response to a request for comment, a representative for Garcia shared a tweet he posted Wednesday, after his Tuesday "lawyer up" warning, that referenced affordability:

"People can’t afford gas, groceries, and rent because Donald Trump and his family are ripping off the American people and enriching themselves. Taking on corruption is about making life more affordable for working families," Garcia said in the tweet.

Before the election, "Squad" Rep. Delia Ramirez, D-Ill., wrote in a PBS-Chicago voters guide that there is "no question that the rising cost of living is the number one issue" for a "working people’s agenda."

After the election, however, her tone appeared to change:

Several respondents pushed back, including one of her stated targets, former Border Patrol Cmdr. Gregory Bovino.

Bovino went on to suggest Ramirez instead relax with a bottle of whiskey from a brand the former immigration official launched upon retirement.

Other respondents also pointed out that Ramirez’ post-election missive didn’t mention her affordability priority:

SCHUMER PREACHES AFFORDABILITY IN DEM MIDTERM PITCH WHILE SABOTAGING GOP FIXES FOR SOARING COSTS

Rep. Delia Ramirez, D-Ill., speaks during a news conference with immigration experts, DACA recipients, and Dreamers. Over the weekend, she attended a conference in Mexico City where she said she was a proud Guatemalan before an American. (Getty Images)

"Notice nothing about how she is going to help her constituents but ‘get Trump’," said one.

"So, you guys never really gave a s--- about affordability," added former Energy Department staffer Matt van Swol.

Rep. Analilia Mejia, D-N.J., who now represents the longtime Republican-held seat of former Rep. Rodney Frelinghuysen, made both affordability and immigration policy part of her campaign message.

"We’re going to toss out subpoenas like Mardi Gras beads," Mejia’s first X post Wednesday read.

Rep. Tony Wied, R-Wis., responded it showed Democrats "have no plans to make life better for you," eliciting a response from Mejia in which she dubbed him "Mr. Weird" and only then mentioned an "economy that works for" Americans.

In April, Rep. Yassamin Ansari, D-Ariz., released a lengthy statement announcing a "New Affordability Agenda" and highlighting her role on the Congressional Progressive Caucus’ "Lowering Costs Task Force."

On Election Night, Ansari posted: "Thank you Mr. President. Our thank-you will come in January with subpoenas." An ensuing tweet called for the impeachment of War Secretary Pete Hegseth.

On Wednesday, Ansari ultimately posted a policy-related pledge to curtail AI.

Sen. Edward Markey, D-Mass., stated during the midterms that his priorities were "groceries, gas prices energy costs" and the like.

However, his post-election missive remarking on how many "new forests" will need planting for "all of the subpoenas we’ll be printing," instead signaled a priority to investigate tech executives like Elon Musk.

"Affordability," quipped former Virginia Del. Nick Freitas, R-Culpeper, in a reply.

Ramirez, Mejia, Markey and Ansari did not respond to requests for comment on their apparent pivots. Garcia’s representative responded by providing his subsequent post on affordability. Both Garcia and Ramirez had previously identified government accountability and immigration oversight, respectively, as priorities, but their immediate post-election statements emphasized investigations rather than the affordability measures they had highlighted on the campaign trail.

DHS appeared to take the newfound priority in stride in comments to Fox News Digital.

"It is unfortunate that Democrats are more interested in political shenanigans than in governing," said DHS’ top attorney James Percival.

"Rest assured, however, that we are well prepared to deal with this nonsense so Secretary Mullin can continue focusing on protecting the homeland," the counsel said.

A Justice Department spokesperson echoed Percival, saying the agency is "not afraid of threats from Democrats" and assured its staff has followed the law.

"It is no surprise that rather than focus on bringing down costs for Americans, Democrats in Congress are picking up where their weaponization efforts left off when they were last in power," the spokesperson said.

Meanwhile, the White House told Fox News Digital that Trump remains willing to work with Democrats on issues they can collaborate on to help "hardworking Americans."

"If Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical-left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people," spokeswoman Lauren Bis said.

Immigration hawks signaled preparations for what Democrats foreshadowed.

The Mass Deportation Coalition, whose leaders have been critical of Biden-era open-border policies and have asserted that the Trump administration has not done enough on the issue in some areas, told Fox News Digital they are prepared to defend officials amid the onslaught.

"We know what’s coming," said Mass Deportation Coalition leader Mike Howell. "A lot of people are going to be cashing-out and charging patriots expensive legal fees to the most vulnerable."

"We have been through this before and are ready to sacrifice for the patriots who are targeted by weaponized harassment."

Former House Oversight Committee counsel and immigration judge Andrew Arthur said Congress has the prerogative to investigate DHS’ work but added that it may not be what Americans are looking for as a priority.

Citing Ramirez’ mention of Border Czar Tom Homan, Arthur noted that the onetime Obama official long held "positive" ratings from Republicans and Democrats.

"He was commonly viewed as the guy who came in and cleaned things up after Noem left, got things a little bit better. So that's probably not going to be a terribly popular thing," he said.

"This isn't really affordability but anything that shows waste in government technically goes to affordability and it all depends on how willing the media is to accept that talking point," said Arthur, now at the Center for Immigration Studies.

Arthur said DHS can largely proceed as usual with its previously established funding while any investigations take place, adding that much of what Mullin and Trump have done already falls under established law that Congress itself passed.

Analilia Mejia, US Democratic House candidate for New Jersey, speaks to supporters and members of the media at Paper Plane Coffee Co. in Montclair, New Jersey, US, on Thursday, Jan. 29, 2026 (Heather Khalifa/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Referencing the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1952, Arthur said that, short of "amending the law itself – which they can’t do if [Trump] vetoes it" Democrats can probe and try to paint the agency in a "bad light" over ICE-involved shootings and similar incidents, but that their larger agenda would be buttressed by the INA.

A 2026 whitepaper by Federal Reserve Bank researchers found elevated "unauthorized" immigration contributed to rising housing costs between 2021 and 2024, estimating that the influx increased home prices by 6.6% and rents by 4.3% in the average metropolitan area.

The researchers attributed the increases to additional housing demand that was not matched by sufficient new construction, lending indirect empirical support to arguments that illegal immigration can have adverse effects on key affordability metrics.

Born and raised in Allentown, Pennsylvania, worked in both the New York and Washington bureaus for Fox News since 2013.

#6177. U.N. Peacekeepers Are Leaving Western Sahara. What Does That Mean?

Africa Brief: U.N. Peacekeepers Are Leaving Western Sahara. What Does That Mean?

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s Africa Brief.

The highlights this week: A United Nations deadlock ends the 35-year-old peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara, local elections take place in South Africa, and Moscow tries to project an illusion of a successful Russia-Africa Summit.

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s Africa Brief.

The highlights this week: A United Nations deadlock ends the 35-year-old peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara, local elections take place in South Africa, and Moscow tries to project an illusion of a successful Russia-Africa Summit.

A deadlock between the United States and Russia at the United Nations Security Council on Friday ended a 35-year-old peacekeeping mission in the disputed African territory of Western Sahara.

The U.N. Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara, known as MINURSO, was established in 1991 to monitor a cease-fire after a 15-year armed conflict between Morocco, which claims sovereignty over the territory, and the Algeria-backed Polisario Front, which seeks Sahrawi independence. It was also tasked with organizing a referendum for Sahrawi self-determination.

The referendum has stalled for decades. Last month, a U.S. draft resolution for the Security Council sought to remove “referendum” from the mission’s name and make semi-autonomy under Moroccan sovereignty the sole basis for future political negotiations over Western Sahara. It would have also scaled back the peacekeeping force by April 2027.

Russia vetoed the plan, instead putting forth a rival proposal to grant the standard one-year extension without imposing terms that favored Morocco. That, in turn, was voted down by the United States. The mission’s mandate subsequently expired on Sunday.

Morocco annexed Western Sahara, a former Spanish colony, in 1975, displacing more than 100,000 people. An International Court of Justice ruling the same year found no historical basis for Morocco’s claim over the area. Rabat now controls around 80 percent of the territory, which boasts rich Atlantic fishing grounds and phosphate reserves.

Currently more than 160,000 Sahrawi refugees live in camps hosted by Algeria. International aid groups have denounced the U.N. Security Council’s failure to renew the mission and find a solution to the severe humanitarian crisis caused by the political stalemate.

Traditionally, Western powers maintained a neutral position on Western Sahara’s status. But in 2020, during U.S. President Donald Trump’s first term in office, Washington broke with precedent by recognizing Rabat’s sovereignty over the territory in exchange for Morocco reestablishing diplomatic relations with Israel under the Abraham Accords.

At the same time, Russia’s stance has been largely driven by its close geopolitical and economic alliance with Algeria, which backs the Sahrawi liberation movement.

The U.S. midterm elections on Tuesday, in which Democrats took control of both the House of Representatives and Senate, could eventually lead to a more nuanced stance from Washington on Western Sahara, especially since many Democrats have expressed support for the U.N.-led process. But any immediate reversal is unlikely.

Washington and Moscow have traded barbs in the wake of Friday’s deadlock. Mike Waltz, the U.S. ambassador to the U.N., said that Russia’s veto prevents “historic steps toward finally ending a 50-year conflict.” His Russian counterpart, Vassily Nebenzia, said the U.S. plan would have “set back the entire process of resolving the Western Sahara issue” by disregarding “a just, free and fair settlement based on the principle of self-determination.”

Sidi Omar, the Polisario Front’s U.N. representative, also warned that the U.S. resolution would “not only torpedo the foundations of the U.N. peace process but would also have set a very dangerous precedent that threatens broader regional and international peace and security.”

Some analysts have echoed these criticisms. “Eager for a quick diplomatic win,” wrote Hugh Lovatt, a senior policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations, Washington has “closed the space for negotiations and risks creating regional instability.”

A small U.N. team is now supervising a phased withdrawal of U.N. peacekeepers and the return of military vehicles and other assets to troop-contributing nations, including Egypt, Ghana, and Pakistan.

Security observers fear that MINURSO’s departure could lead to renewed fighting in the territory. Amid a security vacuum, some analysts fear Morocco may be emboldened to send in troops in a bid to grab more territory.

Wednesday, Nov. 4: South Africa holds local government elections.

Friday, Nov. 6: Zambian Finance Minister Situmbeko Musokotwane presents a delayed 2027 budget.

South African elections. Analysts are predicting that South Africa’s local elections on Wednesday will show growing political fragmentation. The country is already ruled by a coalition government after the African National Congress (ANC) lost its 30-year parliamentary majority in a historic general election in 2024.

A few days before the election, Trump announced that South Africa, the largest beneficiary of the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA), would be removed from the duty-free trade agreement starting in January. But with less than 1 percent of South Africa’s total goods entering the U.S. market under AGOA, the decision will likely have little impact on the vote. Instead, domestic issues such as crime, corruption, and a lack of jobs are expected to be voters’ priority.

Voters will elect councils in all 257 municipalities, but a heavily indebted Johannesburg—the country’s biggest city—is the key battleground.

Johannesburg’s debt has spiraled in recent years, with consumer bills and other debt still owed to the city amounting to 72 billion rand (about $4.5 billion), with Johannesburg owing more than $1.5 billion to its immediate creditors. The city has struggled to collect trash and provide enough drinking water. By some estimates, nearly half of the city’s treated drinking water is lost to underground pipe leaks due to infrastructure neglect and commercial losses.

Currently, the white-led, pro-business Democratic Alliance (DA) is leading the pack in Johannesburg, where its former federal chairperson, Helen Zille, is campaigning for mayor. (Zille was also mayor of Cape Town from 2006 to 2009.)

Yet no party is predicted to win an outright majority. Most polls suggest the DA will win less than 40 percent of the vote in Johannesburg, followed by the ANC and two far-left parties: the uMkhonto weSizwe Party and Economic Freedom Fighters. The DA refuses to work with the latter two, which means it will likely form a coalition with the ANC or other smaller parties.

Déjà vu in Moscow. Moscow made a series of high-profile announcements around last week’s Russia-Africa Summit, including those concerning the sale of fighter jets to Ethiopia, Sudan’s offering of investment opportunities, and Russia’s support in modernizing Eritrea’s ports. Yet while some analysts have concluded that these evince Moscow’s rapidly growing role in Africa, there is reason to be skeptical.

None of these plans are new. Instead, Russia has highlighted and repackaged long-standing agreements to project an illusion of a successful summit. For instance, the delivery of 12 Russian Sukhoi Su-35 fighter jets and the planned acquisition of four S-400 air defense batteries to Ethiopia stem from a prior agreement signed several years ago; they are not, as the Moscow Times described it, “the summit’s highest-profile deal.”

Meanwhile, proposals for Moscow to modernize Eritrea’s ports have been floated since 2018. And Sudan, in order to secure military backing, has offered strategic cooperation with Moscow since the country’s civil war began in 2023.

At the summit, Moscow also announced nuclear power plant deals with several African nations, including Ghana. Yet apart from Egypt’s $29 billion El Dabaa project, decade-old nuclear power agreements between Russia and African nations remain unplanned. Russia agreed to build a nuclear plant for Ghana in 2015, for example, though it never came to fruition.

Congo mining dispute. California-based KoBold Metals, a mining start-up backed by Bill Gates and Jeff Bezos, has asked the United States for help in seeking U.N. Security Council approval to use aerial surveillance technology to map the location of critical minerals in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

The company accuses China of using a U.N. arms embargo—which blocks the supply of arms and related equipment to nongovernmental entities and individuals operating in Congo—to prevent it from using the technology, according to a Financial Times report. China has said the allegations are “inconsistent with the facts.”

Congo, the world’s largest exporter of cobalt, has faced decades of armed fighting over its mineral resources. Chinese companies currently control around 80 percent of the country’s cobalt output.

Sudan’s fragmented war. In Africa Is a Country, Doha Ali, who fled Sudan’s civil war, argues that framing the situation in the country simply as a “humanitarian crisis” flattens its complex history and obscures the foreign interventions and proxy dynamics, including European anti-migration policy, that established the conditions for endless warfare.

“Wars do not simply happen; they are built. Sometimes they are built through weapons. Sometimes through money. Sometimes through diplomatic agreements signed years before the first shot is fired,” Ali writes.

Ali’s article is part of the series We Are Here: Sudanese Girls and Youth Hold Their Ground in Resistance and Remembrance, a collection of stories by young Sudanese people documenting their lived experiences of war and displacement.

Egyptian media repression. On Oct. 27, an Egyptian court ordered the immediate closure of Mada Masr, one of the country’s last prominent independent news outlets, and fined its editor in chief, Lina Attalah, 3 million Egyptian pounds (around $53,450) for operating without a license. Attalah will soon face a criminal trial and possible imprisonment.

This forms part of a wider crackdown against independent news agencies in Egypt, which has detained or jailed more than 20 journalists. In New Lines Magazine, a Cairo-based journalist using the pseudonym Anne Mostafa details Egyptian authorities’ 13-year campaign against Mada Masr and what it means for the country.

Nosmot Gbadamosi is a multimedia journalist and the writer of Foreign Policy’s weekly Africa Brief. She has reported on human rights, the environment, and sustainable development from across the African continent. X: @nosmotg
