On Sept. 29, King Mohammed VI named Fatima Ezzahra Mansouri as Morocco’s head of government, making the country the second in the Arab world after Tunisia to appoint a woman to lead its executive branch. Soon, images of Mansouri meeting with the king, both of them dressed in traditional outfits of the same light-blue shade, circulated around the world. It’s a moment that would have been unimaginable not so long ago.

Mansouri’s appointment brought excitement to an otherwise uneventful election that was largely ignored by many Moroccans. The vote, which took place on Sept. 23, had an abstention rate of almost 62 percent, the country’s highest in almost 20 years. The low turnout was the culmination of decades-long apathy toward elections, with citizens feeling increasingly disconnected from Morocco’s political parties.

Yet while Mansouri’s new role is symbolically important, she will have limited power, as executive authority rests with the king. Still, her leadership comes at a pivotal moment for the country, and she will have a chance to influence issues that are important to many citizens, including the much-anticipated reform of Morocco’s family status law. If she succeeds in shaping policies that improve Moroccans’ lives and support gender equality, she may very well leave her mark on a country that is striving to modernize even as it has long leaned conservative.

Mansouri’s nomination has not been particularly surprising to observers of Moroccan politics. Although women historically did not hold key government positions, that has started to change over the last three decades. In 1993, the first two women were elected to the House of Representatives. Women have also occupied more government roles since 2000, when the late Zoulikha Nasri became the first female royal advisor to the king. Currently, although women still lag in political representation, 107 of the House’s 395 seats are filled by women.

Moroccan women have also become increasingly prominent in civil society. In 2007, the Moroccan Association of Human Rights (AMDH), perhaps the region’s most influential rights organization, elected its first woman president, Khadija Ryadi. (It is currently led by another woman, Souad Brahma.) Five years later, Nabila Mounib became the first elected female secretary-general of a political party, the Unified Socialist Party (PSU). And the National Human Rights Council, whose leaders are appointed by the king, has been led by Amina Bouayach since 2018.

These trends have coincided with Morocco’s transition to a more democratic constitutional monarchy. Before the Arab Spring, the king could choose anyone he wished to be prime minister. This changed after the “February 20 Movement” demonstrations in 2011 shook the country, leading to democratic practices taking root. The new 2011 constitution enshrined gender equality and gave more power to the prime minister—now called the head of government—and parliament. Morocco’s king now has to choose a head of government from the party that wins the general election, though he maintains control over certain divisions of government, such as the ministries of the interior and foreign affairs.

In the lead-up to this year’s election, the possibility of Mansouri’s nomination loomed over the end of the campaign, because she is a prominent figure in the Authenticity and Modernity Party (PAM), which was widely expected to win. A liberal party that describes itself as “modernist,” the PAM was created in 2008 by current royal advisor Fouad Ali El Himma, and many Moroccans have since associated it with the country’s real decisionmakers in the royal palace. Its political purpose was to rival the Islamist party, the Justice and Development Party (PJD). The PJD led Morocco’s coalition governments from 2011 to 2021, when it suffered a major defeat. In September, the PAM won 97 seats, securing a major victory, though it had to form a coalition to govern.

Mansouri, who is 50 years old, is no newcomer to politics. Her father, Abderrahmane El Mansouri, led the Marrakech bar association, served as the city’s “pasha,” a high-ranking city administrator, and later became Morocco’s ambassador to the United Arab Emirates. She followed in his footsteps, becoming a lawyer before moving into politics. In 2007, she joined the Mouvement de tous les démocrates, which laid the groundwork for the PAM. Since then, she has become one of the PAM’s three leaders, and at the time of her appointment, she was serving as both mayor of Marrakech and Morocco’s housing minister.

Mansouri is not known as an outspoken women’s rights advocate, though she openly celebrated her appointment as a historic event and a victory for Moroccan women in her first declaration as head of government. And of the new government’s 32 ministers, only six are women, including Mansouri. Nevertheless, when it comes to women’s rights, the political elite has sent a clear message: Soon after her nomination, many possible political allies in her coalition government expressed their support for a woman occupying the role.

While Mansouri will have only limited room for decision-making, she will still play an important role in the coming months as Rabat tries to find its footing and implement highly anticipated reforms in a delicate political climate.

First, she will oversee new reforms to the Moudawana, or family status law, which is an extremely sensitive topic in Moroccan politics. The Moudawana law is inspired by Islamic principles and concerns issues such as women’s rights, child custody, and the legal age of marriage. The law underwent major revisions in 2004, in a process that sparked significant societal tensions. In recent years, King Mohammed VI has called for another reform, which will address inflammatory subjects such as divorce and equality in inheritance rights, which Moroccan conservatives and Islamists will surely oppose.

It will take political courage for Mansouri to modernize the Moudawana, as she will certainly face considerable opposition. But how she approaches it will impact Moroccan society for decades and represents a unique opportunity to enact radical change for gender equality.

In addition, Morocco’s government will have to manage co-hosting the 2030 FIFA World Cup amid deep socioeconomic tensions. Last fall, the country was shaken by the Gen Z 212 protests, a movement that called for investment in education and health reforms instead of the billions of dollars slated for building and modernizing soccer stadiums. This led to a wave of detention, with some 2,500 people prosecuted—at least 580 of whom are currently incarcerated, according to Omar Arbib of AMDH.

Mansouri will also have to tackle the related issues of the high cost of living and youth disillusionment, illustrated by more than 70,000 Moroccans fleeing to the Spanish exclave of Ceuta in July. (Most have since been returned, and at least 145 have died.)

Although Morocco boasts strong GDP growth of around 4 percent, according to the High Commission for Planning, many citizens aged 15 to 24 have been largely left behind, with a 30 percent unemployment rate. Moreover, 3 million Moroccans between the ages of 15 and 29 are characterized as NEET (Not in Employment, Education, or Training), and many young Moroccans show political apathy; 18- to 24-year-olds account for 12 percent of the population but just 4 percent of the country’s 15.8 million registered voters.

So far, Moroccans have been largely in a state of anticipation. “Let’s see what she does, and then we’ll judge,” has been a common refrain over the last few weeks. Some young people I spoke to approve of Mansouri because of her gender but added that it wasn’t “the woman of their choice.” (They would have preferred Mounib, who openly supported Gen Z 212 and called for the release of detainees.)

In activist circles, meanwhile, having a woman leading the government hasn’t been as important a subject of discussion as the struggle against corruption and the push for further democratization. At least some critics even see the discussion around Mansouri as a diversion from important political debates. Although they welcome a woman leader, leftists in the PSU and the Federation of the Democratic Left believe that structural political reform, social justice, and democratization are far more important than identity politics. Indeed, many Moroccan citizens seem more concerned about the reforms Mansouri will implement to ease the cost-of-living crisis than the gender dynamics at play.

Regardless, the royal nature of the decision leaves little room for open criticism. If Mansouri succeeds in overseeing reforms that improve both gender inequality and the socioeconomic climate, her premiership could have a considerable impact on Morocco’s evolution in the 21st century. At the same time, because she does not fully hold the reins of power, she could remain confined to a political role that critics view as an impediment to genuine democratic improvement. After all, if Morocco undergoes a meaningful transformation, it will be at the hands of the king, not Mansouri herself.

Ilhem Rachidi is a freelance reporter based in Morocco. She worked as a correspondent for four years at the French media site Mediapart and has written for Orient XXI, Rue89, Al-Monitor, and the Christian Science Monitor. X: @Ilhemrachidi

#6158. Democrats better hope they don’t have another Manchin in their midst

Ever since the Covid-19 pandemic, America has been in a funk. The whole country has seemed to be in a sour mood, unhappy with everything, feeling as if the world has gone off its axis and life is out of balance. The trauma of that experience was probably far deeper and more injurious than we wanted to admit, so we just sort of sleepwalked as events cascaded around us, feeling emotionally distanced and impotent.Â

We finally woke up and shook it off. For the first time in six years, the American people took back control of their own destiny and issued a stunning, overwhelming rebuke to the Republican Party, which had fallen back into power during that period of national somnolence and took a wrecking ball, figuratively and literally, to the country. America, it seems, decided to save itself.Â

The historic landslide Democratic victory in Tuesdayâs midterms elections is far more thorough than even the most positive polls had indicated. Analysts assured us that while it looked likely the party would gain at least a House majority, the so-called real victory would be if Democrats reduced the margins in red states, which would serve as a warning to Republicans that they had gone too far. Nobody really expected that Democrats would actually win in places like South Carolina, Kansas, Iowa or perhaps even Mississippi, where, as I write this, Democrat Scott Colom has a 43-vote lead over GOP incumbent Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith.Â

Political polarization was assumed to be set in stone; the GOPâs redistricting gambit and the Supreme Courtâs gutting of the Voting Rights Act meant that Democrats could not expect to flip more than a handful of seats, and the party was facing one of the most inauspicious midterm Senate maps in recent memory. At this moment, they are expected to end up with 245 to 255 seats in the House and possibly 55 seats in the Senate, an unthinkable outcome as recently as yesterday morning.Â

It will be a while before we see the final tally, but the results are so obviously decisive that even Donald Trump cannot fatuously claim that this election was stolen. All the threats against election workers and plans to contest the outcome are empty in the face of such a victory. It is finally, once and for all, clear that the country does not want the insanity and chaos that Trump has wrought.Â

According to voter polls â formerly known as exit polls â the top issue for voters was the cost of living, as expected. Reversing the tariffs and putting an end to the war with Iran would be the obvious ways to begin to alleviate some of the stress, followed by restoration of funding for healthcare and other vital safety net programs. Rolling back Trumpâs tax cuts for the wealthy would go a long way as well. But the president Trump has already promised to be âMr. Veto,â so the prospect for a new era of bipartisan comity with the White House does not look good.Â

Itâs always possible that congressional Republicans will feel chastised enough that they will work with Democrats to create veto-proof majorities on those issues, but I wouldnât hold my breath. The best the Democrats can hope for is that Trump decides he needs to do something positive for his legacy besides building his ballroom and renaming the Atlantic Ocean, and he agrees to compromise on something. I wouldnât hold my breath on that either. But that doesnât mean Democrats shouldnât pass the legislation âÂ and make Trump and Republicans block it.Â

Progress is hard to attain when, to maintain a majority, your coalition must include some who are opposed to it.

As great as it is that Democrats will decisively control both houses of Congress, that big tent brings with it some perennial problems that are likely to manifest themselves again. The red state-blue state divide represents a structural problem that has always been around, and it has been a specific problem for Democrats going back to at least the time of Franklin Roosevelt. Progress is hard to attain when, to maintain a majority, your coalition must include some who are opposed to it. During Rooseveltâs long presidency, the Democratic coalition included powerful southerners who controlled many congressional committees, and they would simply not pass anything that included civil rights or equitable federal programs. By the end of the 1930s, they had successfully joined with northern Republicans to block much of what remained of the New Deal agenda.Â

Eventually, as we know, most of that bloc migrated to the GOP, but until fairly recently itâs always been a somewhat fluid dynamic with a few conservative states in the heartland, the West, Southwest and even the South that would elect conservative Democrats. In the last Congress, we dealt with West Virginiaâs Joe Manchin and Arizonaâs Kyrsten Sinema in the Senate, and it was like pulling teeth to get legislation passed as they used their leverage to extract concessions and block progressive initiatives.Â

In the not too distant past, Sen. Zell Miller, D-Ga., cosponsored tax cuts, supported the Iraq War resolution and even delivered a keynote speech at the 2004 Republican National Convention. Centrist senators Ben Nelson of Nebraska and Joe Lieberman of Connecticut, along with the conservative Blue Dog Caucus in the House, successfully blocked progressive provisions of the Affordable Care Act. There were other so-called mavericks throughout the 1990s and 2000s who would join with the GOP or leverage their position to thwart liberal initiatives.

I only bring this up to remind people that with the addition of these red state legislators will come a whole set of problems. But given the alternative, they are good problems to have. While the pundits have already begun their ritual of handwringing over the possibility of progressives âoverreading the mandate,â the reality is that everyone else understands that the most important priority for Democrats, as a now powerful force of opposition, is to put a check on Trump and begin the critically important process of oversight and accountability. One suspects that on this issue there will likely be unity among all the factions. MS NOW reports that their voter poll showed that 90% of voters said that government corruption was a crucial or major factor in their House vote. That also tracks with the findings of a recent Gallup poll. I would say thatâs a pretty clear mandate and a good place to start.Â

Whatever problems await the Democrats, and there will be many, this was the result we have needed ever since Trump first won the presidency 10 years ago. The damage he has caused in this decade of destruction is immeasurable, but maybe, just maybe, we have finally reached the beginning of the end of our long national nightmare, and we can begin the process of renewal and reformation.

#6157. The Post-Midterms AI Reckoning

Analysis: The Post-Midterms AI Reckoning

Barely 60 seconds into his 60 Minutes interview on Sunday—two days before the U.S. midterm election—Abdul El-Sayed was asked to pick the most important issue he was hearing about from voters in Michigan, where he ran for Senate.

“I think right now we are barreling toward a world where the most important issue I hear about every day is AI,” El-Sayed said, listing a well-documented series of potential risks from artificial intelligence, including massive economic disruption to AI escaping human control. He laid out a list of proposals to mitigate those risks, including a “cabinet-level agency” to regulate AI, partial public ownership of AI companies, and “terms of engagement” for data centers that would be negotiated with local communities. He also advocated for a “full-on pause” on so-called frontier AI development, referring to the world’s most advanced models made by Silicon Valley giants such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Microsoft.

Barely 60 seconds into his 60 Minutes interview on Sunday—two days before the U.S. midterm election—Abdul El-Sayed was asked to pick the most important issue he was hearing about from voters in Michigan, where he ran for Senate.

“I think right now we are barreling toward a world where the most important issue I hear about every day is AI,” El-Sayed said, listing a well-documented series of potential risks from artificial intelligence, including massive economic disruption to AI escaping human control. He laid out a list of proposals to mitigate those risks, including a “cabinet-level agency” to regulate AI, partial public ownership of AI companies, and “terms of engagement” for data centers that would be negotiated with local communities. He also advocated for a “full-on pause” on so-called frontier AI development, referring to the world’s most advanced models made by Silicon Valley giants such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Microsoft.

Come January, El-Sayed will have the opportunity to put that talk into action, having won one of the most high-profile races in the Democratic sweep of Congress. But he’s not the only Democratic candidate whose views on AI helped propel them to victory.

While the national blue wave is largely being seen as a repudiation of U.S. President Donald Trump’s agenda, it also served as a referendum on AI and the data centers required to support them.

NBC exit polls found that 57 percent of voters believed that AI would do more harm to society than good, with 56 percent deeming the technology as “crucial or a major factor” in determining their vote. From Texas to Georgia to Ohio, voters opted to support candidates—mostly Democrats—who promised to rein in AI development and slow the data center buildout.

Strikingly, the Democratic blowout came despite Silicon Valley bigwigs—including Elon Musk, venture capitalists Marc Andreessen and Ben Horowitz, and OpenAI co-founder Greg Brockman along with his wife, Anna—spending more than half a billion dollars to back Republicans, who have widely been seen as less favorable to regulating AI over the past two years.

Many Republican candidates tried to backpedal their support for the unbridled AI development that Trump has advocated, but—as with many other issues—their association with the U.S. president appears to have outweighed those efforts in voters’ minds.

“I think this is the public doing the only thing it really can in the context of a governance regime in which there’s no real regulation in the United States,” Alondra Nelson, the former acting director of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy under former President Joe Biden and the lead architect of the Biden administration’s Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights, told Foreign Policy.

Nowhere is the opposition to AI more palpable than with data centers, whose numbers have exploded in the United States. These facilities, which house computing infrastructure, support the internet as we know it, underpinning everything from video streaming to web purchases. But the Trump administration’s push for AI dominance has led to the proliferation of bigger and more powerful facilities, including the “hyperscale” data centers used by tech giants.

More than 1,500 data centers are now being developed across the country, joining more than 3,000 facilities already in operation, according to the Pew Research Center. The boom has mostly centered on a handful of hot spots—namely Virginia, Texas, and California—although planned construction is now spreading to more regions.

Backlash has been fierce. From Maine to Utah, opposition has grown over the sheer pace of the buildout and the facilities’ impact on energy bills, water usage, jobs, land, and local pollution. Even before the midterms, polls suggested that more than two-thirds of Americans are against local construction of AI data centers, and at least 15 states have weighed moratoriums.

“You can’t fight against a Silicon Valley company, but you can fight against a data center being developed in your area,” said Joshua Rhodes, a research scientist at the University of Texas at Austin. “If that’s the only lever you have to pull, then that’s the lever you’re going to look to pull.”

And pull that lever they did. In Tuesday’s election, there were 41 local measures on the ballot across 10 states that would in some way restrict data center construction. In all but one of the cases, Americans voted against data centers, according to CNBC.

One of Democrats’ most stunning victories came in Texas, which has been a Republican stronghold for decades but has seen fierce debates play out over the state’s embrace of data centers. Texas Gov. Greg Abbott once courted data center investment in his pledge to make the state the “epicenter of AI development.” But so many data centers were built that they strained the state’s electrical grid, prompting public outrage. In June, Abbott told state regulators to make data centers bear the cost of the electrical infrastructure they need; in August, he ordered regulators to stop data center grid connections and directed audits.

Yet his late-stage pivot wasn’t enough to save him. On Tuesday, Abbott was unseated by Gina Hinojosa, who has urged an immediate moratorium on data center development. Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico, too, has called for stronger data center regulations. “Texas should be a leader when it comes to innovation and technology, but that only works if Texans get a say and get a share of that economic growth—and that’s not what’s happening right now,” he said in July.

Hinojosa’s call for a data center moratorium has been echoed by Keisha Lance Bottoms, the former mayor of Atlanta who won the race to be Georgia’s governor.

In Ohio, former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown defeated his Republican opponent, Jon Husted, despite millions in spending by tech billionaires to defeat Brown and support Husted’s campaign. Brown repeatedly criticized Husted as “the face of data centers” during his campaign. Democrat Annie Andrews also won the South Carolina Senate seat previously held by the late Sen. Lindsey Graham in another big upset—in part by dubbing her opponent, Graham’s sister, as “Data Center Darline.”

The techlash extended to the House, where two candidates in key races who centered AI safety issues—Manny Rutinel of Colorado and Scott Wiener of California—both won.

So what happens now? While there is broad recognition across the Democratic Party that AI regulation is needed, there is a wide range of proposals from current and prospective lawmakers on what form that regulation should take.

The midterm results could give more power to individual states to further their AI regulation and ensure more cohesion between the state and federal level. Trump administration orders to nationalize AI rulemaking have received significant Democratic congressional pushback over the past year, and New York, California, and Illinois have all put forward their own legislation to regulate AI. “What these three [states] share is that they are led by Democratic governors,” said Nelson. She suggested that we could now see regulations that states have piloted “being advanced at the federal level in a more accelerated way.”

Much of the immediate scrutiny and restrictions will likely target data centers, said Rhodes, given how much of a lightning rod they have become. “I imagine we’re still going to build a lot of data centers in this country,” he said, “but the scrutiny over cost allocation, water consumption, and community benefits are going to become real drivers in which projects get green lighted.” (Musk, who alone spent almost $450 million to help Republicans in the midterms, sardonically posted on X that “Data centers in space” were “looking pretty appealing right now.”)

But Ami Fields-Meyer, an author and political strategist who previously served as a senior policy advisor on AI and technology in the Biden administration, believes that voters are demanding action on far more than just data centers.

“It would be a big mistake for Democrats to misread these results as being only about data centers. This is about power and agency,” Fields-Meyer said. “After the [2008] financial crisis, we focused on providing immediate relief but failed to turn the rage the public felt at Wall Street into a broader reckoning,” he added. “But if congressional Democrats are smart, if they want to get the politics right, they won’t make that mistake again and they’ll see this as a much broader mandate to deal with corporate power in the tech industry.”

#6156. As Democrats look to next era, the veto and the filibuster await

As Democrats continue their victory lap after their big wins on election night, outside groups and incoming freshmen are already turning up the pressure — and laying out competing visions of what the next two years should look like.

For Senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer, it bears repeating that “the Democrats aren’t all exactly the same.”

“The most important lesson of this whole election, and one we all need to internalize if we’re going to truly build a durable majority, is populism and moderation are not mutually exclusive,” he said at a Center for American Progress Action Fund event on Thursday.

Voters are expecting results as Democrats claim a mandate to address costs and corruption. “Our majority will be measured against one test and one test only: Have we made your life better?” Schumer said.

He acknowledged, however, that their plans could run into a President Donald Trump-sized wall: the presidential veto.

“Will everything pass? Will Trump sign all of it into law? Knowing Trump’s and Republicans’  intransigence, of course not. But I will promise the American people: The Democratic Party will fight to make your life more affordable, your government more competent, your capital less corrupt, bill by bill, brick by brick, for as long as it takes for you to feel the difference,” Schumer said, hinting the road could be a long one.

But several progressive lawmakers and groups say the next Congress cannot be business as usual.

Indivisible, a progressive political organization that has described the Trump administration as a “fascistic clown show,” sent a memo to Senate Democratic offices Thursday morning urging them not to “squander” their momentum and to “fight at a level that matches the public’s demand for action.”

“Who leads the party in this era must be an open question, not a coronation. It’s time to define what the next era of the Democratic Party will be,” the memo reads.

The group has been encouraging voters to speak up and demand their senators hold “a contested leadership election, not a cleared field for Schumer.”

Meanwhile, Schumer has projected confidence he will keep his spot atop the caucus, especially after he helped pave the way for Tuesday’s blue wave. “I’ll be reelected as majority leader,” he said Wednesday. But the pressure campaign points to some tough math and harsh realities for the top Democrat — including some that mirror the woes of the outgoing Republican Majority Leader John Thune.

Among the demands outlined by Indivisible is one with a troubled recent history: “Breaking the filibuster on the first day of the new session.”

Democrats need to leverage “every procedural tool” if they “want the public to believe their campaign promises weren’t just more talk from politicians who are just like the old politicians they hated,” the memo reads.

The group isn’t alone in floating a new approach to the chamber’s 60-vote threshold for invoking cloture and ending debate. Some current and incoming lawmakers have signaled they would be open to going “nuclear” and abolishing the legislative filibuster, following in the footsteps of past majorities in both parties who have similarly changed how other Senate business is handled, like judicial nominees.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., argued in an op-ed in Time this week that Democrats could in some cases use existing tools, like a party-line process known as budget reconciliation, to pass their priorities. For non-budget items, like “bills to ban stock trading by federal officials or crack down on Trump’s corruption in plain sight,” Democrats should start by putting them up for a vote on the floor and letting “Republicans decide if they want to stay tied to such corruption.”

“And, if they do, then let’s clear away Senate filibuster rules and pass the laws anyway,” she wrote.

Sen.-elect James Talarico of Texas told NBC News on Monday ahead of his victory, “I believe the majority has the right to govern in this country, and the filibuster, which is not in the Constitution and is a Jim Crow relic, is leading to gridlock in our nation’s capital.”

Schumer ignored a question about nuking the filibuster at Wednesday’s event, saying instead, “The first thing we’ll do is reduce costs and work the legislative process.”

It would take 51 votes in the Senate for Democrats to go “nuclear” and establish a new precedent, a math problem that Thune knows all too well. The Republican from South Dakota faced loud criticism from conservatives online and hard-liners in his own party who said he wasn’t doing enough to try to pass a sprawling voter ID bill known as the SAVE America Act. But Thune repeatedly insisted he didn’t have the votes to change the chamber’s filibuster rules.

Many senators fear that blowing up the 60-vote threshold would fundamentally change the role of the Senate and its ability to tap the brakes on legislation that doesn’t have durable bipartisan support. Democrats went through a similar debate over the filibuster in 2022, during Schumer’s first stint as majority leader. Even as others in their party pushed to pass sweeping voting rights legislation by any means necessary, Kyrsten Sinema and Joe Manchin, then moderate Democratic senators, held firm against filibuster changes.

And Schumer will have at least one Democrat on his hands who has already spoken up in defense of the filibuster, reversing his previous position. “I now recognize how important the filibuster is and the state our country would be in without it,” Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania wrote in a Washington Post op-ed earlier this summer, praising Sinema and Manchin as “courageous” holdouts who were wrongly “vilified” for holding the line.

None of that points to an easy ride for the incoming Democratic majority leader. And if fights over the filibuster weren’t enough, the caucus is also bracing for a different kind of intraparty angst, this time over impeachment.

The next likely House Judiciary Committee chairman, Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., told reporters on Thursday: “I have not had a single member of Congress or even a candidate say we’ve got to start out by impeaching Donald Trump.”

“For us, impeachment is not a fetish. It’s certainly not a taboo. We’ve impeached the guy twice,” he said, referring to Democrats’ efforts during the first Trump administration. “The problem has been over on the Senate side, and for us, it is a tool in the constitutional toolkit.”

Even if the House were to impeach Trump, a conviction would require a two-thirds supermajority vote in the Senate. And some Democrats are eager not to waste their hard-earned political capital on an impeachment quest that could alienate moderate voters and do nothing to bring down costs for everyday Americans.

Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, who boosted candidates in battleground races and recently released a roadmap for the new Congress, said at the CAP event on Thursday that lawmakers should “hold oversight hearings and expose the corruption of this administration. I’m not suggesting that that necessarily leads to impeachment. Maybe it does.”

Sounding more certain for Democrats in both chambers is their desire to impeach Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth over the war in Iran.

But that could be dealt with in the lame duck if Rep. Thomas Massie’s, R-Ky., resolution prevails next week. His proposal includes eight articles of impeachment, including allegations that Hegseth violated the 1973 War Powers Resolution in his prosecution of the Iran war and acted illegally in military campaigns in Venezuela, Yemen, the Caribbean Sea and the eastern Pacific Ocean.

Hegseth said in a video on Thursday of impeaching: “Didn’t work against President Trump. Won’t work with me. You can rest assured of that.”

Indivisible’s memo names impeaching Hegseth as a priority, as well as blocking a “business-as-usual” National Defense Authorization Act in the lame duck and refusing to fund the Department of Defense if “it doesn’t cut off money for the war.”

But it’s not clear that Democrats in Congress are ready to play that kind of hard ball. As they weigh their approach to the next era, they’re still half-stunned themselves by their larger than expected wins — and trying to put themselves in the best position ahead of the next elections in 2028.

GOP Rep. Christopher H. Smith of New Jersey told reporters on Thursday at the Capitol he hopes Democrats don’t hold up the NDAA “for the good of the country.”

“The NDAA is such an important bill for our national security, and it’s usually very bipartisan. I hope it is,” he said.

John Donnelly and Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

#6155. MAGA media scrambles to form a circular firing squad

Forty-five minutes before the first polls closed on Tuesday, Greg Gutfeld was still doing what Fox News does best, acknowledging reality just long enough to replace it with a culture-war hallucination. “Gas prices are so high, I’m going to vote for the party that wanted to trans my kids,” he joked on “The Five,” adding that he didn’t see Democratic wins on the horizon. “There is no blue wave materializing,” Clay Travis, the Outkick founder and Fox contributor, posted at 3 p.m. EST, adding that Republicans were surging in Florida and the polls were about to be proven wrong yet again.

Then the polls closed, and MAGA’s delusions were pulverized. The country that right-wing media had spent two years describing as angry, ascendant and permanently realigned voted in an avalanche that crushed years of manufactured MAGA hype. American voters told the president to take his $5,000 “Trump Dividend” checks and shove them. Elon Musk, who moved to Texas to get away from Democrats and then spent a reported $150 million to deliver the Lone Star State for Republicans, saw his early Tuesday post urging people to vote red disappear from his profile by Wednesday.

The country woke up to results that few expected — and a long list of historic firsts. Georgia elected Keisha Lance Bottoms, the first Black woman governor in American history. Michigan sent Dr. Abdul El-Sayed to Washington as the first Muslim senator. New Hampshire elected Chris Pappas as the first openly gay man in the Senate. New Mexico made Deb Haaland the first Native American woman governor, and Peggy Flanagan became Minnesota’s first Native American woman senator. Texas elected Gina Hinojosa over three-term Gov. Greg Abbott — the state’s first Latina governor and its first Democratic governor in more than three decades. Ohio got its first woman governor in Dr. Amy Acton. South Carolina tapped Dr. Annie Andrews as its first elected woman senator. Democrats won a Senate seat in Kansas for the first time in 94 years. While votes are still being counted in key races, solid majorities in both the Senate and House are assured, and Democrats are set to make Hakeem Jeffries the country’s first Black speaker.

Even the New York Post, Rupert Murdoch’s tabloid and a loyal Trump house organ, refused to mince words on its front page: “Trump suffers historic rebuke as Dems romp in midterms,” with “BLUE TSUNAMI” blaring beneath it. On “Fox and Friends” Wednesday morning, Ainsley Earhart warned viewers that “your wallet and your way of life” are now in the crosshairs.

The deeper truth the conservative media apparatus could never say out loud is that MAGA was always a Trump-specific phenomenon. It does not transfer to his imitators, and it only ever worked when the economy let voters treat Trump as entertainment.

It is no surprise that Trump 2.0, stripped of its previous establishment Republican guardrails like Mike Pence and Mitch McConnell, has culminated in such total structural collapse. The deeper truth the conservative media apparatus could never say out loud is that MAGA was always a Trump-specific phenomenon. It does not transfer to his imitators, and it only ever worked when the economy let voters treat Trump as entertainment. Right-wing media spent years confusing its ability to dominate a conversation with its ability to represent a country. When Tuesday’s returns exposed the difference, its leading voices reached for almost everything except accountability. They blamed immigration. They blamed insufficient restrictions on voting. They blamed each other. Alex Jones even decided Trump might secretly be a Democrat.

For the network’s election night coverage, Fox News seated former New York Mayor Bill de Blasio between two of Trump’s former press secretaries, Kayleigh McEnany and Karoline Leavitt, and he told them to their faces that they were “missing the plot.” He said, “The American people are looking at a war they do not believe in, and they did not authorize. They’re looking at prices that are making it impossible for middle-class people, let alone working-class people, to live.”

Trump, watching at the White House, raged on Truth Social — “Why does FoxNews have deBlasio” — and seethed at the panel’s lone liberal: “I can’t stand Jessica Tarlov’s voice — DUMB AS A ROCK, but it’s the voice that gets me.” After Gutfeld read the president’s text on air — which is as good a diagram as exists of what Fox News is now: a suggestion box the president monitors live — Tarlov answered on X, not on Truth Social: “Reality is a tricky thing,” and the president “should get better at dealing with it.”

On Newsmax, things were somehow worse. Political strategist Dick Morris argued that Trump’s problem was effectively excessive success: He had solved the major problems that would otherwise motivate Republican voters. The influencer ecosystem, meanwhile, went straight for the circular firing squad, and every faction picked a different target.

Jones, livestreaming as the returns buried his movement, said Trump himself is the plant: “I think he’s a Democrat. I’m 100% at war with Trump. He’s not that r*tarded. He did this on purpose. I think he’s the ultimate Democrat sleeper cell and he works for them.” Benny Johnson and Libs of TikTok reached for the great replacement theory, and Fox’s Lawrence Jones supplied the broadcast version, surveying Texas and concluding, “Texas, there is a lesson here. Don’t be so welcoming.”

So much for celebrating people voting with their feet and the U-Hauls leaving California.

Laura Loomer went straight doomer: “America is over and so is the American Dream.” Others blamed Sen. John Thune for failing to pass the SAVE Act and shrink the electorate further, as though the answer to such a broad repudiation were fewer voters. The Daily Wire’s Ben Shapiro posted the “everything is fine” fire GIF — “Just checking in to see how things are goi—” — and the Federalist’s Sean Davis answered with the hot-dog-suit meme, the one where the man in the costume insists everyone else is the problem.

The recriminations got personal fast. Rep. Nancy Mace told Fox’s Mark Levin to “STFU,” blamed his “beloved” war for the losses and called the night “devastating . . . for the hard-working American who can’t afford to buy a home, or fill their tank with gas or put food on the table.” Levin returned fire: Mace was a “washed up political loser” and “one of the most mentally unhinged POS to ever be in Congress.” She was angry, he said, “because you’ll actually have to now work for a living . . . Good riddance, crackpot.” Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis gloated that with governors’ races lost in Texas and Ohio and Georgia, the Sunshine State would stand alone among the ten most populous states with a Republican governor. And Katie Miller — podcaster, administration wife, professional MAGA explainer — told CBS’s Norah O’Donnell that she had not voted at all. “I did not vote in Virginia because in Virginia when you vote, you dox your own address, and so I prefer my own safety and security over giving that up.”

In the end, the movement’s loudest voices spent the cycle performing for each other. Some of them couldn’t even be bothered to vote.

#6154. The Israel Netanyahu Made

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

DALIA DASSA KAYE is a Distinguished Visiting Fellow at Perry World House at the University of Pennsylvania and a Senior Fellow at the UCLA Burkle Center for International Relations.

Why Bibi’s National Security Vision Will Endure

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has dominated his country’s politics for the last four decades, and his influence will not end even if Israelis vote him out of office. Over the course of his tenure as Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, Netanyahu has dramatically reset the terms of the country’s national security politics. His persistent rejection of Palestinian statehood has helped push the idea firmly out of mainstream debates, and his longtime agitation for war against Iran is now widely accepted policy across Israel’s political and security establishment.

Before his first term as prime minister, Netanyahu was already a divisive figure. In 1993, as the leader of the opposition, he likened Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin’s Oslo agreement with Palestine Liberation Organization leader Yasir Arafat to British Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain’s appeasement of Hitler ahead of World War II. His inflammatory rhetoric emboldened Israelis who considered any territorial compromise with the Palestinians to be treasonous, including the assassin who killed Rabin in 1995. Today, extreme policies and positions have become normalized under Netanyahu’s watch. He has presided over a three-year campaign of mass destruction and displacement in Gaza and the killing of more than 70,000 Palestinians. His government includes one politician, National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, who was barred from serving in the army in his youth because of his involvement in terrorist groups, and another, Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, who has said Israel needs “to wipe out Gaza” and that it should repeat what it “did in Gaza” in the West Bank. Defense Minister Israel Katz has made similar calls for applying the “Gaza model” to the West Bank and even southern Lebanon.

Netanyahu might soon lose power. His attacks on Israel’s judiciary, corruption trials, and refusal to take responsibility for security lapses ahead of Hamas’s terror attack on Israel on October 7, 2023, have generated significant opposition among Israelis. A change of leadership could have profound consequences for domestic policy. But whether Netanyahu leaves politics this week or years down the road, his national security vision will outlast him. He has had catastrophic success in crushing domestic support for Palestinian national aspirations and gaining mainstream backing for a permanent war footing to confront Iran. Netanyahu has changed the baseline of how Israelis think about their country’s security and turned his own uncompromising positions into an institutionalized reality. Future leaders may bring their own styles to Israeli security policy, but for the foreseeable future, at least, they will be coloring within lines that Netanyahu has drawn for them.

Netanyahu is not the first Israeli prime minister to reject Palestinian national aspirations. In a 1969 interview, Golda Meir famously asserted that there was “no such thing” as a distinct Palestinian nation. Menachem Begin embraced the 1978 Camp David accords with Egypt only because the agreement did not require him to come to terms with the Palestinians. Yitzhak Shamir refused to allow independent Palestinian representation at the 1991 Madrid Peace Conference.

The difference today is that the idea of Palestinian statehood is not even up for debate. This change did not happen overnight. Rabin’s assassination led to the dismantling of the Oslo model, which intended to produce a Palestinian state but in practice produced limited Palestinian self-government and continued Israeli control over much of the West Bank. Attacks by Palestinian terrorist groups throughout the 1990s deepened Israelis’ skepticism about the prospects of peace, which helped to bring Netanyahu to power in 1996.

Still, when Netanyahu’s first term ended in 1999, some politicians sought to keep the possibility of a political settlement alive. Israelis elected leaders such as Ehud Barak and Ehud Olmert who were open to territorial concessions to the Palestinians and who engaged in serious, albeit unsuccessful, U.S.-backed peace negotiations. Barak also spearheaded a unilateral Israeli withdrawal from southern Lebanon in May 2000. Even the hawkish Ariel Sharon, whose controversial visit to the Temple Mount in Jerusalem later that year helped spark the second Palestinian intifada, evacuated around 9,000 Israeli settlers and initiated the withdrawal of ground forces from Gaza in 2005.

But in the absence of a negotiated solution, the conflict worsened on all fronts. Hamas won the 2006 elections in Gaza and took full control of the territory by 2007. Military conflict between Israel and Hamas became routine, with major wars erupting in 2008, 2012, 2014, and 2021. Netanyahu became prime minister again after the first of those wars, in 2009. As Israel contended with frequent rocket fire from Gaza and missile attacks by the Lebanon-based Hezbollah in the north, Netanyahu linked the deteriorating security conditions to Israel’s earlier withdrawals from these areas, bolstering his case against territorial compromise.

Netanyahu’s policies also changed realities on the ground in the West Bank. Even before his return to power, after the second intifada broke out, Israel built a concrete wall to separate Israel from the West Bank that encroached substantially on internationally acknowledged Palestinian territory. Israeli checkpoints throughout the West Bank also severely limited Palestinians’ freedom of movement and access to East Jerusalem. In office, Netanyahu accelerated policies, including continued settlement expansion, that threatened the viability of a future Palestinian state. And he encouraged a growing divide between Hamas in Gaza and the Palestinian Authority in the West Bank by facilitating Qatari payments to Hamas-run Gaza for more than a decade, further undermining the Palestinian national project.

Even the coalition led by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid that briefly removed Netanyahu from power from 2021 to 2022, and which promised change, did not substantially depart from Netanyahu’s positions. It is telling that this coalition—the only one able to push Netanyahu aside in the last decade and a half—boasted strong right-wing security credentials; Bennett was a longtime opponent of Palestinian statehood. Rather than taking steps to advance peace with the Palestinians, Bennett and Lapid focused on the Abraham Accords, the agreements negotiated by the first Trump administration in which several Arab states committed to normalizing relations with Israel without requiring concrete progress toward Palestinian statehood in return.

Few vocal supporters of Palestinian statehood remained within the political establishment on the eve of October 7, 2023. The attacks that day all but ensured that opposition to a Palestinian state would become the norm. No Israeli political leader, even in the opposition, speaks anymore about ending Israeli occupation of Gaza and the West Bank. After destroying much of Gaza and killing tens of thousands of Palestinians, Israel has regained military control of nearly 70 percent of the strip. Israeli settlers in the West Bank, whose numbers have more than doubled since the Oslo accords were signed, have been attacking Palestinians with alarming frequency. The settlers have ravaged Palestinian villages as the Israeli government and military look the other way, if not outright condone the violence. Palestinians, as a result, are now more focused on survival than statehood. Whether Netanyahu wins or loses this election, there is no clear path to the two-state future he has been so determined to avoid.

Netanyahu’s hardline position on Iran has been just as consistent as his hardline attitude toward the Palestinians. As early as 1992, as a member of the Knesset, he warned that Iran was “racing to develop nuclear weapons” and that the “threat must be uprooted.” More than three decades later, Netanyahu finally found in Donald Trump a U.S. president willing to launch the military campaign against Iran he had long sought. The first attack went forward in June 2025, when the United States and Israel struck key nuclear sites in Iran. Then, on February 28, they began a larger war targeting the Iranian leadership itself. As Netanyahu announced in a video message at the start of hostilities, “Together with the U.S., we will strike the terror regime hard and create the conditions that will enable the brave Iranian people to cast off the yoke of this murderous regime.”

The Israeli public and Israeli politicians expressed near-uniform support for the war in its early months; Lapid, the leader of the opposition, declared it a “just war.” By June, polls showed more public criticism of Netanyahu’s handling of the war. But few Israeli politicians have questioned the need to maintain military pressure on Iran, and active planning for renewed attacks continues. When Yair Golan, the leader of the left-wing Democrats party, called Israel’s killing of Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khameini a “mistake” that led to an even more extremist Iranian leadership, politicians across the political spectrum condemned him.

There used to be more debate among Israel’s military, intelligence, and political elite about how to deal with Iran. When Netanyahu’s government began seriously considering a conventional military strike on Iran’s nuclear facilities in 2012, for instance—a development that drew concern in Washington—Israeli leaders did not all immediately coalesce around the idea of attacking Iran. Notable voices such as Meir Dagan, the former head of Israel’s intelligence agency, the Mossad, were arguing against a military strike and questioning what such a move could accomplish. The debate over military options became moot, however, once the Obama administration announced an interim nuclear deal with Tehran, negotiated in 2013 via back-channel diplomacy through Oman. The deal surprised and infuriated Netanyahu, who tried without success to scuttle the final nuclear agreement, which was signed in 2015.

Netanyahu’s strident opposition to U.S. President Barack Obama’s diplomacy was not supported by all Israeli politicians, either. Many worried that campaigning against the nuclear deal would damage Israel’s relations with Washington and that Netanyahu’s growing alignment with the U.S. Republican Party threatened bipartisan support for Israel. Although the Israeli government officially opposed the agreement, several prominent political leaders and members of the security establishment argued that the deal could have upsides. Benny Gantz, the former chief of staff of the Israel Defense Forces, called the deal an “achievement” that could postpone Iranian nuclear capabilities for ten to 15 years. Some Israeli officials even argued against a U.S. withdrawal from the deal when Trump, with Netanyahu’s enthusiastic support, threatened to do so without first establishing an alternative arrangement. Even Barak, who had supported military strikes on Iran in the past and criticized the nuclear deal when it was signed, questioned whether Trump’s pulling out of the agreement was the “optimal” way to deal with Iran.

But these debates largely dissipated after Trump withdrew from the deal in 2018. When Iran resumed its nuclear enrichment program and with diplomatic efforts at a dead end, Netanyahu seized the opportunity to renew Israel’s shadow war with Tehran. Explosions at Iran’s Natanz nuclear facility in July 2020 and April 2021 were widely attributed to Israeli intelligence, as was the killing of Iran’s top nuclear scientist in November 2020, after the election of U.S. President Joe Biden, who had promised to restore the nuclear deal during his campaign. Even when the Bennett-Lapid coalition took over, Israeli positions on Iran remained consistent. The new government was less confrontational than Netanyahu’s, but it opposed a U.S. return to the nuclear deal. Bennett argued, as Netanyahu had done before, that an agreement would channel funds into “the Iranian terror machine.”

After October 7, with Netanyahu back in power, Israel escalated its attacks on Iran and its proxies. These actions included strikes in Tehran and Beirut that killed the heads of Hamas and Hezbollah, as well as tit-for-tat missile exchanges with Iran in April and October 2024. Aside from criticism that Netanyahu was timing the attacks to serve his own political interests, opposition figures such as Lapid and Gantz supported Netanyahu’s actions and the public backed what had become open military confrontation between Israel and Iran.

Israeli leaders have rallied behind Netanyahu’s preference for military confrontation over diplomacy, and not only with Iran. The idea that preventive military action should be used to manage any potential threat has guided Israel’s campaigns not only in Palestinian territories but also in southern Lebanon and in Syria after the fall of the Assad regime. Israel has been crossing new lines: it launched its first military attack on a Gulf Arab state in September 2025 with an airstrike in Doha targeting Hamas leaders. War has become Israel’s normal state of affairs.

Even if Netanyahu loses power, Israel’s approach to national security is unlikely to change. The opposition has articulated clear differences from the current government on matters of domestic policy, but major fissures on the Palestinian conflict, Iran, and Israel’s wider regional military campaigns are less apparent. As many Israeli analysts have put it, the political spectrum of the opposition is in essence “50 shades of right.”

Gadi Eisenkot, who has emerged as Netanyahu’s main rival, might slow settlement expansion in the West Bank and crack down on settler violence if he becomes prime minister. But those steps would amount to tactical adjustments, not strategic shifts. Eisenkot is not suggesting that Israel end its occupation of the West Bank or make a serious effort to advance a two-state solution. He has called the idea of a Palestinian state “delusional” in the wake of October 7. Other leading opposition figures, such as Bennett, not only oppose a Palestinian state but also avidly support settlement expansion.

A new government would not overhaul Israel’s policy in Gaza, either. There is widespread resentment among opposition politicians and the Israeli public over how Netanyahu waged the war, especially his resistance to cease-fire agreements that could have saved the lives of more hostages. Many believe Netanyahu prolonged the war to stay in power. But there is far less concern about the war’s effect on Palestinians; only a small number of Israeli human rights groups say Israel has committed genocide in Gaza. An Eisenkot government might be more inclined to advance the stalled Trump peace plan for Gaza, which has yet to make meaningful progress on reconstruction, Palestinian governance, or other key objectives. But like Netanyahu, Eisenkot does not support giving up Israeli control of Gaza without the full disarmament of Hamas.

More fundamentally, Israeli leaders across the board now consider control of territory to be essential to national security—whether in Gaza, the West Bank, southern Lebanon, or Syria. As the Middle East scholar Nathan Brown has observed, to the extent that debate about Israel’s security doctrine remains, it “is increasingly about how Israeli predominance should be exercised, not whether it should be maintained.” A new government might be willing, with Washington’s backing, to strike a nonaggression agreement with Syria that would require the removal of Israeli forces from border areas. Many leading Israeli politicians oppose such a withdrawal, however, lowering the odds of a deal going through. And it is even less likely that Israel would cede ground anywhere else.

No major Israeli politician is arguing for a change of course on Iran. The only significant domestic criticism of Netanyahu’s Iran policy has been about his failure to prevent diplomatic agreements, such as the short-lived memorandum of understanding the Trump administration reached with Tehran in June, which most Israelis see as favoring Iran and as failing to remove Tehran’s nuclear and missile threat. Israeli military leaders are already planning for the next round of war, including for a possible scenario in which Israel has to fight Iran on its own. Maintaining this war footing seems to have broad political support, too. Lapid has argued that Israel should go even further in its attacks on Iran, including by bombing “all energy facilities” to make sure the “Iranian economy is demolished.”

Netanyahu would have found it far more difficult to bring his hardline vision into the mainstream had he faced a political opponent who could powerfully advocate for a fundamentally different vision for Israel’s place in the region and path to peace. There have been no Rabins in the Israeli opposition, no leaders willing to pivot from their own previous positions, tell the public the truth about what a real peace would require, and invest in the painstaking work of diplomacy. Instead, Netanyahu’s governing style has stifled robust debate on national security questions and lined up Israel’s defense leadership behind the prime minister’s own uncompromising worldview that favors continuous reliance on military force.

Neither did Netanyahu face serious pushback from Washington as he pursued policies that thwarted any hope for peace with the Palestinians, including the relentless destruction of Gaza. Even though U.S. public attitudes toward Israel have grown increasingly unfavorable, on both sides of the political divide, American presidents have become less willing to use diplomatic and economic leverage to cajole Israeli leaders to end dangerous activities such as settlement expansion. The lack of pressure from the United States—and some Arab states’ willingness to normalize relations with Israel without demanding serious progress toward reconciliation with the Palestinians—made it easier for Netanyahu to pursue hardline policies without making concessions. It weakened dissenting voices within Israel, too, who could not convincingly criticize those policies on the grounds that they would damage Israel’s security or relationships with its most important partners.

Of course, regional realities complicate Netanyahu’s worldview. The plight of the Palestinians continues to resonate with foreign publics, limiting how far pivotal countries such as Saudi Arabia will go in normalizing relations with Israel. Yet future Israeli leaders may not be overly concerned about that problem, convinced that Israel, with its military might and technological edge, has too much to offer potential partners to be ignored or isolated. Many Israeli politicians today are dismissive of the increasingly common view in the region that Israel is as great a security threat as Iran.

A serious reversal of Netanyahu’s security policies will not be possible until a new Israeli leader emerges with a bold alternative plan for how Israel achieves lasting peace—and with the ability to bring the Israeli public on board. And as long as the United States remains Israel’s closest political and security partner, helping this shift along will require U.S. policies that stop enabling and start pushing back on Israeli settlement expansion, territorial occupation, and reckless military escalation.

None of this is happening during the current Israeli election season. In fact, there is little chance of it happening any time soon. Netanyahu has triumphed in squashing Israeli support for Palestinian national aspirations and normalizing military confrontation with Iran. It’s a powerful legacy. But it is not one that will make Israel, the region, or the world better off.

#6153. Trump names Stephen Miller new White House chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles

Former Trump White House chief of staff Mark Meadows joins 'America Reports' to discuss Susie Wiles stepping down as White House chief of staff and being replaced by White House Deputy Chief of Staff for Policy Stephen Miller.

President Donald Trump named Stephen Miller his new White House chief of staff, calling him one of his "most trusted advisors" on Friday.

Miller will ascend to the role on Monday, officially replacing Susie Wiles, who Trump said will be moving to his political operation.

"I want to thank her for her service as Chief of Staff — She has done a great job!" Trump wrote.

Moments after Trump's announcement, Wiles issued a statement of her own.

"Today is my last day as White House Chief of Staff," Wiles said.

HEGSETH'S FUTURE DRAWS OMINOUS PREDICTIONS FROM INSIDERS AFTER GOP LOSSES, BUT TRUMP ISN'T BUDGING YET

Susie Wiles, White House chief of staff, walks on the South Lawn of the White House before boarding Marine One in Washington, DC, US, on Friday, Oct. 9, 2026. Trump is heading to Syracuse on Friday to boost Republican gubernatorial candidate Bruce Blakeman, who is trailing Governor Kathy Hochul in polls ahead of November's election. Photographer: Aaron Schwartz/Bloomberg (Getty Images)

"Serving President Trump in the White House has been the honor of a lifetime. I’m so proud to have been a part of what we’ve accomplished together from securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America First," she added. "More than anything, I’m grateful for the extraordinary people I’ve had the privilege of working alongside. While my role may be changing, my commitment to the President and the mission never will."

Trump told reporters Friday, before departing on Marine One. that Wiles did a "great job."

"I think [she's] done a very good job. Great job. But I just wanted to make this even been great.  We got to make. We've got to make those. So sometimes in life, we have to make [moves]," said Trump.

In March, Wiles announced she had been diagnosed with early-stage breast cancer upon early detection and received a strong prognosis. Six months later, in September, she shared that she was cancer free.

"With grit, determination, faith and the support of extraordinary people, it is possible to fight this disease while continuing to embrace the work, relationships and sense of purpose that make you who you are," Wile wrote in a USA Today op-ed in September. "For me, that means serving my president and my country. I will always be grateful to President Donald Trump for the kindness and compassion while I was undergoing treatment."

TRUMP PLEDGES TO VETO 'INSANE' DEM BILLS, PINPOINTS ISSUE PARTIALLY TO BLAME FOR REPUBLICAN LOSSES

The Friday announcement came after Republicans lost control of both the House and Senate in the midterm elections, dealing a major blow to President Donald Trump after the war with Iran and persistent affordability concerns loomed large over elections, as voters weighed the economic toll of the conflict.

A White House official told Fox News Digital the decision was "very amicable" and Wiles handed her resignation on Thursday night.

"A great pick. He has the trust of millions of Americans who understand that reversing mass migration is the crisis of our time," an administration official told Fox News Digital.

Wiles worked on Trump’s 2016 and 2020 campaigns, making history as the first woman to serve as chief of staff. She is a longtime Trump ally, first throwing her support behind him in 2015 when she became the Trump campaign's co-chairwoman in Florida.

"As a card-carrying member of the G.O.P. establishment, many thought my full-throated endorsement of the Trump candidacy was ill-advised — even crazy," Wiles told the New York Times in a rare public statement back in 2016.

Wiles has served in her role for 21 months, making her Trump’s longest-serving chief of staff across both of his terms. Trump cycled through four chiefs of staff during his first term, with John Kelly serving the longest—about 17 months.

'POD SAVE AMERICA' HOSTS CALL DEMOCRATIC PARTY'S MIDTERM WINS 'THE END OF THE TRUMP ERA'

She has been dubbed the "Ice Maiden" by Trump, which he noted in his 2024 victory speech, for her hard-nosed approach to handling business.

Wiles was seen as Trump’s behind-the-scenes enforcer, sitting in on high-level meetings and standing by his side at events, while Wiles rarely spoke directly to the public.

Current and former Trump administration officials posted on social media to thank Wiles and congratulate Miller.

"Very grateful to Susie for her friendship and service to the president and our country. Stephen Miller is an amazing patriot and will do great things. Congrats to him on a well deserved promotion," wrote Vice President Vance.

"Stephen Miller is a Trump OG, someone who has been with the President since the very beginning. There is no bigger advocate for the Trump agenda than Stephen, and he will help the Administration deliver on monumental victories for the rest of this historic second term," wrote White House communication director Steven Cheung.

"A huge thank you to Susie Wiles for her incredible service to our nation! She’s a rockstar and will no doubt continue working to make our country great. Looking forward to continuing our work with my good friend Stephen Miller as Chief. Together we’ve reduced crime to historic levels, enhanced public safety throughout our communities, and continue to root out the massive fraud that has taken advantage of American taxpayers. We’re not slowing down," wrote Attorney General Todd Blanche.

President Donald Trump, and Susie Wiles, White House chief of staff, during an Invest America roundtable in the State Dining Room of the White House in Washington, D.C., on Monday, June 9, 2025. (Yuri Gripas/Abaca/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Wiles played a central role in engineering Trump's return to the White House, earning a reputation as one of his most trusted political strategists. But her transition from campaign mastermind to White House chief of staff has also brought its share of challenges, with a few high-profile controversies drawing scrutiny during her tenure.

Wiles faced scrutiny during her tenure over several controversies, including her involvement in a Signal group chat in which Secretary of War Pete Hegseth shared sensitive details about impending U.S. military strikes against Houthi militants in Yemen. The chat inadvertently included the editor-in-chief of The Atlantic, who later exposed the discussions. The administration denied that classified information had been shared.

White House deputy chief of staff for policy Stephen Miller has offered to appear on CNN to discuss any topic. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)

Wiles also drew attention in December 2025 after Vanity Fair published a series of candid interviews in which she offered blunt assessments of Trump and senior administration officials.

Ashley J. DiMella reports on politics for Fox News Digital.

#6152. Texas Republicans’ gerrymander backfires as Democrats gain ground in U.S. House delegation

This article originally appeared on The Texas Tribune.

In 2025, Texas Republicans, pushed by President Donald Trump, redrew the state’s congressional map before the midterms, converting five Democratic-held districts into ones Trump would have carried by at least 10 percentage points.

The move backfired: GOP candidates lost four of five seats their new congressional map was designed to flip and lost two of their own.

That means Texas Republicans will head to Washington in January with 24 U.S. House seats, one less than they had at the start of the current Congress. When the state Legislature in Austin pursued the controversial mid-decade gerrymander, Republicans had hoped for a 30-8 split in the delegation but will end up instead at 24-14.

In South Texas, moderate Democratic Reps. Henry Cuellar of Laredo and Vicente Gonzalez of McAllen both won reelection, surviving the redraw that put more Trump voters in their districts. Republicans also lost ground in the lone Rio Grande Valley district they already held, as Tejano musician Bobby Pulido ousted two-term Rep. Monica De La Cruz, R-Edinburg.

Democrats picked up another seat with Katy Padilla Stout’s win over YouTuber and gun-rights activist Brandon Herrera in the 23rd Congressional District, a sprawling seat covering San Antonio to the outskirts of El Paso. The district has been vacant since former GOP Rep. Tony Gonzales resigned in April over a sex scandal with a staffer. Despite the district’s 15-point lean for Trump, Padilla Stout, a San Antonio attorney and former teacher, made it onto the radar of national Democrats who saw opportunity in the district’s majority-Hispanic status and Herrera’s history of edgy, controversial comments.

Democrats held fast to districts elsewhere, despite their incumbents being displaced due to the redraw. In the San Antonio area, Bexar County sheriff’s deputy Johnny Garcia beat Republican Carlos De La Cruz, the brother of Monica De La Cruz, in the newly crafted 35th Congressional District, a GOP target that Trump carried by 10 points.

In Houston, the grassroots campaign of Democrat Leticia Gutierrez topped Army veteran and former investment banker Alex Mealer, despite being vastly outspent in a district that Trump won by 20 percentage points two years ago. Gutierrez raised just a fraction of Mealer’s $2.8 million haul over the midterm cycle, as of mid-October, according to Federal Election Commission filings.

Republicans had high hopes for the redraw, which Democrats fought by fleeing the state, keeping the map in limbo by temporarily denying Republicans the headcount to pass it. But the new lines could not withstand the blue wave that swept through much of the country Tuesday, driven in part by the leftward swing of Latino voters. Texas’ new map banked on the GOP holding most of Trump’s 2024 gains with Latino Texans, who made up a majority of the eligible voting population in four of the five targets.

Nor did the redraw deliver what the White House wanted from it: a buffer that would preserve Republicans’ slim U.S. House majority. Trump’s push for the Texas map kicked off a tit-for-tat redistricting war across the country, producing similarly skewed maps in a number of states.

After Texas, Republicans were most hopeful to flip four Democratic seats they redrew in Florida. Three of them stayed blue, and the other was within a one-point margin. In California, where Democrats retaliated with new congressional maps of their own, they had picked up three of the five they targeted and were leading in the remaining two.

With GOP-leaning congressional maps powerless in the face of the blue wave, Democrats won the U.S. House and are set to have a substantial majority.The party has also wrested control of the U.S. Senate, leaving Trump to reckon with a Congress under full Democratic control for his last two years in office.

Under less dramatic circumstances, a number of new faces will join the ranks of Texas’ congressional delegation to replace ten U.S. representatives who are either retiring, gave up their seats to run for other offices or lost their primaries for reelection. Most of the races were in noncompetitive general election districts.

Two sitting representatives ran for U.S. Senate but lost in their respective primaries: Rep. Jasmine Crockett, D-Dallas, fell to James Talarico while GOP Rep. Wesley Hunt, R-Houston, finished behind Sen. John Cornyn and Ken Paxton.

Reverend Frederick Haynes III won Crockett’s endorsement to succeed her in the heavily Democratic 30th District. A Dallas native, Haynes has been pastor of the city’s Friendship-West Baptist Church for more than 40 years. He sailed his way into Congress in the deep blue district Tuesday.

Mortgage loan officer Jon Bonck will succeed Hunt in the safely red 38th District. Bonck received endorsements from Trump, Sen. Ted Cruz and other influential Republicans leading up to his victory in the general election.

The tenure of Rep. Chip Roy will also come to an end in January after the congressman ran for Texas attorney general, a contest he lost in a primary runoff to Mayes Middleton. This election left the staunchly Republican 21st District in the hands of Mark Teixeira, a former professional baseball player who started his 14-season Major League career as the fifth overall draft pick for the Texas Rangers in 2001.

And one incumbent, Rep. Dan Crenshaw, was forced into an early exit from his safe Republican seat by his primary rival, state Rep. Steve Toth of Conroe. The business owner defeated investment banker and Democratic nominee Shaun Finnie, and will be joining the U.S. House after five total terms, including the last eight years, as a state legislator.

Among the six soon-to-be retirees, two are Democrats. The seats of Reps. Lloyd Doggett and Marc Veasey will be filled, respectively, by Rep. Greg Casar, who ran for Doggett’s Austin seat after his own district was scrambled, and former Rep. Colin Allred. Both are returning to Congress — Allred after two years out of office — in new districts.

A new cast of Republicans will take over in four other safe districts.

Five-term Rep. Jodey Arrington will leave his seat to Tom Sell, who worked in the office of former Rep. Larry Combest. Sell worked at a law firm he founded with Combest before running for the U.S. House.

Rep. Michael McCaul will be succeeded by Chris Gober, who, before running for office, worked as the chief lawyer of Elon Musk’s America PAC that has channeled $216 million toward Republicans this cycle.

Rep. Morgan Luttrell also chose not to run for reelection after two terms. That opened the door for Jessica Steinmann, an attorney who previously worked in Cruz’s office as well as in the first Trump administration’s Department of Justice.

And a deceptively familiar face will replace Rep. Troy Nehls – that of his identical twin brother, Trever Nehls, who served in the U.S. Army for more than three decades and retired from the military as a Colonel. He’ll represent the Houston-area 22nd Congressional District.

This article first appeared on The Texas Tribune.

#6151. Hoax Bomb Threats Disrupt Air Traffic Across Europe

This issue is preventing our website from loading properly. Please review the following troubleshooting tips or contact us at [email protected].

World Brief: Hoax Bomb Threats Disrupt Air Traffic Across Europe

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.
