#6143. The grocery store shortcuts that make weeknight dinners easier

A version of this recipe first appeared in The Bite, Salon's food newsletter. Sign up for early access to articles like this, plus recipes, food-related pop culture recommendations and conversations about what we're eating, how and why.

There is a particular little sequence to my autumn evenings that Iâve come to adore.

I finish work, head to a dance class or the gym, and come home ready to cook. I pour myself a little cooking-time spritz â my current favorite is ginger-flavored sparkling water mixed with iced green tea and a squeeze of lemon â put on an old sitcom Halloween episode and open the refrigerator to see what weâre working with.

I love this part of the day. I love gathering ingredients, turning on the stove, deciding what sounds good. I especially love sitting down to something delicious afterward, knowing Iâve fed the muscles I just worked.

What I donât particularly love? Dirtying three separate bowls to bread chicken cutlets on a Tuesday night. Or peeling and chopping a pile of vegetables when Iâm already hungry. Or washing an enormous stack of dishes by hand, which has become an especially relevant consideration since my dishwasher gave up the ghost over the summer (and its replacement is currently in apartment maintenance limbo).Â

Which brings me to one of my more firmly held beliefs about home cooking: We canât be domestic goddesses for everything, you know?

And over the past several months, Iâve received a handful of emails from readers asking what packaged, prepared and otherwise convenient foods I actually buy. As it turns out, I have surprisingly strong opinions about groceries.

So, a little disclosure before we get into it: Nobody is paying me to recommend these products, and neither Salon nor I will earn money from these recommendations. These are simply the things I buy, use and genuinely enjoy. Some are specific brands; others Iâll happily buy from whichever label happens to be on sale.

For me, eating well right now means a dinner that takes less than an hour, includes at least two vegetables and some protein, ideally gives me a little more fiber, doesnât leave the kitchen looking like a crime scene and, above all, tastes really, really good.

And if spending a little extra on a convenience ingredient keeps me from placing an impulsive takeout order? Well, thatâs a pretty good investment, too.

Hereâs whatâs earning its keep in my kitchen lately.

Whole Foods frozen fried garlic breaded chicken breast fillets: I cannot overstate my affection for these things. Frankly, theyâre better than the breaded cutlets I usually make myself, and they eliminate the entire flour-egg-breadcrumb production, along with its accompanying dishes. Iâll serve them over pasta and vegetables, chop them into Caesar wraps or turn them into absolutely gorgeous fried chicken sandwiches. A box in the freezer is several possible dinners.

Frozen miniature meatballs: Any brand, really! I love these little guys for their versatility. For a quick stroganoff-ish dinner, Iâll simmer them with mushrooms, frozen aromatics, a gravy packet and fresh thyme, then finish everything with sour cream. Spoon the result over egg noodles, mashed potatoes or rice. Theyâre also excellent browned and added to Mediterranean-inspired bowls with rice, lemon hummus, feta, olives and a chopped cucumber-tomato salad. And when I want something comforting, Iâll toss them into pastina with finely diced vegetables for what I think of as âtiny everything soup.â

Heyday Canning Saucy Beans: Oh, how I love these. The beans come swimming in almost velvety sauces that are good enough that Iâd aspire to make them myself. The cans suggest simply heating and eating, which I wholeheartedly endorse. In fact, Iâve been known to sneak a cold bite of the tomato alla vodka beans straight from the can. No regrets. That variety is especially good as the foundation for a cozy skillet dinner, while the enchilada-flavored beans are excellent warmed and spooned over a rice bowl.

Laoban Popcorn Chicken with Soy Garlic Sauce: This freezer find really does scratch the takeout itch. The chicken pieces cook up light and crisp, while the sauce is a little bit of sticky heaven. I love serving them over rice with whatever vegetables I have waiting in the freezer, perhaps some steamed edamame, corn and shredded cabbage.

Jennyâs Tofu Organic Smoked Five Spice Tofu: Jennyâs tofu is made about 10 minutes from my Chicago apartment, and interviewing Jenny herself a few years ago helped convince me that many people who think they dislike tofu have simply never had really good, fresh tofu. The smoked variety is particularly wonderful for sandwiches. I love a barbecue smoked-tofu wrap with shredded red cabbage and corn relish, or a bÃ¡nh mÃ¬-inspired sandwich with crunchy vegetables.

Frozen scallion pancakes: Again, Iâm not especially brand-loyal. I like to treat these almost like tostadas, crisping them up and piling them high with toppings. One favorite is a sesame-scented chicken salad made with Kewpie mayonnaise, plenty of scallions and a little sesame oil. Spoon that over a hot scallion pancake for a delightful contrast of crisp, creamy and savory.

I once heard a piece of advice about eating more vegetables that Iâve never forgotten, although I wish I could remember who said it: Find the vegetables you can add to a meal almost automatically. The ones that make you say, âWhy the hell not?â

For me, those are pre-shredded cabbage and carrots.

Pre-shredded red and green cabbage: I put this on practically everything. Tacos, rice bowls, steak chili, prepared grain salads â anything that could benefit from a little crunch, color or freshness. I also love tossing green cabbage with miso butter, roasting it until the edges begin to brown, and finishing it with lemony, toasted panko breadcrumbs. Itâs inexpensive, keeps beautifully in the refrigerator and requires very little effort to turn into something special.

Pre-shredded carrots: These get tossed into stew bases, pasta sauces and curries, particularly anything Iâm planning to blend. Theyâre also the foundation of my current obsession: hibachi-style carrot-ginger dressing, which becomes almost laughably easy when you use frozen ginger and onion cubes, too.

Then thereâs my increasingly substantial frozen vegetable collection.

Fire-roasted corn, peas and carrots, mixed vegetables, edamame, spinach and cubed butternut squash: These are all regulars in my freezer. A note: Frozen vegetables are best with a little love. Iâll make compound butter to toss with them before roasting, whip up a herby sauce to coat them after steaming or finish them with a drizzle of brown butter, which is, in my opinion, king of nearly everything.

Iâve also become a fan of using prepared specialty cheese spreads to make indulgent broccoli. Break the florets â fresh or frozen â into small pieces, coat them with a good cheese spread (smoked Gouda and whipped Asiago have both been winners), and bake until bubbly, adding breadcrumbs if you like.

The philosophy is pretty simple: Iâd rather spend my energy making vegetables taste wonderful than spend all that time chopping them.

Now, hereâs where Iâm willing to get a little spendy.

I will not pay a premium for a bag of frozen vegetables that Iâm going to zhush up anyway. Generic peas are perfectly fine by me.

But sauces, pastes, condiments, good jams? Thatâs another story.

Sauz Lemon Pepper Pesto: One of my current favorites. Itâs creamy, acidic and provides a really distinct little lift to almost anything I spoon it over. I love tossing it with cubetti pasta, peas and canned white beans for a quick pasta salad, but itâs also fantastic smeared on sourdough toast and piled with olive oil-marinated vegetables.

Sun-dried tomato pesto: Another little jar of concentrated goodness. I love its deep, savory tomato flavor in pasta, sandwiches and vegetables. It also happens to be a key player in one of my favorite semi-homemade chicken sandwiches, which weâll get to shortly.

Curry paste: A good curry paste is an invitation to improvise. Add protein, vegetables, some coconut milk or stock, and youâre already well on your way to something fragrant and satisfying.

Mekhala Lemongrass Turmeric Paste: Just this week, I stirred a spoonful into a soup base of frozen onions, garlic and ginger, then added coconut cream, frozen mushrooms, shredded carrots, leftover rice and shredded rotisserie chicken. I finished the bowls with scallions, salted roasted peanuts and lime. The paste gave the whole thing an aromatic depth that would have required considerably more shopping and chopping to achieve from scratch.

Pacific Foods chicken miso ramen broth: The foundation of one of my favorite recent semi-homemade dinners. I like to doctor it with a little additional miso and coconut cream for richness, then pile on noodles, protein, vegetables and toppings.

Brown or mushroom gravy packets: Listen. I know how to make gravy. I also know that sometimes a packet of gravy is exactly what a weeknight cottage pie or a skillet full of meatballs needs. There is absolutely no shame in that.

Frozen ginger, onion and garlic cubes: Perhaps the least glamorous but most indispensable items on this list. They eliminate chopping, cut down on dishes and make the first few minutes of cooking almost frictionless. Iâm happy to buy whichever brand happens to be available or on sale.

Of course, a grocery list is only so useful without a little inspiration. Here are five dinners that show how these ingredients make their way onto my table.

These arenât formal recipes. Think of them as invitations to improvise.

This one is a little more ambitious, but itâs an excellent example of how convenience ingredients can leave more room for creativity.

I started with Pacific Foods chicken miso ramen broth, adding extra miso and coconut cream for richness, then used chicken Iâd already grilled earlier in the week for protein.

While the broth heated, I tossed frozen mushrooms, ginger and onions with oil, soy sauce and red pepper flakes, then roasted everything until the edges were almost charred. I steamed frozen corn and edamame, and tossed a generous pile of shredded red cabbage with sesame oil.

Into the bowls went noodles, broth, chicken, vegetables and roasted toppings, along with soy sauce eggs Iâd marinated earlier that day. I served a salad with homemade carrot-ginger dressing alongside.

Not exactly a five-minute dinner, but a beautiful one. And because so much of the prep was already done, I could spend my time on the little details that made the meal feel special.

This is the dinner for when I want something cozy and substantial but do not want to peel a single potato.

Brown ground beef or chicken in a skillet with frozen onions, garlic and mushrooms. Once everything has developed some color, stir in a brown or mushroom gravy packet, a splash of stock and a generous quantity of frozen mixed vegetables.

Let the filling simmer until thick and savory, then transfer it to a baking dish (or keep it in an oven-safe skillet, if you have one). Spread deli-counter mashed potatoes over the top and bake until the filling is bubbling and the potatoes are golden in spots.

Hearty, comforting and full of vegetables, without having to peel, chop or mash a thing.

This is one of those dinners that started with a can and became something much more interesting.

I browned a little hot Italian sausage in a skillet, then added sun-dried tomatoes, a can of tomatoes, Heydayâs tomato alla vodka beans, a splash of cream and frozen spinach.

Everything simmered together into a rich, savory, slightly spicy skillet situation. I served it with toasted sourdough tips for scooping up all that lovely sauce.

The beans bring both flavor and fiber, the sausage adds richness and heat, and the spinach practically disappears into the sauce. I would happily eat this again tomorrow.

This is the sort of thing I love making when I want something fresh, bright and satisfying without spending much time at the stove.

Cook some small pasta â Iâm fond of cubetti here â and add frozen peas and carrots, cooking them just long enough to heat through. Drain, cool slightly and toss with canned white beans and a generous amount of Sauz Lemon Pepper Pesto.

You can eat it slightly warm or chill it for later. Either way, the creamy, lemony pesto ties everything together, while the vegetables and beans make the whole thing more substantial.

Sometimes you just need one very good sauce.

Remember those Whole Foods chicken cutlets I was raving about earlier? Hereâs one of my favorite things to do with them.

While the cutlets cook, toast some soft potato buns and make a quick lemon-garlic mayonnaise. I use Kewpie, into which I stir freshly grated lemon zest and one of those handy frozen minced-garlic cubes, thawed.

When the chicken is nearly done, melt a slice of Muenster cheese over each piece.

To assemble, spread sun-dried tomato pesto on one half of the bun and the lemon-garlic mayo on the other. Add the cheesy chicken cutlet, then pile on an almost unreasonable quantity of fresh arugula. My beloved shredded cabbage would also be wonderful here if youâre in the mood for extra crunch.

The result is creamy, tangy, savory, crunchy and a little peppery. Itâs the sort of sandwich Iâd happily pay a cute restaurant a slightly unreasonable amount of money to make for me.

Instead, Iâm standing in my own kitchen, feeling very pleased with myself.

#6142. How 4 states voted on election-related ballot measures

More than 100 statewide ballot measures went before voters this week, including a handful that could shape future elections in their states.

Here’s a look at how those measures fared, including one in Alaska that hasn’t been called as yet:

Voters in Maryland on Tuesday approved an amendment to the state’s constitution that will make it easier for the state’s Democrat-controlled legislature to redraw the congressional map for the 2028 elections.

The outcome was a victory for Democrats, who could potentially eliminate the state’s lone Republican-held seat – the 1st District on Maryland’s Eastern Shore, represented by Rep. Andy Harris, the chair of hard-line conservative House Freedom Caucus.

The Old Line State emerged as a bright spot in Democrats’ plan to counter the redistricting wars initiated by President Donald Trump and turbocharged by the spring Supreme Court ruling that diluted Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act and set off a slew of Republican-led map-remaking across the South.

But those GOP-led redistricting efforts appeared to backfire this week, with Democrats holding many of the redrawn seats in states such as Texas, Florida, Alabama and North Carolina.

Still, Maryland Gov. Wes Moore told reporters Wednesday that he was “ready to engage” with the legislature on a new map, citing the threat of further redistricting in Republican states.

“Donald Trump is not done. He has already been very clear about his intention to go after additional states, to go after places like Mississippi and South Carolina and Indiana,” Moore said, according to video posted by WBAL-TV 11 News.

Following an unsuccessful attempt to redraw the Maryland map in February, Moore called a special August legislative session during which state lawmakers voted to put the redistricting amendment, known as Question 3, on the November ballot.

The move faced immediate legal challenges from Republicans. Two Maryland courts ruled to block the measure from appearing on the ballot, finding that lawmakers had missed the legally imposed deadline to refer the ballot measure. The state’s Supreme Court, though, allowed the redistricting amendment to go before the voters, with changes to the ballot text.

State and national Democrats campaigned heavily for Question 3 as some public polling pointed to skepticism among voters. Former President Barack Obama even appeared in an ad urging voters to approve it.

Voters in the Show-Me State overwhelmingly rejected a Republican-drawn congressional map that sought to dismantle a safely Democratic seat in the Kansas City area.

Missouri Republicans enacted the new lines in 2025, aiming to give them an advantage in seven of the state’s eight House districts, including the 5th District held by Democrat Emanuel Cleaver II.

A protracted legal and political tussle over the map ensued.

The group People Not Politicians Missouri started a citizen petition to put the adoption of the map to a statewide vote. While the petition effort was pending, the state held its August primaries under the new lines. But in September, the state Supreme Court ruled that the 2025 map could not be used in the general election because of the pending ballot measure and ordered state officials to hold November’s election under the previous boundaries, first enacted in 2022.

Attempts to challenge the ruling in federal court ultimately proved unsuccessful, with the U.S. Supreme Court issuing an order that reinstated the 2022 map.

Groups on both sides of the ballot measure, known as Proposition A, reportedly spent millions to persuade voters. But St. Louis Public Radio reported last week that while opponents of the 2025 map were actively campaigning against it, organized efforts in favor of Proposition A appeared “nearly nonexistent.”

Republican efforts to try again and enact a new congressional map for 2028 could be complicated by a constitutional amendment, approved by voters Tuesday, that curtails the power of state legislators to override the result of a voter-approved initiative.

Voters in Massachusetts opted this week not to join states such as California and Washington and adopt a nonpartisan primary system.

The ballot initiative, known as Question 3, would have replaced the state’s partisan primaries with an open primary under which all candidates would appear on the same ballot, with the top two vote-getters, regardless of party, advancing to the general election.

The outcome was a victory for the chorus of labor unions and progressive groups, including the Working Families Party, that opposed the measure. Holding so-called jungle primaries, the groups argued, could make it harder for candidates without financial resources or high name recognition to run for office.

A bipartisan coalition that included the NAACP of New England and Republican former Gov. Charlie Baker supported the measure, arguing that open primaries would give voters more choice and create more competitive elections in a state dominated by Democrats.

Alaskans weighed in this year for the second time as many cycles on a ballot measure to revert to partisan primaries and repeal the state’s top-four ranked choice voting system.

With over 70 percent of the vote in, The Associated Press had yet to call the ballot initiative, known as Measure 2, which would also roll back certain campaign finance disclosure requirements. As of Thursday evening, the “no” side, which supports keeping the current election system, was narrowly ahead. The state has until Nov. 18 to finish counting outstanding ballots.

Under Alaska’s voting system, all candidates ran on the same ballot during the primary. Then the top four candidates, regardless of party, advance to the general election, which is decided by ranked choice voting if no one takes a majority of the vote.

In 2024, Alaska voters narrowly voted to keep the current system in place.

National Republicans, though, have largely opposed ranked choice voting, including President Donald Trump, who has characterized Alaska’s voting system as a “scam.”

The state’s use of open primaries and the top-four ranked choice system has drawn fresh scrutiny this year.  Outside groups spent big sums trying to boost underdog candidates during the Senate primary in an effort to hurt the front-runners. And several candidates in the Senate, House and governor’s races dropped out before the deadline to finalize the general election ballot, again trying to prevent splitting votes with their party front-runners.

Then last week, the Senate race was upended by a New York Times investigation that revealed operatives aligned with the Senate campaign of Democratic Mary Peltola helped recruit a candidate with a similar name to her opponent, Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in an attempt to stack the four-candidate ballot with two Republicans with the same first and last names. The revelations have fueled an ongoing debate there about whether ranked choice voting encourages this kind of campaign chicanery.

“We would not be having this conversation at all if we didn’t have a thing in place called ranked choice voting,” Mike Dunleavy, Alaska’s outgoing Republican governor, told Fox News last week.

Dunleavy has ordered an investigation into the revelations, as has the Justice Department. The DOJ also sought to block the certification of the state’s Senate results if the incumbent Sullivan loses. Last weekend, a federal court dismissed the lawsuit.

Alaska and Maine are the only two states that currently use ranked choice voting in regular federal elections, along with the District of Columbia.

Michael Macagnone contributed to this report.

#6141. How Will the Blue Tsunami Affect Latin America?

Latin America Brief: How Will the Blue Tsunami Affect Latin America?

Welcome back to Foreign Policy’s Latin America Brief.

The highlights this week: Democrats lay out plans to challenge U.S. President Donald Trump’s approach to the region, Paraguay’s president abruptly resigns, and Salvadoran troops deploy to Haiti.

Welcome back to Foreign Policy’s Latin America Brief.

The highlights this week: Democrats lay out plans to challenge U.S. President Donald Trump’s approach to the region, Paraguay’s president abruptly resigns, and Salvadoran troops deploy to Haiti.

The Democrats’ resounding victory in the U.S. midterm elections on Tuesday could spell change in the Trump administration’s approach to Latin America. It has also kicked off a debate about how the next U.S. president might approach the region.

Latin America has already received significant attention from U.S. lawmakers pushing for foreign-policy accountability for President Donald Trump. They have called for subpoenas related to Trump’s opaque oil deal in Venezuela, introduced a resolution to block deadly boat strikes in the region, and demanded hearings on deportee detentions in El Salvador.

Without legislative majorities, those efforts have moved slowly. That will change in January, when the new Congress is sworn in.

With control of Congress, Democrats could aim to “shut down” Trump’s boat strikes by attaching a funding prohibition to must-pass legislation, former State Department legal advisor Brian Finucane told FP’s John Haltiwanger. As an example of this tactic, Finucane pointed to Congress’s 1973 threat of a government shutdown to halt the U.S. bombing of Cambodia.

Republican Rep. Thomas Massie, who will leave office in January, has said he plans to introduce articles of impeachment for Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth as soon as next week, unless Hegseth resigns first. Unnamed Republican sources told CNN that they expect the attempt to pass. Massie is targeting Hegseth primarily over the Iran war, alleging that the conflict contravenes the War Powers Resolution.

The defense secretary is also a vocal champion of the boat strikes in the Western Hemisphere and has said he is trying to elevate “lethality” over “legality” in military operations. Without Hegseth, the metrics for whether the United States views the strikes as a success could shift.

A bigger earthquake would be the early departure of U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who is steering Trump’s Venezuela policy. The Independent reported on Thursday that Rubio was “on resignation watch” as he mulled a run for president in 2028; the White House and State Department have denied the report.

Though Democrats hope their oversight will moderate Trump’s foreign policy, some analysts have argued that the opposite is possible. After Republican losses in the midterms, Trump may double down on an area where the executive branch has more leeway to act alone.

But the U.S. president could face new pushback from foreign leaders who see him as a lame duck. Right-wing Latin American presidents who have otherwise hewed close to Trump showed a taste for acting independently last week, when most swiftly recognized left-wing Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s reelection victory. (Trump has yet to do so.)

The midterms mark the unofficial start of the 2028 U.S. presidential campaign, with prospective candidates already staffing up. Recent weeks have seen a round of think pieces by policy wonks about how the next U.S. administration should run its Latin America policy.

Last month, the Council on Foreign Relations, which has seeded staffers to both parties, published proposals that included expanding some elements of the U.S.-Mexico-Canada trade deal to northern South America, building out a more robust critical minerals strategy, and supporting a democratic transition in Venezuela that outlasts intense U.S. control.

On the progressive side of the spectrum, Matt Duss, a former advisor to U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders, recently edited a collection of foreign-policy essays. One proposes burden-sharing on immigration policy among countries across the hemisphere. Another calls for a return to U.S. efforts to fight crime by prosecuting high-ranking white-collar criminals.

Latin America still has two more years of the so-called Donroe Doctrine to endure. But its staying power looked weaker after Tuesday.

Friday, Nov. 6, to Tuesday, Nov. 17: Pope Leo XIV visits Uruguay, Argentina, and Peru.

Sunday, Nov. 29: Ecuador holds midterm elections.

Riot police stand guard in front of Paraguay’s Congress in Asuncion, Paraguay, on Nov. 5.Daniel Duarte/AFP via Getty Images

Peril for Peña. Paraguayan President Santiago Peña abruptly resigned on Thursday after the collapse of a digital bank that left millions of people in the country unable to access money from their accounts. Until last year, Peña was an investor at Ueno Bank’s parent company. He named an executive linked to the bank as Paraguay’s central banker in 2023.

A series of investigations in recent weeks revealed that Ueno may have grown in prominence through connections with people in power. Regulators took control of Ueno on Tuesday.

Much of the political spectrum turned against Peña this week, even as he denied wrongdoing and said most of the bank’s customers would get their money back. On Wednesday, protesters took to the streets, including in front of the presidential palace. The next day, the top power broker in Peña’s party, Horacio Cartes, came out in support of an impeachment trial against the president.

Peña announced his resignation on Thursday shortly before being impeached, saying he was stepping aside for “the stability of our country.” Vice President Pedro Alliana is expected to take over until Paraguay’s next presidential election in 2028.

Green shipping pilot. The Brazilian Port of Santos began regularly using ethanol-based shipping fuel for a small number of ships last month, becoming the first port in Latin America to do so. The move comes amid a slow global rollout of low-carbon fuels in the shipping sector—and jockeying among producers about which types of fuel will become widespread.

The International Maritime Organization aims for 5 to 10 percent of shipping fuels to come from no or low-carbon sources by 2030 as part of a draft target up for an approval vote next month. In the meantime, countries that produce biodiesel and ethanol are making the case that their fuels should be adopted as part of those efforts.

Proponents of biodiesel argue that ship engines do not need to be refitted to use their fuel, while ethanol—made from starch, corn, or sugar alcohol—requires a retrofit. That is what the cohort of ships stopping in Santos have undertaken.

Baseball’s regional roots. Last week, the Milwaukee Brewers won the U.S. baseball World Series against the Tampa Bay Rays. The final featured players born in Cuba, the Dominican Republic, Mexico, and Venezuela, as well as the United States. It was a showcase of the sport’s deep roots in Latin America, former U.S. diplomat Steven E. Hendrix wrote in Foreign Policy.

Strained political relations between the United States and Latin American countries have often complicated baseball ties. Trump’s first-term “maximum pressure” strategy on Cuba blocked an MLB deal to ease the signing of players. And amid Venezuela’s political crisis over the last decade, many U.S. baseball academies in the country withdrew.

The Brewers’ Jackson Chourio, from Maracaibo, Venezuela, made it to the United States through a more roundabout route, first playing baseball in the Dominican Republic.

“Baseball is not a substitute for diplomacy, trade agreements, or immigration policy,” Hendrix wrote. But he argued that it shows a powerful cultural interconnectedness. In another sign that baseball has become not just America’s pastime but also Latin America’s, Venezuela defeated the United States in the World Baseball Classic in March.

Which of the following National Baseball Hall of Famers is not from the Dominican Republic?

Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori walks visits the Terrorism Confinement Center in San Vicente, El Salvador, on Oct. 29. Alex Peña/Getty Images

Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori was in El Salvador last week to visit the country’s Terrorism Confinement Center, a maximum-security prison known by its Spanish acronym CECOT. Her trip follows a visit last month by Costa Rican President Laura Fernández.

Both Fujimori and Fernández are expanding their own countries’ prison infrastructure in an anti-crime push. They also hope for the popularity boost that Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele experienced after he carried out a mass detention campaign beginning in 2022, targeting suspected gang members and criminals.

Now, Bukele is exporting more than sweeping detentions. He dispatched more than 2,000 security forces to Haiti over the past few weeks to fight gangs in the country, most of whom are not bound by a United Nations Security Council-approved framework that governs visiting forces.

Since 2024, Haiti’s interim authorities have welcomed international security reinforcements to help with anti-gang efforts. Many have operated under a framework approved by the U.N. Security Council, though private military contractors are also common.

Four Salvadoran troops were working under the U.N.-backed framework in mid-October when they were ambushed by Haitian gangs and disappeared. Bukele said he would send in extra forces to recover them. The prospect of a large-scale confrontation with Salvadoran troops led a Haitian gang leader this week to plea for outside mediation.

#6140. Trump reversed the Pied Piper’s bargain, and voters stiffed him

When the pied piper loses his audience, we must ask whether the people have rediscovered their conscience or simply found a new tune to follow.

On Tuesday night, Donald Trump and his MAGA movement saw what happens when political influence collides with the everyday realities of the people it seeks to lead.

The 2026 midterm elections brought a dramatic shift in political power. Democrats won control of both the House and the Senate, flipping Senate seats in states such as Texas and Kansas, which were long thought to be out of reach, and winning House districts Trump easily carried just two years ago.Â

Voter polls placed the presidentâs approval at approximately 38%, with roughly six in 10 voters saying he was a factor in their vote. But beneath those numbers lies a more consequential story. Americans are confronting the cost of living, the economic consequences of tariffs, the uncertainty of war with Iran and diminishing confidence in American leadership abroad.

Trump promised his voters he would drain the swamp, end foreign wars and bring prices down. Yet many Americans went to the polls questioning whether those promises had been kept. Unlike the Pied Piper of Hamelin, who rid the town of its rats, Trump now faces an electorate concerned that the problems he promised to eliminate have instead multiplied.Â

In the original story, the Piper fulfilled his bargain. He played his pipe, led the rats into the river and freed the town. But when the townspeople refused to pay him, he returned to exact revenge by leading away their children.Â

Over and over again throughout the midterm campaign, Trump urged supporters to vote as though he were personally on the ballot. In this telling, the Piper did not eliminate the rats. He added to them, and still he expected to be paid.

Critics argue that Trump reversed that bargain. Rather than delivering the relief promised to ordinary Americans, the administration has left many struggling with economic uncertainty while continuing to demand political loyalty. Over and over again throughout the midterm campaign, Trump urged supporters to vote as though he were personally on the ballot. In this telling, the Piper did not eliminate the rats. He added to them, and still he expected to be paid.Â Â

Trumpâs supporters see a different story. They point to immigration raids and mass deportations, deregulation and challenges to established political institutions as evidence that the president delivered on important commitments. From their perspective, voters who rejected those policies after experiencing the consequences resemble townspeople who accepted the Piperâs services, but refused to honor their bargain.Â

Both interpretations expose a fundamental ethical question: When does political loyalty cease to be an expression of shared principles and become an abdication of independent judgment?Â

In a democracy, voters are not obligated to follow the music indefinitely. They retain the right to question the destination, reconsider promises and withdraw their support. Political loyalty is not a debt citizens owe their leaders. It is a trust that leaders must continually earn.

Albert Hirschman, an American economist and author of âExit, Voice, and Loyalty: Responses to Decline in Firms, Organizations, and States,â distinguished between voice (working to change an organization from within) and exit (abandoning it). A vote against an incumbent is often itself an act of a voice. But where voters withdrew their allegiance from a party or movement altogether, Tuesday looked more like an exit. Hirschman saw loyalty as what keeps members inside, speaking up rather than leaving. His framework suggests that when loyalty silences voice instead, exit becomes the only remaining option.Â

But elected officials carry a different and greater responsibility.Â

Like the children of Hamelin, many Republican lawmakers followed the music toward an uncertain destination. Unlike those children, however, they had the authority â and the responsibility â to question where they were being led. Some embraced the presidentâs direction; others followed him despite reservations, knowing that dissent could invite a primary challenge. After all, they had seen others who challenged his leadership pay a considerable political cost. Kentucky Rep. Thomas Massie and Louisiana Sen. Bill Cassidy lost their Republican primaries to Trump-backed challengers.Â

Political cooperation is essential to governing. But cooperation becomes ethically troubling when loyalty to an individual displaces the obligation to question, deliberate and act independently. The oath of office is not a pledge of allegiance to a president, a party or a political movement. It is a commitment to uphold the Constitution. A president can command attention, share public debate and place enormous pressure on members of his own party. But the ability to demand loyalty does not create a moral entitlement to receive it.Â

The children of Hamelinâs Pied Piper tale had no part in the broken bargain, yet they paid its price. In our democracy, ordinary Americans and future generations often inherit the consequences of political decisions, and today they are paying a price. Economic instability, weakened public trust and the costs of war do not disappear when an election ends. A leaderâs success cannot be measured solely by the number of people willing to follow along with them. It must also be measured by what happens to those who never chase the tune.Â

The election has shifted power in Washington. Democrats, after winning sizable, historic victories throughout the country, will soon have an opportunity to exercise congressional oversight and reinforce the institutional independence our constitutional system requires.Â

But changing who holds the instrument does not necessarily change the music.Â

Democrats now face their own ethical test. Will they exercise power with the transparency, accountability and respect for constitutional checks they demanded from their opponents? Will they welcome dissent within their own ranks? And will they resist the temptation to substitute partisan loyalty for independent judgment?Â Â

An election can change the balance of power overnight. It cannot, by itself, restore public trust or guarantee ethical leadership. That requires leaders willing to place constitutional responsibility above political convenience, institutions prepared to exercise meaningful oversight, and citizens who refuse to surrender their judgment to the most compelling voice in the room. The first six months of the 120th Congress must be defined not merely by a change in political power, but by a demonstrable commitment to ethical reform, transparency, and accountability. The American people did not vote simply for a change in leadership. They voted for a government worthy of their trust.

The Pied Piperâs greatest power was not simply his ability to play a captivating tune. It was his ability to persuade others to follow without questioning where their journey would end.Â

Political ethicist Dennis Thompson called this the problem of many hands: When many officials each contribute a small part to a collective outcome, responsibility seems to dissolve until no one bears it. So, when political loyalty becomes more important than independent judgment, who bears responsibility â the leader who plays the tune, or those who willingly follow? Thompsonâs framework does not allow individual lawmakers to hide behind presidential leadership, party discipline or collective decisions. Nor does it assign blame equally. Responsibility depends on each officialâs authority, knowledge, contribution and the alternatives available to them. By that measure, those who knew better and had the power to act cannot claim they were merely following the music from the leader in the red hat.

When the music finally stops, the question is not simply who will lead next.Â

It is whether we have learned to listen differently.

#6139. The Backdoor to American Innovation

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

SAM MULLINS is a Professor at the Daniel K. Inouye Asia-Pacific Center for Security Studies.

MICHAEL MAYO is Special Agent and Division Chief for Pacific Operations with the U.S. Naval Criminal Investigative Service and Fellow at the Daniel K. Inouye Asia-Pacific Center for Security Studies.

NIEL KANESHIRO is a Professor at the Daniel K. Inouye Asia-Pacific Center for Security Studies.

How Military Partnerships Make Washington Vulnerable to Its Adversaries

Sam Mullins, Michael Mayo, and Niel Kaneshiro

In late May, a shipment of F-35 stealth fighter jet parts heading for the United States from Australia was misrouted to Hong Kong and into Chinese hands. Since 2007, Chinese intelligence operatives and their proxies had been stealing data to do with the F-35. Now, some of the jet’s closely guarded components, including a cockpit canopy and weapons-bay door, had landed on Chinese soil—handing Beijing stealth technology that only the United States and its allies have access to. China will surely attempt to reverse-engineer the technologies it was lucky to acquire. U.S. officials do not believe there was foul play here and they think the delivery was likely an accident: the result of a shipping delay and a missed email. But even without active foreign interference, the mere logistics of coordinating F-35 production and delivery among Washington, Canberra, Lockheed Martin, and a third-party shipping company exposed defense secrets to the greatest U.S. rival.

The U.S. defense industrial base—the network of domestic and international companies and organizations responsible for the research, production, delivery, and maintenance that undergird American military operations—is growing at a pace not seen in decades, as Washington seeks to place arms manufacturing back on a “wartime footing,” in the words of U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. The United States is working with allies, notably in the Indo-Pacific, to expand military production and make supply chains resilient to shocks. South Korea has begun performing maintenance and repairs on U.S. naval vessels, Japan is set to quadruple its production of vital antiballistic missiles, and American Precision Strike Missiles will soon be rolling off assembly lines in Australia.

Although this expansion is sensible and necessary, it also carries significant risks. As the U.S. defense base spreads, it becomes more exposed to espionage, theft, and sabotage.

Since the Cold War, U.S. adversaries have targeted the research and infrastructure that give the United States its military advantage. Now, the likes of Russia, China, and North Korea can also learn about American capabilities by mounting espionage campaigns against U.S. allies. Because the U.S. military is more dependent on supply chains that snake around the world, it has become more vulnerable to the disruptive actions of hostile powers.

If the United States fails to safeguard its deepening military partnerships, adversaries will have more opportunities than ever before to at once undermine American defenses and improve their own militaries. Washington must help its partners raise their security standards, share intelligence and best practices more widely, and fortify monitoring programs. If pursued judiciously, this emphasis on security will not hinder cooperation between the United States and its allies but rather strengthen it. But if the United States does not address this threat, one of the country’s great advantages will become a perilous weakness.

In the 1990s, the United States began working more closely with allies to bolster defense production and supply chains amid post–Cold War cuts to military spending. Washington established the National Technology and Industrial Base in 1993, a policy framework that institutionalized cooperation between U.S. and Canadian defense companies. In the following decades, the United Kingdom, Australia, and New Zealand were added to the agreement. But until recently, a number of legal, bureaucratic, and cultural barriers among the five countries hampered this partnership, keeping it from fulfilling its potential.

Over the last five years, however, Washington’s efforts to expand its defense base have begun to speed up. In 2021, the trilateral AUKUS security pact between the United States, the United Kingdom, and Australia—in which the three countries pledged to work together to produce advanced military technologies, including nuclear-powered submarines—was a milestone for defense industrial cooperation. In the 2023 National Defense Industrial Strategy, Washington outlined its commitment to further collaboration with allies, arguing that “the global activity of pacing threats increasingly requires a global approach to defense industrial relationships, concerns, and competition.”

The next year, the United States helped launch the Partnership for Indo-Pacific Industrial Resilience, a forum that brings together some Western and Asian countries to coordinate defense manufacturing and protect important supply chains. Washington has supplemented these multilateral initiatives with bilateral defense production agreements, including pacts with Australia, Japan, South Korea, and Taiwan to partner on critical defense systems, missile production, and shipbuilding. The United States is also planning to accelerate collaboration with India, Indonesia, and the Philippines. Washington has a growing appetite for defense industrial cooperation in the Indo-Pacific, and its partnerships there can thrive—as long as they can be adequately secured.

States have long used espionage to gauge enemy weaknesses and steal cutting-edge technologies. They have also executed sabotage operations to disrupt opponents’ supply chains and hinder their battlefield performance. The Soviet Union, for instance, gained nuclear weapons in part by penetrating the Manhattan Project; more recently, China stole secrets related to the F-22 and F-35 stealth fighter jets and the C-17 cargo plane. Galloping advances in technology invite subterfuge and theft. New breakthroughs in artificial intelligence and quantum computing could have strategic implications on par with the atomic bomb, and U.S. rivals are tenacious in seeking to acquire such technologies themselves.

Today, the American defense base is “under a state of constant, multivector siege” in cyberspace, according to a February report by the Google Threat Intelligence Group. U.S. adversaries are working to steal sensitive information, trade secrets, and intellectual property at every possible level, from recruiting individual employees to hacking manufacturers’ IT networks.

In addition to staging digital attacks, foreign governments such as China and North Korea are cultivating sources inside firms and research institutions focused on defense and dual-use innovation. Governments hostile to the United States, notably China, have sought to establish seemingly legitimate business and academic relationships to gain access to proprietary information. A September 2025 report from the U.S. House Select Committee on China found more than 100 academic partnerships between American universities and Chinese entities that pose a national security risk. State-sponsored actors have also embedded themselves inside American firms and research departments; for instance, North Korean remote IT workers in 2024 infiltrated a U.S. defense contractor and stole data about export-controlled technology. Perhaps most strikingly, U.S. adversaries have used foreign investment, mergers, and even the acquisition of entire companies—sometimes using subsidiaries to mask their involvement—to gain control of critical dual-use technologies. The Times reported that the 2008 buyout of the British-based Dynex Semiconductor by a subsidiary of a Chinese state-owned railway company, for example, gave the Chinese navy access to technology crucial to developing rail guns and electromagnetic launch systems for aircraft carriers.

As the United States has deepened its defense cooperation efforts in the Indo-Pacific, China and North Korea have increasingly targeted U.S. allies in the region. In 2024, South Korea’s National Police Agency revealed that North Korean hackers had mounted all-out cyberattacks against South Korean defense companies for over a year, breaching their networks and stealing technical data. Last January, the agency reported a 40 percent increase in illegal technology transfer cases—that is, of insiders leaking proprietary information on critical technologies to do with semiconductors, batteries, and shipbuilding. Many of those leaks were connected to China.

Japan, which the KGB nicknamed “spy heaven” during the Cold War, remains a hub for espionage. A July New York Times investigation found that members of a Tokyo-based Russian military intelligence unit called the 20th Directorate have spent years posing as diplomats and businesspeople to help Moscow acquire defense technologies that it is banned from importing. This equipment—which includes Japanese components used to guide Russian Kh-101 cruise missiles—has been essential to Russia’s war effort in Ukraine. From 2019 to 2024, the Chinese hacking group MirrorFace conducted over 200 cyberattacks against Japanese defense, national security, and advanced technology targets. And in February 2025, the Japanese military discovered that some of its members had unknowingly circulated for over a year USB sticks that carried malware used by Chinese hacker groups.

In Australia, U.S. adversaries have worked to infiltrate AUKUS in a number of ways. Last year, the Iranian-backed Cyber Toufan hacker group mounted a series of cyberattacks on Israeli defense contractors that gave it access to sensitive material on Australian weapons programs, including the multibillion-dollar Redback infantry fighting vehicle. Mike Burgess, the director general of Australia’s domestic intelligence service, has repeatedly warned that Australia has become a priority espionage mark where “defense personnel are being targeted in person and online.” In 2024, Burgess revealed that a spy ring run by an unspecified foreign government, referred to as “the A-team,” had cultivated and recruited a former Australian politician to assist them. In one scheme, the A-team invited Australian academics and political figures to an all-expenses-paid overseas conference to build intelligence relationships—a tactic often associated with China. The group also offered to pay Australian defense sector employees for information on AUKUS and sensitive technologies such as submarines and missile systems.

American rivals also use sabotage to weaken the broader U.S. defense base. Since 2022, Russian military intelligence has targeted European weapons manufacturers, transportation, and logistics. Moscow even planned to assassinate Armin Papperger, the CEO of the German defense giant Rheinmetall, to undermine the continent’s support for Ukraine. American security services worry adversaries may introduce malicious products into U.S. and allies’ supply chains to steal or alter data, disrupt operations, or interrupt communications. In a wartime scenario, when the defense industrial base is needed most, compromising American production lines or weapons systems could provide opponents with enormous advantages.

The United States and its allies have systems in place to protect against spying and sabotage, but these systems are not always successful. Within the United States, the Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency is the lead organization for implementing the National Industrial Security Program, which protects the domestic defense industry by governing security clearances, cybersecurity safeguards, and the detection of espionage. But even domestically, many of the most vulnerable parts of the military supply chain—notably, smaller companies that provide specialized software, parts, or services—operate beyond the government’s field of vision and often cannot afford to install sufficient cybersecurity protections. Outside the United States, these problems are magnified.

Although bilateral security agreements establish standards for safeguarding classified military and industrial information, U.S. partners still have vastly different legal regimes, security cultures, and capabilities. Australia is arguably Washington’s most capable Indo-Pacific ally: it is part of the Five Eyes Alliance, an Anglosphere intelligence-sharing agreement; works closely with the American and British militaries through AUKUS; and has a robust, albeit relatively new program focused on securing the defense industry. Still, Burgess has cautioned that the country faces “unprecedented levels of espionage” that will only increase as AUKUS collaboration grows.

South Korea and Japan, while both technologically advanced and capable U.S. partners, have long-standing legal and counterintelligence vulnerabilities that they are only belatedly addressing. Until South Korea passed an expanded espionage statute last February, a loophole in the country’s law meant its government could generally bring espionage charges only in cases related to North Korea, forcing it to rely on different laws to prosecute spies from other countries. As a result, South Korean security services have long been operating with one hand tied behind their back in dealing with Chinese subterfuge; most Chinese nationals caught filming sensitive installations in recent years, for instance, have faced little or no punishment. For its part, Japanese law still does not explicitly prohibit individuals from serving as clandestine agents for a foreign power or accepting payment from a foreign intelligence service, creating a permissive environment for foreign spies to operate in Japan.

Japan is aware of these problems and is reforming its security architecture: Tokyo recently established two bodies to oversee its intelligence agencies and is pursuing a new “anti-spy” law that will finally give authorities an appropriate set of tools to counter espionage. Still, these measures face domestic opposition and will take time to come into effect. Although American allies and partners in the Indo-Pacific are making meaningful progress, regional security standards still lag behind those of the United States.

The United States needs its Indo-Pacific allies to support its military goals in the coming years. But weaknesses in one country’s security architecture create vulnerabilities for all. Washington must help its allies better protect their defense industries. Although the United States has acknowledged this need before, it has not treated it with sufficient urgency and has focused too narrowly on cybersecurity. To be sure, absolute security is impossible, and too rigidly enforcing U.S. standards on allies would slow technological cooperation. Still, the United States must ensure that allies’ security programs are comparable to its own and that any glaring gaps are filled as swiftly as possible.

To launch these efforts, the United States should develop a comprehensive grading system for defense industrial security—a framework that assesses allies’ ability to safeguard critical technologies and identifies areas for improvement. The State Department already uses such a system to evaluate global efforts to counter narcotics and human trafficking. A grading system for defense industrial security would gauge the strength of the entirety of allies’ security apparatuses—including the efficacy of their legal frameworks, cybersecurity, personnel vetting, protection of classified information, foreign investment screening, and supply-chain security—and their resilience against foreign interference and espionage.

At the operational level, Washington should expand existing programs that oversee international defense industrial security. Counterintelligence special agents from organizations such as the Naval Criminal Investigative Service and the Air Force Office of Special Investigations already enforce security standards at home and abroad by guarding critical infrastructure, strengthening cybersecurity, and neutralizing foreign intelligence threats in collaboration with host-country partners. As the defense industrial base expands internationally, more resources will be needed to sustain these operations at scale and ensure that security standards keep pace with joint manufacturing and innovation.

The United States should also expand its information-sharing efforts to alert allies about potential threats and vulnerabilities. Foreign partners currently have limited access, for instance, to Department of Defense cybersecurity information-sharing programs. The United States should consider allowing international defense organizations to access these programs, or else work with allies to develop similar, multilateral information-sharing platforms focused on securing defense production.

Finally, Washington should use the Partnership for Indo-Pacific Industrial Resilience to develop a work stream dedicated to defense industrial security, which would provide a forum for regional partners to establish common security standards and share intelligence best practices. Although nonbinding, policy recommendations from this collaboration would provide authoritative guidance on how to strengthen defense industrial security.

The F-35 parts debacle is a reminder of the inherent vulnerabilities of globalized supply chains, which U.S. adversaries are increasingly eager to exploit. The United States must rely on international partnerships to revitalize its defense industrial base—but true burden sharing is possible only if U.S. partners can keep critical technologies secure. The United States and its allies must strive to stiffen the security of their military research, production, and supply chains. Only with those protections can they realize the gains that come from working together.

#6138. Gay candidates won where it was supposed to be impossible

On Tuesday night, two things happened at once, and the country will be tempted to remember only one of them.

The first made me go quiet at my kitchen table. Chris Pappas won election to the U.S. Senate in New Hampshire, becoming the first openly gay man ever sent to that chamber, and part of the margin that handed Democrats the Senate. In Indiana, J.D. Ford, the first openly gay person ever elected to that stateâs legislature, unseated a Republican incumbent and is headed to the House. In Texas, of all places, James Talarico beat Ken Paxton to become the first Democrat to win statewide in more than thirty years, after a campaign in which anti-LGBTQ+ messaging was reportedly Paxtonâs single largest category of advertising, and in which the vice president of the United States stood on a stage and used âgayâ as a punchline against him. Talarico is straight, and he won anyway.

And on Long Island, in a district Donald Trump carried, a gay Democrat named Chris Gallant, whose private photographs were leaked against him precisely because someone believed that seeing him would be enough to end him, came within about two points of flipping a seat the forecasters had rated safely Republican. He conceded the election on Wednesday, down by roughly 6,700 votes in the closest race of the incumbent Republican Nick LaLotaâs career. In the same breath, Gallant called LaLota a brother in arms and told the district he was still their neighbor, which is to say he refused the shame he was supposed to feel from the photo leak to the very end. Whatever that is, it is not the story of a man sunk by leather. It is the story of a man who nearly won the unwinnable while carrying the exact weight that was supposed to be disqualifying.

In 2026, you cannot reliably win an American election by making a manâs gayness, real or invented, the center of your campaign. Republicans tried it in Texas and lost the whole state. They tried it on Long Island and watched a red seat nearly flip.

Put those results next to one another and a sentence forms that would have been unimaginable a decade ago: In 2026, you cannot reliably win an American election by making a manâs gayness, real or invented, the center of your campaign. Republicans tried it in Texas and lost the whole state. They tried it on Long Island and watched a red seat nearly flip. The oldest weapon in the drawer â the one that raised me, the one that could empty a lunch table in the 1990s â is losing its edge at the ballot box. Voters keep looking at the openly gay candidate and sending him to Washington.

That is the headline, and it is real, and I am not going to let anyone talk me out of being moved by it.

But here is the second thing that happened Tuesday night. In the same hours, often on the same ballots, and it is the part the rainbow-wave coverage is already rushing past. In Arizona and Nebraska, voters approved measures to bar transgender girls from girlsâ sports. In Colorado, two measures aimed at transgender young people, one on sports and one restricting certain surgical care for minors, are narrowly passing. In Washington State, an initiative to keep transgender girls out of girlsâ sports passed comfortably. The same electorate that refused to punish a Senate candidate for being gay reached down the ballot and punished trans kids for existing.

This is the thing I need people to see before the celebration hardens into a story we tell ourselves. The contempt did not disappear on Tuesday. It relocated. A political movement that has learned it can no longer win by hating gay men has not given up the strategy. It has updated the target. The MAGA machine that aired the Paxton ads and laughed at Vanceâs joke is the same one now writing ballot measures about 11-year-olds, because cruelty still tests well when it is aimed at the group with the least power to answer back. Gays are simply the part of the community that got powerful enough to be left alone.

I know this pattern in my body, because I have watched it my whole life. The fear moves. First it was the plague, then it was the gay man as predator, then it was marriage as the end of the world, and each time the broader culture eventually got bored or ashamed and the fear went looking for a new address. Right now the address is a trans child in a locker room. The people who found that child did not arrive by accident. They are the same people, running the same play, because it is the only play they have ever had.

So I want to be careful about the victory lap, even as I take one. It is a genuine and hard-won thing that Chris Pappas will be a senator and J.D. Ford will be a congressman, and that a straight man in Texas could not be destroyed by being called gay. Those wins are not small, and the people who did the work to make them real earned every bit of the joy.Â

But a movement does not get to accept its own seats at the table while the youngest and most defenseless members of its own community are voted off the field in four states on the same night. This is not a win we get to keep cleanly. It is a split screen, and if we only look at our half of it, we become exactly the kind of people who could be bought off with a little representation while someone else pays the bill.

The refusal to be ashamed won some rooms on Tuesday. I felt it. The task now is to extend that refusal to the people the machine has decided to hunt next, to say as loudly for trans kids what the voters of New Hampshire and Indiana and Texas just said for us: that you do not get to make a personâs existence a punchline, or a wedge, or a ballot measure. We learned that lesson about gay men the slow and brutal way. The whole point of learning it is to spare the next group from learning it alone.

Chris Gallant did not quite win. But he came close enough to prove the old weapon is dulling. The question Tuesday really asked is whether we will hand the people wielding it a new one, or finally take the thing out of their hands.

#6137. The International Power Broker Trying to Normalize Hamas

This issue is preventing our website from loading properly. Please review the following troubleshooting tips or contact us at [email protected].

Analysis: The International Power Broker Trying to Normalize Hamas

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

In 2006, the last time that Palestinians voted in an election, national power broker Mohammed Dahlan fiercely opposed the new Hamas-led administration in Gaza. Dahlan has been in exile in the United Arab Emirates since 2011. But he is now setting out again to win political power in Gaza by uniting the fractious Palestinian movement—this time by including Hamas. And he is suspected of doing so with the support of influential Arab leaders and Israelis and Americans across the political spectrum.

Earlier this month, when Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas postponed elections scheduled for November to next autumn, it wasn’t surprising. Every attempt since the last election 20 years ago has run into trouble either due to Abbas’s fear of losing or Israel’s refusal to allow voting in East Jerusalem. Fatah and Hamas, the two main Palestinian factions, clashed in 2006, which resulted in a de facto division of Palestinian territories into the West Bank and Gaza.

In 2006, the last time that Palestinians voted in an election, national power broker Mohammed Dahlan fiercely opposed the new Hamas-led administration in Gaza. Dahlan has been in exile in the United Arab Emirates since 2011. But he is now setting out again to win political power in Gaza by uniting the fractious Palestinian movement—this time by including Hamas. And he is suspected of doing so with the support of influential Arab leaders and Israelis and Americans across the political spectrum.

Earlier this month, when Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas postponed elections scheduled for November to next autumn, it wasn’t surprising. Every attempt since the last election 20 years ago has run into trouble either due to Abbas’s fear of losing or Israel’s refusal to allow voting in East Jerusalem. Fatah and Hamas, the two main Palestinian factions, clashed in 2006, which resulted in a de facto division of Palestinian territories into the West Bank and Gaza.

Israel has exploited Palestinian divisions, citing the absence of a unified Palestinian political entity as a reason it could not move forward on peace. Most Palestinians have relentlessly called for unity among Palestinian factions. Dahlan’s party, the Democratic Reform Bloc (DRC) is now trying to achieve that elusive aim. However, including Hamas in any political alliance risks rattling Israel, which is suspected of deploying myriad tools at its disposal to influence Palestinian politics.

Born in Khan Younis, the same town as former Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar, who plotted the attack against Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, Dahlan is seen as a son of the soil. He learned the ropes from Yasser Arafat, the architect of the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO), when Israel deported him to Jordan. In 1994, as the Oslo Accords were set in motion, Abbas appointed Dahlan to manage the enclave’s security as head of the Palestinian Authority’s (PA) Preventive Security organization. His reputation and reach soon earned him a reputation, and Gaza was often referred to as “Dahlistan.”

Dahlan dealt with Israeli intelligence officials and quickly made a name for himself as someone who anyone could work with. He fought against Hamas in 2006, but it was Abbas who later exiled him on corruption charges. Abbas was wary of Dahlan’s ambition and access, fearing that he might be a fierce competitor one day.

Dahlan relocated to the UAE and became a security advisor to the ruler of Abu Dhabi, Mohammed bin Zayed. He was close to the sheikh when the Abraham Accords were signed and during the military escalation in Gaza following Oct. 7, when the UAE maintained its diplomatic commitment and didn’t walk out of the deal. His proximity to Abu Dhabi’s leadership made him appealing to Israel. Could he be a Trojan horse in the Palestinian movement?

“Many Israeli intelligence officials, even those close to [Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin] Netanyahu, have met him,” said Eran Lerman, a former Israeli deputy national security advisor and retired intelligence colonel who serves as vice president of the Jerusalem Institute for Strategy and Security.

Dahlan played an instrumental role in convincing Hamas to decommission its weapons during talks with U.S. President Donald Trump’s Board of Peace—although the fate of that proposal hangs in balance as Israel demands full disarmament. Muhammad Shehada, a visiting fellow with the European Council on Foreign Relations, said that Dahlan was brought into the negotiations to build trust with Israel.

Israel has signed peace treaties with both Egypt and the UAE, and it sees them as firm opponents of the Muslim Brotherhood, a pan-Arab movement that Israel views as an ideological fountainhead of Hamas. Dahlan maintains open channels with both Abu Dhabi and Cairo, and those relationships make him an interesting figure for Israeli strategists.

In a 2024 interview with the New York Times, Dahlan laid out his vision for Palestine, declaring, “No Abbas, no Hamas,” and calling for a new generation to take charge of the PA.

Dahlan has funneled Emirati funds into Gaza, helping him revive his standing and expand his reach. He has maintained a political base through the DRC.

Dimitri Diliani, a DRC spokesperson, said that Dahlan was meeting with former Hamas chief Ismail Haniyeh in Doha when the Times article was published, yet Hamas raised no objections. “That was the first sign that Hamas was willing to give up control of Gaza,” Diliani said. “But neither the U.S. nor Israel took notice.”

Hamas might accept a relegated status in Palestinian governance, but observers have questioned whether there is more than meets the eye. Some have argued that Dahlan is throwing Hamas a lifeline, ostensibly to challenge Abbas but also allowing it to survive another day as a political entity.

The DRC has formed an alliance comprising Hamas, Palestinian Islamic Jihad, and Fatah breakaway factions to support a unified electoral list of independent candidates to compete against Abbas. “Hamas agreed they will not participate directly and will support whatever list we announce,” Diliani said. “It will be a national list that represents us, but none of our political figures will be in it.”

That offers little comfort to Israel, which demands Hamas’s complete exit from Gaza rather than political influence by proxy. A former senior Israeli security official, who previously spoke highly of Dahlan as someone who could be acceptable to Israel to lead Gaza, now warned about his motives. The official described him as “a thief” who “can play both sides.”

Is Dahlan playing Israel, or is there a larger strategy at play behind the scenes? When asked whether he could convince Israelis to discuss a two-state solution, Dahlan struck a harsh tone. “It’s not my job to convince the Israelis,” he told the Times. “Let them go to hell.”

Adopting a firm stance against Israel remains a political necessity for any Palestinian leader—lest they be labeled as a puppet. Yet Dahlan has positioned himself as a rare figure capable of liaising between Israel, the United States, and Hamas.

Dahlan maintains he has no desire to officially run the Palestinian territories but that is standard political speak to hide real intentions. However, Lerman noted that with business ventures spanning Belgrade and beyond, Dahlan is financially well-off and may have little interest in returning to Gaza and enduring the privations that come with it.

Israel is also running out of options. It is unhappy with Abbas and sees him as ineffective in managing armed resistance, and it has called on the European Union to pressure Abbas to reform the PA and link European aid to reforms. A different version of PA reforms has been discussed in Palestinian circles. They wish to downgrade the PA, which was formed as part of the Oslo process to pave the path for a Palestinian state, and revive the PLO, which is the umbrella movement for self-determination. Palestinians argue that they didn’t get a state; instead, the PA has eroded the movement. In this vision, the PLO includes Hamas.

Diliani said that it was pointless to seek Hamas’s decimation. Even if Hamas gives up weapons, another armed rebellion will rise. “As long as Israel occupies Palestinian lands, resistance will persist in one form or another,” he said. “Dahlan has an inclusive vision.”

Israel may have to choose between Dahlan’s broader alliance that includes Hamas as a political actor or backing Abbas and his familiar operatives—such as Hussein al-Sheikh, the PA’s second-in-command, or Majed Faraj, the PA’s intelligence chief who recently called on Hamas to apologize for Oct. 7. Dahlan has a year to navigate these competing pressures and decide if he wants to jettison Hamas or risk being outmaneuvered by Israel.
